Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 1–4:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. (Makkiyyah) According to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir, it is Meccan. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: except for one verse, which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114]. [[See p. 109 of this part. And in a report from Ibn 'Abbas, it is entirely Meccan; this is the view of al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah.]]

Abu Muhammad al-Darimi narrated in his Musnad, from Ka'b, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite Surat Hud on Friday." Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have grown grey!" He said: "Hud, al-Waqi'ah, al-Mursalat, 'Amma yatasa'alun, and when the sun is wound up have greyed me." He said: this is a hasan gharib hadith, and something of this has been narrated as mursal.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi Abu 'Abd Allah also reported it in Nawadir al-Usul: Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Bishr narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Salih, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Juhayfah, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we see you have grown grey!" He said: "Hud and its sisters have greyed me." Abu 'Abd Allah said: Fright produces greyness, because fright distracts the soul and dries up the moisture of the body, and beneath every hair there is a root, and from it comes sweat. When fright drains its moisture, the roots dry up, the hair dries and whitens, just as you see green crops whitening when their water is gone. The hair of an old man turns white only because its moisture departs and its skin dries. So the soul is distracted by the threat of Allah and the terrors of what the report from Allah brings, and it withers, and that threat and terror which has come drains its water, and from it one greys. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a Day that will make the children grey-haired﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 17], for they greyed from fright.

As for Surat Hud, since it mentions the nations and what befell them of Allah's swift punishment, the people of certainty, when they recite it, see upon their hearts His dominion, His authority and His glances, and the seizing of His enemies. Were they to die of fright, it would be right for them, but Allah, blessed and exalted is His name, shows them gentleness in those moments until they finish reading His words. As for its sisters, the surahs resembling it, such as ﴿al-Haqqah﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1], ﴿A questioner asked﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1], ﴿When the sun is wound up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1] and "al-Qari'ah" [al-Qari'ah: 1], in the recitation of these surahs is what reveals to the hearts of those who know Him His authority and His seizing, so the souls are distracted by it and the heads turn grey.

[I say:] It has been said that what greyed the Prophet (ﷺ) from Surat Hud is the saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112], as its explanation will come, if Allah wills.

Yazid ibn Aban said: I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in my dream, and I recited Surat Hud to him. When I finished it he said: "O Yazid, this is recitation, so where is the weeping?"

Our scholars said: Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: It is said "hadhihi Hudu" without tanwin, as the name of the surah, because if you named a woman Zayd you would not give it diptote treatment; this is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. But 'Isa ibn 'Umar says: "hadhihi Hudun" with tanwin, as the name of the surah, and likewise if one names a woman Zayd, because when its middle is vowelled with sukun it becomes light and receives tanwin. If you intend omission, you give it tanwin according to all, and say: "hadhihi Hudun" while meaning Surat Hud. Sibawayh said: The proof of this is that you say "hadhihi al-Rahman," and had you not intended "this is the surah of al-Rahman" you would not have said "hadhihi."

Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim.

Alif-Lam-Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm, then detailed, from One Wise and All-Aware. (1) That you worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings. (2) And that you seek forgiveness of your Lord and then turn to Him in repentance; He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term and will give every person of virtue his virtue. But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day. (3) To Allah is your return, and He is over all things competent. (4)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾. Its discussion has already preceded [see vol. 8, p. 304].

(Kitab) means "hadha kitab" (this is a Book). "(uhkimat ayatuh)" is in the position of raf' as an adjective of kitab. The best of what has been said regarding the meaning of "uhkimat ayatuh" is the saying of Qatadah, i.e., they were made muhkam entirely, with no defect in them and no falsehood. Ihkam (making firm) means preventing speech from corruption, i.e., they were arranged in a firm arrangement, no contradiction or defect reaching them. Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., no book abrogated it, unlike the Torah and the Gospel. In this sense, He made some of its verses muhkam by making them abrogating and not abrogated. This has been discussed before [see vol. 4, p. 10].

The generic noun may sometimes denote a species, as one says: "akaltu ta'am Zayd" (I ate Zayd's food), meaning some of his food. Al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah said: "uhkimat ayatuh" by command and prohibition.

"(Thumma fussilat)" by promise and threat, reward and punishment. Qatadah said: Allah made them firm from falsehood, then detailed them with the lawful and the unlawful. Mujahid said: they were made firm as a whole, then clarified verse by verse with all that is needed of proof concerning tawhid, prophethood, resurrection and other matters. It has also been said: they were gathered in the Preserved Tablet, then detailed in the revelation. It has also been said: "fussilat" means they were sent down piece by piece so that they might be pondered. 'Ikrimah read "fusilat" with light pronunciation, meaning judged with truth. "(Min ladun)" means "min 'indi" (from with Him). "(Hakim)" means one who makes affairs firm.

(Khabir) means aware of every existing and non-existing thing. His saying, Exalted is He: (Alla ta'budu illa Allah). Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: i.e., bi-'alla: it was made firm and then detailed so that you worship none but Allah. Al-Zajjaj said: li-'alla, i.e., it was made firm and then detailed lest you worship other than Allah. It has been said: He commanded His Messenger to say to the people: "Worship none but Allah."

"(Innani lakum minhu)" i.e., from Allah.

"(Nadhir)" i.e., one who warns of His punishment and His might to those who disobey Him.

"(Wa-bashir)" with pleasure and Paradise for those who obey Him. It has also been said: this is from the speech of Allah at the beginning and the end, i.e., "Worship none but Allah; indeed I am to you from Him a warner," i.e., Allah is a warner to you from worshipping other than Him, as He said: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28] [see vol. 4, pp. 58 and 210].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you seek forgiveness of your Lord﴾ is coordinated with the first.

"(Thumma tubu ilayh)" i.e., return to Him through obedience and worship. al-Farra' said: "thumma" here means "wa" (and), i.e., "and repent to Him," because seeking forgiveness is repentance and repentance is seeking forgiveness. It has also been said: seek forgiveness from your past sins, and repent to Him from what you commit in the future whenever it occurs. Some of the righteous said: seeking forgiveness without giving up (sin) is the repentance of liars. This meaning has been fully discussed before in "Al 'Imran" [see vol. 4, pp. 58 and 210], and in "al-Baqarah" [see vol. 3, p. 156] at His saying: ﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in jest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. It has also been said: the mention of seeking forgiveness is placed first because forgiveness is the sought-after goal, and repentance is the means to it; so forgiveness is first in what is sought and last in the means. It may also mean: seek forgiveness from minor sins, and repent to Him from major sins.

"(Yumatti'kum mata'an hasanan)" this is the fruit of seeking forgiveness and repentance, i.e., He will let you enjoy benefits such as abundance of provision and comfortable living, and will not destroy you with punishment as He did to those who were destroyed before you. It has also been said: "yumatti'kum" means "yu'ammirukum" (He will let you live long); the original sense of imta' is prolongation, and from it comes "amta'a Allah bika" and "matta'a." Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: the good enjoyment is leaving creation and turning to the Truth. It has also been said: it is contentment with what is present and not grieving over what is lost.

"(Ila ajalin musamma)" it has been said: this is death. It has been said: the Resurrection. It has been said: entering Paradise. According to this last view, the good enjoyment is protection from every hateful thing and frightening matter, of what occurs in the grave and elsewhere, and the terrors and distress of the Resurrection. The first view is more apparent, because of His saying in this surah: ﴿And, O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength to your strength﴾ [Hud: 52] [see p. 50 onward of this part]; and this ends with death, which is the specified term. And Allah knows best. Muqatil said: They refused, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, and they were afflicted with drought for seven years, until they ate burned bones, filth, carrion, and dogs.

"(Wa-yu'ti kulla dhi fadlin fadlahu)" i.e., He will give every doer of righteous deeds the reward of his deed. It has also been said: He will give everyone whose good deeds outweigh his bad deeds "fadlahu," i.e., Paradise, which is Allah's bounty, so the pronoun in "fadlahu" refers back to Allah, Exalted is He. Mujahid said: it is what a person reckons of speech uttered by his tongue, or deed done by his hand or foot, or what he voluntarily gives from his wealth; that is Allah's bounty, which He gives when one believes, and does not accept from him if he is a disbeliever.

"(Wa-in tawallaw fa-innani akhafu 'alaykum 'adhaba yawmin kabir)" i.e., the Day of Resurrection, which is "great" because of its terrors. It has also been said: the Great Day is the Day of Badr and others. "Tawallaw" may be a past form, and the meaning would be: "and if they turn away, then say to them: indeed I fear for you." It may also be a future form, one of the two tas omitted, and the meaning: "Say to them: if you turn away, indeed I fear for you." His saying, Exalted is He: "To Allah is your return" i.e., after death.

"(Wa-huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir)" of reward and punishment.

This has been discussed before [see vol. 4, p. 10].

The generic noun may sometimes denote a species, as one says: "akaltu ta'am Zayd" (I ate Zayd's food), meaning some of his food. Al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah said: "uhkimat ayatuh" by command and prohibition.

"(Thumma fussilat)" by promise and threat, reward and punishment. Qatadah said: Allah made them firm from falsehood, then detailed them with the lawful and the unlawful. Mujahid said: they were made firm as a whole, then clarified verse by verse with all that is needed of proof concerning tawhid, prophethood, resurrection and other matters. It has also been said: they were gathered in the Preserved Tablet, then detailed in the revelation. It has also been said: "fussilat" means they were sent down piece by piece so that they might be pondered. 'Ikrimah read "fusilat" with light pronunciation, meaning judged with truth. "(Min ladun)" means "min 'indi" (from with Him). "(Hakim)" means one who makes affairs firm.

(Khabir) means aware of every existing and non-existing thing. His saying, Exalted is He: (Alla ta'budu illa Allah). Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: i.e., bi-'alla: it was made firm and then detailed so that you worship none but Allah. Al-Zajjaj said: li-'alla, i.e., it was made firm and then detailed lest you worship other than Allah. It has been said: He commanded His Messenger to say to the people: "Worship none but Allah."

"(Innani lakum minhu)" i.e., from Allah.

"(Nadhir)" i.e., one who warns of His punishment and His might to those who disobey Him.

"(Wa-bashir)" with pleasure and Paradise for those who obey Him. It has also been said: this is from the speech of Allah at the beginning and the end, i.e., "Worship none but Allah; indeed I am to you from Him a warner," i.e., Allah is a warner to you from worshipping other than Him, as He said: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28] [see vol. 4, pp. 58 and 210].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you seek forgiveness of your Lord﴾ is coordinated with the first.

"(Thumma tubu ilayh)" i.e., return to Him through obedience and worship. al-Farra' said: "thumma" here means "wa" (and), i.e., "and repent to Him," because seeking forgiveness is repentance and repentance is seeking forgiveness. It has also been said: seek forgiveness from your past sins, and repent to Him from what you commit in the future whenever it occurs. Some of the righteous said: seeking forgiveness without giving up (sin) is the repentance of liars. This meaning has been fully discussed before in "Al 'Imran" [see vol. 4, pp. 58 and 210], and in "al-Baqarah" [see vol. 3, p. 156] at His saying: ﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in jest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. It has also been said: the mention of seeking forgiveness is placed first because forgiveness is the sought-after goal, and repentance is the means to it; so forgiveness is first in what is sought and last in the means. It may also mean: seek forgiveness from minor sins, and repent to Him from major sins.

"(Yumatti'kum mata'an hasanan)" this is the fruit of seeking forgiveness and repentance, i.e., He will let you enjoy benefits such as abundance of provision and comfortable living, and will not destroy you with punishment as He did to those who were destroyed before you. It has also been said: "yumatti'kum" means "yu'ammirukum" (He will let you live long); the original sense of imta' is prolongation, and from it comes "amta'a Allah bika" and "matta'a." Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: the good enjoyment is leaving creation and turning to the Truth. It has also been said: it is contentment with what is present and not grieving over what is lost.

"(Ila ajalin musamma)" it has been said: this is death. It has been said: the Resurrection. It has been said: entering Paradise. According to this last view, the good enjoyment is protection from every hateful thing and frightening matter, of what occurs in the grave and elsewhere, and the terrors and distress of the Resurrection. The first view is more apparent, because of His saying in this surah: ﴿And, O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength to your strength﴾ [Hud: 52] [see p. 50 onward of this part]; and this ends with death, which is the specified term. And Allah knows best. Muqatil said: They refused, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, and they were afflicted with drought for seven years, until they ate burned bones, filth, carrion, and dogs.

"(Wa-yu'ti kulla dhi fadlin fadlahu)" i.e., He will give every doer of righteous deeds the reward of his deed. It has also been said: He will give everyone whose good deeds outweigh his bad deeds "fadlahu," i.e., Paradise, which is Allah's bounty, so the pronoun in "fadlahu" refers back to Allah, Exalted is He. Mujahid said: it is what a person reckons of speech uttered by his tongue, or deed done by his hand or foot, or what he voluntarily gives from his wealth; that is Allah's bounty, which He gives when one believes, and does not accept from him if he is a disbeliever.

"(Wa-in tawallaw fa-innani akhafu 'alaykum 'adhaba yawmin kabir)" i.e., the Day of Resurrection, which is "great" because of its terrors. It has also been said: the Great Day is the Day of Badr and others. "Tawallaw" may be a past form, and the meaning would be: "and if they turn away, then say to them: indeed I fear for you." It may also be a future form, one of the two tas omitted, and the meaning: "Say to them: if you turn away, indeed I fear for you." His saying, Exalted is He: "To Allah is your return" i.e., after death.

"(Wa-huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir)" of reward and punishment.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 1–4:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. (Makkiyyah) According to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir, it is Meccan. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: except for one verse, which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114]. [[See p. 109 of this part. And in a report from Ibn 'Abbas, it is entirely Meccan; this is the view of al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah.]]

Abu Muhammad al-Darimi narrated in his Musnad, from Ka'b, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite Surat Hud on Friday." Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have grown grey!" He said: "Hud, al-Waqi'ah, al-Mursalat, 'Amma yatasa'alun, and when the sun is wound up have greyed me." He said: this is a hasan gharib hadith, and something of this has been narrated as mursal.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi Abu 'Abd Allah also reported it in Nawadir al-Usul: Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Bishr narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Salih, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Juhayfah, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we see you have grown grey!" He said: "Hud and its sisters have greyed me." Abu 'Abd Allah said: Fright produces greyness, because fright distracts the soul and dries up the moisture of the body, and beneath every hair there is a root, and from it comes sweat. When fright drains its moisture, the roots dry up, the hair dries and whitens, just as you see green crops whitening when their water is gone. The hair of an old man turns white only because its moisture departs and its skin dries. So the soul is distracted by the threat of Allah and the terrors of what the report from Allah brings, and it withers, and that threat and terror which has come drains its water, and from it one greys. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a Day that will make the children grey-haired﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 17], for they greyed from fright.

As for Surat Hud, since it mentions the nations and what befell them of Allah's swift punishment, the people of certainty, when they recite it, see upon their hearts His dominion, His authority and His glances, and the seizing of His enemies. Were they to die of fright, it would be right for them, but Allah, blessed and exalted is His name, shows them gentleness in those moments until they finish reading His words. As for its sisters, the surahs resembling it, such as ﴿al-Haqqah﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1], ﴿A questioner asked﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1], ﴿When the sun is wound up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1] and "al-Qari'ah" [al-Qari'ah: 1], in the recitation of these surahs is what reveals to the hearts of those who know Him His authority and His seizing, so the souls are distracted by it and the heads turn grey.

[I say:] It has been said that what greyed the Prophet (ﷺ) from Surat Hud is the saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112], as its explanation will come, if Allah wills.

Yazid ibn Aban said: I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in my dream, and I recited Surat Hud to him. When I finished it he said: "O Yazid, this is recitation, so where is the weeping?"

Our scholars said: Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: It is said "hadhihi Hudu" without tanwin, as the name of the surah, because if you named a woman Zayd you would not give it diptote treatment; this is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. But 'Isa ibn 'Umar says: "hadhihi Hudun" with tanwin, as the name of the surah, and likewise if one names a woman Zayd, because when its middle is vowelled with sukun it becomes light and receives tanwin. If you intend omission, you give it tanwin according to all, and say: "hadhihi Hudun" while meaning Surat Hud. Sibawayh said: The proof of this is that you say "hadhihi al-Rahman," and had you not intended "this is the surah of al-Rahman" you would not have said "hadhihi."

Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim.

Alif-Lam-Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm, then detailed, from One Wise and All-Aware. (1) That you worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings. (2) And that you seek forgiveness of your Lord and then turn to Him in repentance; He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term and will give every person of virtue his virtue. But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day. (3) To Allah is your return, and He is over all things competent. (4)

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 11, verse 5:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold their breasts to conceal themselves from Him﴾. He informs of the hostility of the polytheists toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, and that they think their states are hidden from Allah. "They fold their breasts" means they fold them over their enmity toward the Muslims, and there is an ellipsis (ḥadhf) in this phrase. Ibn 'Abbas said: they conceal what is in their breasts of rancor and enmity, while displaying the opposite. It was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who was a man sweet of speech and sweet of tongue; he would meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with what pleased him, while his heart harbored what was displeasing. Mujahid said: "they fold their breasts" means doubt and disputation. Al-Hasan said: they fold them over the disbelief that is in them. It was also said: it was revealed concerning some of the hypocrites, who, whenever he passed by the Prophet (ﷺ), would bend his chest and back, lower his head, and cover his face, so that the Prophet (ﷺ) would not see him and invite him to faith. This meaning is related from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad. So the pronoun in "minhu" (from Him) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: the hypocrites said, "When we shut our doors, wrap ourselves in our garments, and fold our breasts over enmity toward Muhammad, who will know about us?" Then the verse was revealed. It was also said: some of the Muslims used to practice asceticism by covering their bodies and not exposing them under the sky, so Allah the Exalted explained that asceticism is not what the hearts contain of belief, and what they manifest of speech and action. Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Abbad ibn Ja'far, who said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, say: "Unquestionably, they fold their breasts (tathnuwi) to hide from Him (liyastakhfū minhu)" [[In the original: "tathnuwa", without a nun after the waw, in the pattern of tanṭawī. This differs from what is in Sahih al-Bukhari and the tafsir of al-Tabari from Muhammad ibn 'Abbad, so we have corrected it accordingly. As for the reading "tathnuwa" mentioned in the original, Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to Ibn 'Uyayna, and al-Nahhas's I'rab al-Quran (grammatical analysis of the Qur'an) supports this, where he said: Other than Muhammad ibn 'Abbad related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Unquestionably, they fold their breasts (tathnawī ṣudūruhum)" without a nun after the waw, in the pattern of tanṭawī... etc., which is the phrase that follows in the original. Some exegetes criticized this reading as an error in transmission that cannot stand. See al-Ma'ani, al-Bahr, and the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya.]] He said: they used not to have intercourse with women, nor would they relieve themselves in the open, while they were bathing under the sky. So this verse was revealed. Other than Muhammad ibn 'Abbad related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Unquestionably, they fold their breasts (tathnawī ṣudūruhum)" without a nun after the waw, in the pattern of tanṭawī. The meaning of "tathnawī" and the other two readings is close, because the breasts are not folded until they fold them. It was also said: some of them would bend over another and whisper to him about disparaging the Muslims, and their ignorance reached the point that they imagined this was hidden from Allah, the Exalted. "To hide (liyastakhfū)" means to conceal themselves from Him, that is, from Muhammad or from Allah. "To hide (liyastakhfū)" means to conceal themselves from Him, that is, from Muhammad or from Allah.

(﴿Unquestionably, when they wrap themselves in their garments﴾) meaning they cover their heads with their garments. Qatadah said: a servant is most concealed when he bends his back, wraps himself in his garment, and conceals his concern within himself.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on surah 11, verse 6:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾. "Ma" is a negation, "min" is extra (redundant), and "dabbatin" is in the position of the nominative, the implied meaning being: "and there is no creature." "Illa 'ala Allahi rizquha" ("but upon Allah is its provision"): "'ala" here means "min" (from), i.e., its provision is from Allah. This is supported by the saying of Mujahid: "Whatever provision comes to it is from Allah." It was also said: "'ala Allah" means as a bounty, not as an obligation. It was also said: it is a promise from Him, a binding truth. The explanation of this meaning has already been given in (Surah) "An-Nisa'" [see vol. 5, p. 273], and that He, glorified is He, has nothing obligatory upon Him. "Rizquha" is in the nominative by being the subject of the sentence; according to the Kufans, it is in the nominative by being a qualifier. The apparent meaning of the verse is generality, but its real meaning is specificity, because many creatures perished before they were provided for. It was also said: it is general for every creature, and every creature that has not been given provision by which it lives has nevertheless been given its spirit as provision. The connection of the verse with what precedes it is that He, glorified is He, informed of the provision of all of them, and that He is not heedless of their nurture; so how could your conditions be hidden from Him, O company of disbelievers, when He is the one who provides for you?! "Dabbah" is every animal that crawls. "Rizq" in its true sense is what a living being feeds on, and in which the survival of its spirit and the growth of its body lie. It is not permissible for "rizq" to mean ownership, because beasts are provided for, and it is not correct to describe them as owning their fodder; likewise infants are provided with milk, and one does not say that the milk in the breast is the property of the infant. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 22], and we have no ownership in the heaven. Moreover, if provision were ownership, then whenever a person ate from the property of another, he would have eaten from the provision of another, and that is impossible, because a servant eats only his own provision. This meaning has already been discussed in (Surah) "Al-Baqarah" [see vol. 1, p. 177 onward], and praise be to Allah. It was said to one of them: "From where do you eat?" He said: "The One who created the millstone brings it the grain, and the One who split the jaws is the Creator of sustenance."

It was said to Abu Usayd: "From where do you eat?" He said: "Glory be to Allah, and Allah is greatest! Allah provides for the dog, so will He not provide for Abu Usayd?!" It was said to Hatim al-Asamm: "From where do you eat?" He said: "From Allah's presence." He was told: "Does Allah send down dinars and dirhams to you from the sky?" He said: "As if His property were only the sky! O man, the earth belongs to Him and the sky belongs to Him; if He does not bring my provision to me from the sky, He will drive it to me from the earth." And he recited:

"And how should I fear poverty while Allah is my provider,
and the provider of this creation in hardship and ease?

He has taken on the provision of all creatures,
and of the lizard in the desert and the fish in the sea."

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned in "Nawadir al-Usul," with its chain of narration from Zayd ibn Aslam, that the Ash'aris, Abu Musa, Abu Malik and Abu 'Amir, along with a group of them, when they emigrated and came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, had run out of provisions (their food had been exhausted); so they sent a man from among them to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to ask him. When he reached the door of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he heard him reciting this verse: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its place of residence and its place of storage; all is in a clear record﴾. The man said: "The Ash'aris are not the least of creatures in Allah's sight." So he returned without entering upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said to his companions: "Rejoice, relief has come to you!" They did not think except that he had spoken with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and that he had promised them. While they were in that state, two men came to them carrying a bowl between them, filled with bread and meat, and they ate from it as much as they wished. Then some of them said to others: "If we were to return this food to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so that he might meet his need with it..." They said to the two men: "Take this food to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for we have already satisfied our need from it." Then they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have never seen food more abundant or better than the food you sent us." He said: "I did not send you any food." They informed him that they had sent their companion. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked him, and he told him what he had done and what he had said to them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "That is a provision Allah has given you."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and He knows its place of residence﴾: that is, from the earth, where it takes refuge.

(And its place of storage): that is, the place where it dies and is buried. This was said by Miqsam from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "Its place of residence" refers to the days of its life; "its place of storage" is where it dies and where it is resurrected. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Its place of residence" is in the womb, and "its place of storage" is in the loins. It was also said: "He knows its place of residence" in Paradise or Hell, and "its place of storage" in the grave. This is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted, describing the people of Paradise and the people of Hell: ﴿How good a place of residence and station it is﴾ [Al-Furqan: 76] ﴿How evil a place of residence and station it is﴾ [Al-Furqan: 66] [see vol. 13, p. 72 and p. 82].

(All is in a clear record): that is, in the Preserved Tablet.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. Its explanation has already passed in "al-A'raf" (see vol. 7, p. 218 onward), and praise be to God. (And His Throne was upon the water): this shows that the creation of the Throne and the water came before the creation of the earth and the heaven. Ka'b said: God created a green ruby, and He looked at it with awe, and it became water trembling from the fear of God Exalted. Therefore the water still trembles to this day, even when it is still. Then He created the wind and placed the water upon its back, then He placed the Throne upon the water. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: "And His Throne was upon the water," and he said: "Upon what was the water?" He said: "Upon the back of the wind."

Al-Bukhari related from 'Imran ibn Husayn, who said: I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) when some people from Banu Tamim came to him, and he said: "Accept the glad tidings, O Banu Tamim." They said: "You have given us glad tidings, so give us [twice]." [The addition is from Sahih al-Bukhari.] Then some people from Yemen entered, and he said: "Accept the glad tidings, O people of Yemen, since Banu Tamim did not accept them." They said: "We accept. We have come to gain understanding in the religion, and to ask you about this matter: what was it?" [In (ʿ): "We ask you about this religion, and we ask you about the beginning of this matter."] He said: "God was, and there was nothing with Him, and His Throne was upon the water. Then He created the heavens and the earth and wrote in the Reminder (al-Dhikr) everything." Then a man came to me and said: "O 'Imran, catch up with your camel, for it has gone." So I set off seeking it, and behold, the mirage was cutting it off from me. By God, I wished that it had gone and I had not gotten up.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. That is, He created that so that He might test His servants by way of reflection and inference upon the perfection of His power and upon the Resurrection. Qatadah said: the meaning of "which of you is best in deed" is "which of you is most complete in intellect." Al-Hasan and Sufyan al-Thawri said: "which of you is most ascetic regarding this world." It is mentioned that 'Isa, peace be upon him, passed by a sleeping man and said: "O sleeper, get up and worship." He said: "O Spirit of God, I have worshipped." He said: "And with what did you worship?" He said: "I have left this world to its people." He said: "Sleep, for you have surpassed the worshippers." Al-Dahhak: "which of you is most thankful." Muqatil: "which of you is most God-fearing." Ibn 'Abbas: "which of you is most active in obedience to God, the Mighty and Majestic." It is related from Ibn 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: "which of you is best in deed," and said: "which of you has the best intellect, is most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of God, and is quickest in obedience to God." So he gathered all the sayings together. This will also come in "al-Kahf" (see vol. 10, p. 303), God willing. The meaning of trial (ibtila') has already been mentioned.

(And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death"): that is, if you, O Muhammad, give evidence for the Resurrection.

(after death): And if you mentioned that to the polytheists, they would say: "This is magic." "Inna" is pronounced with a kasra because it begins a new statement after the verb of saying. Sibawayh related the fatha (opening vowel).

(those who disbelieved will surely say): the lam is given a fatha because the verb precedes it and has no pronoun in it, and after it comes "la-yaqulanna," because it contains a pronoun. And ("magic") means: false delusion, because of the falsity of magic in their view. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Indeed this is nothing but an evident sorcerer" (inna hadha illa sahir 'alim), referring to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 11, verse 8:

ۥ **His saying, Exalted is He:** ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation﴾. The *lam* in "**لَئِنْ**" (la'in) is the *lam* of oath (*lam al-qasam*), and the response is "**لَيَقُولُنَّ**" (layaqulunna), "they will surely say." The meaning of "**إِلى أُمَّةٍ**" (ila ummatin) is "until a counted term and a known time." So "ummah" here means a period of time. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and the majority of the exegetes (*mufassirun*). The root meaning of "**الأُمَّةُ**" (al-ummah) is "a group," and the word is used for the time and the years because a community (*ummah*) exists within them. It has also been said that the phrase contains an elided genitive (*mudaf mahdhuf*), so the meaning is "until the coming of a generation in which there is no one who believes, so that they deserve destruction," or "until the passing away of a generation in which there are believers, so that after its passing away no one who believes remains."

The word "**الأُمَّةُ**" is a homonym (*ism mushtarak*) used in eight senses:

1. It means a group, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and he found upon it a community of people﴾ [al-Qasas: 23]. [See vol. 13, p. 267.]
2. It also means the followers of the prophets, peace be upon them.
3. It means a man who combines all goodness and is followed as an example, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, upright﴾ [al-Nahl: 120]. [See vol. 10, pp. 197 and 62.]
4. It means religion and creed, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. [See vol. 16, p. 74.]
5. It means a period of time and an age, as in His saying, "**And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation**," and likewise His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and he remembered after a period﴾ [Yusuf: 45]. [See p. 201 of this volume.]
6. It means stature, which is the height and tallness of a person. From this one says: "So-and-so has a good *ummah*," meaning a good stature.
7. It means a man who is alone in his religion, with no one sharing it with him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a *ummah* alone" (ﷺ).
   (*Yub'athu Zayd ummatan*): because he had disavowed the religions of the polytheists and had believed in the Prophet ﷺ before his mission (*mab'ath*).
8. It means a mother. One says: "This is the *ummah* of Zayd," meaning the mother of Zayd.

**His saying:** (**لَيَقُولُنَّ مَا يَحْبِسُهُ**) (layaqulunna ma yahbisuhu), "they will surely say: What is holding it back?" It means the punishment. They said this either as a denial of the punishment because of its delay concerning them, or out of haste and mockery, meaning: what is it that is keeping it from us?

**His saying:** (**أَلا يَوْمَ يَأْتِيهِمْ لَيْسَ مَصْرُوفاً عَنْهُمْ**) (ala yawma ya'tihim laysa masrufan 'anhum), "Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be turned away from them." It has been said that this refers to the killing of the polytheists at Badr, and the killing of the mockers by Gabriel, as will be mentioned.

**His saying:** (**وَحاقَ بِهِمْ**) (wa haqa bihim), "and there befell them": that is, it descended upon them and encompassed them.

**His saying:** (**مَا كانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِؤُنَ**) (ma kanu bihi yastahzi'un), "what they used to mock." That is, the recompense for what they used to mock, and the genitive word is elided (*al-mudaf mahdhuf*).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 9–11:

God's words: ﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us﴾. Al-Insan (man) is a common noun denoting the species, encompassing all disbelievers. It is said that al-Insan here refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and the verse was revealed concerning him. It is also said that it refers to Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya al-Makhzumi. "Mercy" means blessing.

(Then We withdraw it from him) meaning, We strip it away from him.

(Indeed, he is despairing) meaning, he is hopeless of mercy.

(Ungrateful) to blessings, a denier of them. Ibn al-A'rabi said: [...]

Al-Nahhas said: "Ya'us" (despairing) is from ya'isa, yay'asu. Sibawayh reported ya'isa, ya'ISU, on the pattern fa'ila yaf'alu, like hasiba yahsibu and ni'ma yan'amu, and ya'isa yay'asu [[As in the originals. The correct reading is likely yabisa yaybasu, with the letter ba' after the ya'. This is the fourth letter]]. Some say ya'isa yay'isu, and in the Arabic language only these four sound-root verbs come on the pattern fa'ila yaf'alu, and there is disagreement regarding one of them. The form is ya'isa, and "ya'us" is an intensive form, like fakhur, for emphasis.

God's words: ﴿And if We let him taste blessing﴾, meaning health, ease, and abundance in provision.

(After hardship had touched him) meaning, after harm, poverty, and adversity.

(He will surely say, "The evils have gone from me") meaning, the misfortunes that afflict their owner from harm and poverty.

(Indeed, he is exultant and boastful) meaning, he rejoices and boasts of the abundance he has obtained and forgets to thank God for it. One says: "a man is fakhir" when he boasts, and fakhur is for emphasis. Ya'qub al-Qari said: Some people of Medina read "laffaraḥ" with a damma on the ra', as one says rajul fatun, ḥadhar, and nadus. In both dialects, it is permissible to pronounce it with sukun because of the heaviness of the damma and kasra.

God's words: ﴿Except those who are patient﴾, meaning the believers, whom He praises for their patience in hardships. It is in the accusative position. Al-Akhfash said: it is an exception that is not from the first, meaning "but those who are patient and do righteous deeds in both states of blessing and trial." Al-Farra' said it is an exception from "And if We let him taste," meaning from man, since al-Insan means people, and people include both the disbeliever and the believer, so it is a connected exception, and it is good.

(Those will have forgiveness) an inchoative and predicate.

(And a great reward) conjoined.

(Great) an adjective.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verses 12–13:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾, meaning: perhaps, because of the great disbelief and denial you see from them, you imagine that they will turn you away from what you are upon. It was also said: when they said, "Why was a treasure not sent down to him, or an angel not sent with him?", he (ﷺ) intended to give up reviling their gods, so this verse was revealed. Thus the meaning of the statement is interrogative (istifham, a question), i.e., "Will you leave out what contains the reviling of their gods, as they asked you?" The command to deliver the message was emphasised, as in His saying: ﴿O Messenger, deliver what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 67].[[See vol. 6, p. 242.]] It was also said: the meaning of the statement is negation (nafy) in the sense of remote likelihood (istib'ad), i.e., that will not come from you; rather, you will convey to them everything that has been sent down to you. This is because the polytheists of Makkah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you bring us a book that does not contain the reviling of our gods, we will follow you." The Prophet (ﷺ) intended to give up reviling their gods, so this verse was revealed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and your breast is constricted by it﴾ is coordinated (atf, conjunction) with "leaving out" (tārik), and "breast" (ṣadruka) is in the nominative (marfū', raised case) by it. The pronoun in "by it" refers to "what" (mā), or to "some" (ba'ḍa), or to the conveying, or to the denial. He said "ḍā'iq" (constricted) and did not say "ḍayyiq" in order to match "tārik" which precedes it, and because "ḍā'iq" denotes a temporary condition, whereas "ḍayyiq" denotes something more permanent. "(That they should say)" is in the accusative position (manṣūb, objective case), meaning: out of dislike that they should say, [or lest they should say],[[from w.]] like His saying: ﴿God makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [An-Nisa': 176], i.e., lest you go astray. Or it means: because they would say.

(Dhalūlan) i.e., hallā (why not): (a treasure has not been sent down to him, or an angel has not come with him to confirm him), said by Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi. Then God, the Exalted, said: O Muhammad, (you are only a warner). It is only incumbent upon you to warn them, not to bring them what they propose of signs.

(And God is Guardian over all things.) That is, Preserver and Witness.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ "Am" (or) here means "bal" (rather). It was mentioned earlier in Surah Yunus.[[See vol. 8, p. 344.]] The meaning is: you have removed their excuse and their doubt concerning your prophethood by this Qur'an, and you have established the proof against them with it. So if they say, "You have invented it", i.e., you fabricated it, then let them bring a fabrication like it, according to their claim.

(And call upon whomever you can, apart from God), i.e., from the soothsayers and helpers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they do not respond to you﴾, meaning in the matching (mu'arada, the attempt to produce a equal rival), and they are unable to do so, then the proof has been established against them, since they are the eloquent of tongue and the fluent masters of speech.

﴿Then know that it was sent down with the knowledge of Allah﴾, and know the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and that there is no god but He. Will you then submit?﴾ This is a question whose meaning is a command. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already been given, and that the Qur'an is inimitable (mu'jiz) was stated at the beginning of the book, and all praise is due to Allah.

He said: "Say, bring forth..." and after it: "﴿And if they do not respond to you﴾", and He did not say "to you" (singular). It has been said: this is a shift of address from the singular to the plural, for glorification and exaltation, and a leader may be addressed with the form used for a group. It has also been said: the pronoun in "lakum" (to you) and in "fa'lamu" (know) refers to everyone, that is, let everyone know that ﴿it was sent down with the knowledge of Allah﴾; this was said by Mujahid. It has also been said: the pronoun in "lakum" and in "fa'lamu" refers to the polytheists, and the meaning is: if those whom you call upon for help do not respond to you, and the matching is not possible for you, then ﴿know that it was sent down with the knowledge of Allah﴾. It has also been said: the pronoun in "lakum" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, and in "fa'lamu" to the polytheists.

There are three issues here.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿Whoever desires﴾. Some say that "kāna" is redundant (zā'ida). Al-Bahr says: "This may not be correct, for if it were redundant, the conditional verb would be "yurīdu" and it would be in the jussive." For this reason the apodosis is in the jussive: "nuwaffi ilayhim" (We will pay them in full). This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: "man kāna" is in a position of jussive (conditional) and its apodosis is "nuwaffi ilayhim", meaning: whoever should desire. The first is past in form, while the second is future in meaning, as Zuhayr said:

"Whoever shrinks from the causes of death will meet it, even if he tries to climb the causes of the sky with a ladder."

The scholars differed in interpreting this verse. It was said: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers. This is the view of al-Dahhak, and al-Nahhas chose it, based on the following verse: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire﴾ [Hud: 16]. That is, whoever among them performs the joining of kinship ties or charity, We will reward him for it in this world, with health of body and abundance of provision, but he will have no good in the Hereafter. This meaning has already been discussed in full under "Bara'a" [[See vol. 8, p. 161.]]. It was also said: the verse refers to the believers, meaning: whoever intends by his deed the reward of this world, the reward is hastened to him and nothing is diminished from it in this world, and in the Hereafter he will have punishment, because he restricted his intention to this world. This is like the saying of (ﷺ): "Actions are judged only by intentions." A servant is given according to the nature of his intention and what his inner self holds. This is a matter agreed upon among all nations and every religious community. It was also said: it applies to the people of show-off (riya'). It is reported in a khabar that it will be said to the people of riya': "You fasted, prayed, gave charity, fought, and recited, so that it might be said of you," and it has been said. Then (He) said: "The first of these to be cast into the Fire." Abu Hurayra narrated this, then wept intensely and said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke the truth. Allah the Exalted says: "Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment" and he recited the two verses. Muslim recorded it in his Sahih [[From "ع" and "و" (manuscript sigla).]] with similar meaning, and al-Tirmidhi too. It was also said: the verse is general, applying to everyone who intends by his deed other than Allah the Exalted, whether he had the root of faith or not. This is the view of Mujahid and Maymun ibn Mihran, and Mu'awiya (may Allah have mercy on him) also adopted it. Maymun ibn Mihran said: No one does a good deed without being repaid for it. If he is a Muslim, sincere, he is repaid in this world and the Hereafter; and if he is a disbeliever, he is repaid in this world. It was also said: whoever desired [the world] by his campaign with the Prophet (ﷺ) was repaid in it, meaning he was given the reward of the warriors without any deduction from it. This is a particular application, while the correct view is the general one.

The second issue: some scholars said the meaning of this verse is His (ﷺ) saying: "Actions are judged only by intentions." This verse indicates that whoever fasts in Ramadan without intending it as Ramadan does not count as Ramadan fasting, and it indicates that whoever performs wudu' for coolness and cleanliness does not thereby make it an act of worship for the sake of prayer. The same applies to everything of this kind.

The third issue: most scholars held that this verse is absolute (mutlaq), and so is the verse in al-Shura: ﴿Whoever desires the tillage of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tillage; and whoever desires the tillage of this world, We will give him of it﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 18.]] [al-Shura: 20], and likewise: ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 226 and following.]] [Al 'Imran: 145]. The verse in al-Isra' restricts and explains them: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty (life), We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 235 and following.]] [al-Isra': 18], up to His saying: ﴿restricted﴾ [al-Isra': 20]. So He informed, glory be to Him, that the servant intends and desires, while Allah, glory be to Him, decides what He wills. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) concerning His saying "Whoever desires the life of this world" that it was abrogated (mansukha) by His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty (life)﴾ [al-Isra': 18]. The correct view is what we have mentioned: this is a case of the absolute and the restricted (al-itlaq wa al-taqyid). Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqara: 186]. Its apparent meaning is a report that every supplicant is answered always and in every state, but this is not so, because of His saying: ﴿He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾ [al-An'am: 41]. Abrogation (naskh) does not apply to reports, because the rational obligations cannot change, and lying is impossible for Allah the Exalted. As for reports about legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyya), their abrogation is permissible, though there is disagreement on this, as is mentioned in the books of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence). Its explanation will come in "al-Nahl" [[See vol. 10, p. 127.]], if Allah the Exalted wills.

[The commentary of al-Qurtubi on surah 11, verse 16]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire﴾. This is an indication of eternal abiding (takhlid), but the believer does not abide eternally, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that﴾ [An-Nisa: 48], and the verse. So it is to be understood as referring to the case where this show-off dies upon disbelief. And it was said: the meaning is that there is for them nothing but the Fire for known days, then they will be brought out, either by intercession or by the handful (al-qabdah). The verse implies the threat of the loss of faith, and in the hadith that has passed [[In the original (al-ma'asi) which is a distortion; the intended hadith is the earlier hadith of Abu Hurairah concerning the deed of the show-off, "You fasted and prayed..."]] it means disbelief, and especially showing off (riya'), since it is associating partners (shirk), as its explanation has preceded in "An-Nisa" [[See vol. 5, pp. 245 and 422.]] and it will come at the end of "Al-Kahf" [[See vol. 11, p. 69.]].

(And vain is what they used to do) is an inchoative and predicate (ibtida' wa khabar). Abu Hatim said: the pronoun (ha') has been omitted. Al-Nahhas said: this does not need an omission, because it has the sense of the verbal noun (masdar), meaning "and vain is their deed." In the reading of Ubayy and Abdullah, "and vain is what they used to do" [with an accusative, wa-batilan], and "ma" would then be superfluous (za'idah), meaning "and they used to do vain things."

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾. It is an inchoative (mubtada') and the predicate is omitted, meaning: Is he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord in following the Prophet (ﷺ), and who has with him the excellence by which he is distinguished, like others who desire the life of this world and its adornment?! This is related from Ali ibn al-Husayn and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. Likewise Ibn Zayd said: "Indeed, the one who is upon a clear proof [[من ع.]] is the one who follows the Prophet Muhammad [[من ع.]] (ﷺ)."

(And there follows it a witness from Him) from Allah, and he is the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said that what is meant by His saying "Is he who is upon a clear proof from his Lord" is the Prophet (ﷺ), and the speech refers back to His saying: ﴿and your breast is distressed by it﴾ [Hud: 12], meaning: Is he who has with him a clear proof from Allah, and a miracle like the Qur'an, and with him a witness like Jibril, as will come, and whom the earlier scriptures have given good tidings of, one whose breast is not constrained by conveying, for he knows that Allah will not abandon him? The pronoun in "his Lord" refers to him, and so does His saying "and there follows it a witness from Him." Ikrimah related from Ibn Abbas that it is Jibril, and this is the saying of Mujahid and al-Nakha'i. The pronoun in "from Him" refers to Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, meaning: and there follows the clear proof and the demonstration a witness from Allah, may He be mighty and majestic. Mujahid said: the witness is an angel from Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, who protects him and makes him firm. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatadah said: the witness is the tongue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: I said to my father, "Are you the witness?" He said: "I would wish that I were he, but he is the tongue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It has also been said: he is Ali ibn Abi Talib. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: he is Ali ibn Abi Talib. It is related from Ali that he said: There is not a man from Quraysh except that a verse or two verses were revealed concerning him. A man said to him: "What was revealed concerning you?" Ali said: "(And there follows it a witness from Him)." It has also been said: the witness is the form of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his face and his features, because whoever has excellence and intellect, when he looks at the Prophet (ﷺ), knows that he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Accordingly, the pronoun in this view refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), according to the saying of Ibn Zayd and others. It has also been said: the witness is the Qur'an in its composition and eloquence, and the many meanings within a single expression. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: the pronoun in "from Him" refers to the Qur'an. Al-Farra' said: some of them said: "And there follows it a witness from Him" is the Gospel, and although it came before, it follows the Qur'an in confirmation, and the pronoun in "from Him" refers to Allah, may He be mighty and majestic. It has also been said: the clear proof is the knowledge of Allah in which hearts are illuminated, and the witness who follows it is the intellect that is set in the brain and whose breast is illuminated by its light. (And before it) meaning before the Gospel.

(The Book of Musa) is in the nominative by being the inchoative. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: and there follows it, from before it, the Book of Musa, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is described in the Book of Musa: ﴿They find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157] [[راجع ج ٧ ص ٢٩٧]]. Abu Hatim related from some of them that he recited "and before it the Book of Musa" in the accusative, and al-Mahdawi related it from al-Kalbi. It would be conjoined to the pronoun in "yatluhu" (follows it), and the meaning would be: and Jibril, peace be upon him, follows the Book of Musa. Likewise Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the meaning is that before it Jibril recited the Book of Musa to Musa. It is also permissible, according to what Ibn Abbas mentioned in this view, to read "Book" in the nominative, so that the meaning is: and before it the Book of Musa likewise, that is, Jibril recited it to Musa just as he recited the Qur'an to Muhammad.

(As an imam) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

(And a mercy) is conjoined.

(Those believe in it) is a reference to the Children of Israel, meaning they believe in what is in the Torah of the good tidings of you. As for those later ones who disbelieved in you, they are the ones whose promised place is the Fire, as related by al-Qushayri. The pronoun in "his Lord" may refer to the Qur'an, and it may refer to the Prophet (ﷺ).

(And whoever disbelieves in it) that is, in the Qur'an or in the Prophet, upon him be peace.

(Of the factions) meaning of all the religions, according to Qatadah. Likewise Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "the factions" are the people of all the religions, because they form factions against one another. It has also been said: they are Quraysh and their allies.

(Then the Fire is his promised place) meaning he is among the people of the Fire. Hassan recited:

"You brought them to the watering-places of death, the bright ones... so the Fire is their destination, and death is meeting them."

In the Sahih of Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Yunus, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, no one from this community hears of me, a Jew or a Christian [then dies [[زيادة عن صحيح مسلم.]]] and does not believe in what I have been sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire."

(So do not be in doubt) meaning in uncertainty.

(About it) meaning about the Qur'an.

(Indeed it is the truth from your Lord) meaning the Qur'an is from Allah, as Muqatil said. Al-Kalbi said: the meaning is: do not be in doubt that the disbeliever is in the Fire. "Indeed it is the truth," meaning the true word that exists, and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), while the intended meaning is all the responsible persons.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And who does greater wrong than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ That is, no one is more wrongdoing toward themselves than they, because they fabricated a lie against Allah. They attributed His speech to others, claimed that He has a partner and a son, and said of the idols, "These are our intercessors with Allah."

(﴿Those will be presented before their Lord﴾) That is, He will call them to account for their deeds.

(﴿And the witnesses will say﴾) This means the angels who record deeds (al-hafazah), according to Mujahid and others. Sufyan said: I asked al-A'mash about "al-ashhad" (the witnesses), and he said: "The angels." Al-Dahhak said: They are the prophets and messengers. His evidence is the Almighty's saying: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ [An-Nisa: 41]. It was also said: they are the angels, the prophets, and the scholars who conveyed the messages. Qatadah said: they are witnesses over all creation. In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Safwan ibn Muhriz, from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and in it he said: "As for the disbelievers and the hypocrites, they will be called out before all creation: 'These are the ones who lied against Allah.'"

(﴿Surely, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾) That is, His distance, His wrath, and His banishment from His mercy upon those who put worship in other than its proper place.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Who bar from the way of Allah﴾. "Alladhina" may be in the genitive case as an adjective (na't) for "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers), and it may be in the nominative case, meaning "they are those who." It was also said that this is a new statement from Allah, the Exalted, meaning: they are those who bar themselves and others from faith and obedience.

(﴿And they seek to make it crooked﴾) That is, they divert people from it toward sins and polytheism.

(﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾) The word "they" (hum) is repeated for emphasis.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They could not escape (Allah's punishment) in the earth﴾, meaning: they could not escape from the punishment of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "They could not defeat me, were I to command the earth and it would swallow them up."

(And they had no protectors other than Allah) meaning: helpers. Here "min" (from) is extra (ziyadah). It was also said that "ma" means "alladhi" (the one who), with the sense: "Those (people) could not escape, nor could those who had protectors besides Allah." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

(Their punishment will be doubled) meaning: in proportion to their disbelief and their sins.

(They could not bear to hear) "Ma" is in the position of a accusative (nasb), with the meaning: "for what they used to be able to hear."

(Nor could they see) and they did not use that for hearing the truth and seeing it. The Arabs say: "jazaytuhu ma fa'ala" and "bi-ma fa'ala" (I recompensed him for what he did), so they sometimes omit the preposition "ba'" and sometimes affirm it. Sibawayh recited [[The line is by 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib al-Zubaidi. He meant (bi-l-khayr), so he omitted the preposition and the verb connected to the object in the accusative. Al-nashab: stable wealth such as estates and the like. It was also said: al-nashab is all wealth, so its conjunction with the first is for emphasis and intensification.

(Sibawayh's evidences)]]:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded, for indeed I have left you possessing wealth and property."

It is also permissible for "ma" to be a temporal adverb, and the meaning would be: their punishment will be doubled perpetually, that is, at the time of their ability to hear and see; and Allah, glorified is He, will make them in Hell capable of that forever. It is also permissible for "ma" to be a negation with no grammatical position, since the sentence was complete before it, and stopping at "the punishment" is sufficient; the meaning: they were not able in the world to hear a hearing by which they would benefit, nor to see the seeing of one who is guided. Al-Farra' said: "They could not bear to hear" because Allah misguided them in the Preserved Tablet. Al-Zajjaj said: because of their hatred for the Prophet (ﷺ) and their enmity toward him, they could not bear to hear from him nor understand from him. Al-Nahhas said: this is well known in the speech of the Arabs; it is said: "So-and-so cannot bear to look at so-and-so," when that is burdensome to him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 21–22:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾

It is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar).

(And what they used to fabricate has departed from them) i.e., their fabrications were lost and perished for them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Without doubt﴾ (la jarama). The scholars have various opinions regarding it. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "la jarama" means "haqqan" (truly, certainly), so "la" and "jarama" are, in their view, one word, and "anna" (that) is in the position of the nominative (raf'). This is the view of al-Farra' and Muhammad ibn Yazid, related by al-Nahhas. Al-Mahdawi said: "It is also reported from al-Khalil that its meaning is 'la abada' (without a doubt) and 'la mahalata' (undoubtedly), which is also the view of al-Farra', mentioned by al-Tha'labi."

Al-Zajjaj said: "la" here is a negation, and it is a rejection of their saying that the idols benefit them, as if the meaning were: that will not benefit them. "Jarama" means "kasaba" (earned, brought about), i.e., that action earned for them the loss; the subject of "kasaba" is implied, and "anna" is in the accusative governed by "jarama," just as you say: "Your harshness earned (kasaba) Zayd his anger against you." The poet said:

"We fixed his head in a palm trunk
for what his hands had earned (jaramat), and we did not transgress."

i.e., for what they had earned (kasabat).

Al-Kisa'i said: the meaning of "la jarama" is: there is no prevention or hindrance concerning that they [will lose]. It was also said: the meaning is: no cutter cuts, so the subject was omitted when its use became frequent. "Al-jarm" means cutting; one says "jarama al-nakhl" and "ijtaramahu," meaning he cut it off, so he is "jarim"; a people are "wa-jarm" and "jurram"; and this is the time of "al-jaraam" and "al-jiraam" (the time of cutting/harvesting). "Jaramtu sawfa al-shah" means I sheared it, and "jaramtu minhu" means I took from it, like "jalamtu al-shay' jalman," meaning I cut it. "Jalamtu al-jazura ajlimuha jalman" means when I took the meat that was on its bones. "Akhadtu al-shay'a bi-jilmatihi" (with its whole body; the lam is unvocalized) means when I took it entirely, and "jumlat al-jazuri" (with the vowel on the jim) means its meat entirely. This is what al-Jawhari said.

Al-Nahhas said: al-Kisa'i claimed that there are four dialects for it: "la jarama," "la 'an dha jarama," "la anna dha jarama." He said: some people of Fazara say "la jara annahum" without the mim. Al-Farra' related two other dialects for it. He said: the Banu 'Amir say "la dha jarama," and some of the Arabs say "la jurma" with a dammah on the jim.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 23:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾. "Those who" (alladhina) is the subject (ism) of "indeed" (inna), and "believed" (amanu) is the relative clause (silah), meaning: they affirmed the truth (saddaqu).

(And did righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord) is a conjunction (atf) upon the relative clause. Ibn 'Abbas said: "akhbatu" means they turned in repentance (anabu). Mujahid said: they obeyed (ata'u). Qatadah said: they were humble and submissive (khasha'u wa-khada'u). Muqatil said: they were sincere (akhlasu). Al-Hasan said: al-ikhbat is humility (khushu') arising from a steady fear that is fixed in the heart. The original meaning of al-ikhbat is evenness (istiwa'), from al-khabt, which is wide, level ground. So al-ikhbat is humility and tranquility (itmi'nan), or turning in repentance (inabah) to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, continued in that state with evenness. ﴿Before their Lord﴾: al-Farra' said: "ila rabbihim" and "li-rabbihim" have the same meaning, though the meaning may also be: they directed their humbling toward their Lord.

﴿Those﴾ ("ula'ika") is the predicate (khabar) of "indeed" (inna).

The statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿The likeness of the two groups﴾, is a beginning (*ibtida'*, the nominal subject), and the predicate (*khabar*) is (*ka-al-a'ma*, "like the blind man") and what follows it. Al-Akhfash said: that is, "like the likeness of the blind man." Al-Nahhas said: the estimated meaning is that the likeness of the group of the disbelievers is like the blind [*ka-al-a'ma*] and the deaf, and the likeness of the group of the believers is like the hearing and the seeing. For this reason He said, ﴿Are the two equal?﴾, returning the pronoun to "the two groups," which are two. This meaning has been related from Qatadah and others. Al-Dahhak said: the blind and the deaf are an example for the disbeliever, and the hearing and the seeing are an example for the believer. It has also been said: the meaning is, "Are the blind and the seeing equal, and are the deaf and the hearing equal?"

﴿As an example﴾ (*mathalan*) is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*, the accusative of specification that clarifies a preceding general sense) [[In the manuscripts ʿ and Y: "as an explanation" (*ʿalā al-tafsīr*).]].

﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ concerns the two attributes, and [it means] "and reflect."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 25–26:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾. He, glorified is He, mentioned the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, to the Prophet (ﷺ) as an admonition to him to persevere steadfastly in bearing the harm of the disbelievers, until Allah suffices him against their affair.

(Inni) meaning: he said, "Inni" (indeed I), because in "sending" there is the sense of "saying." Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "Anni" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: We sent him with "that I am to you a clear warner." He did not say "innahu" (indeed he) because the address shifted from the third-person absence (ghayba) to the direct address of Noah to his people [[Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "In this there is room for examination; it is rather a quoted address to his people, and this is not truly a shift from absence to direct address. Had the wording been 'that I warn them' or the like, that would be valid."]], as in His saying: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], then He said: "So take them with strength" [[See vol. 7, p. 280.]] [al-A'raf: 145].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾, meaning: abandon the idols so that you do not worship them, and obey Allah alone. As for one who reads "Inni" with a kasra, he makes it a parenthetical insertion in the speech, and the meaning is: We sent him with "that you not worship [none but Allah]."

(Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day.)
