**(He will send the sky upon you in abundance.)** It is apocopated (*jazm*) because it is a response, and it carries the sense of a conditional. **"(upon you in abundance)"** is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*), and it carries the sense of profusion, meaning: He will send the sky with rain, successive, one part following another. The Arabs drop the *ha'* in *mif'al* when used as a relative adjective, and *mif'al* mostly comes from *af'ala*, but here it has come from *fa'ala*, because it is from "the sky poured forth (*darrat*) and pours (*tadirru* and *tadurru*), so it is *midrar*." The people of Hud, that is 'Ad, were people of gardens, crops, and cultivation, and their dwellings were the sands between al-Sham and Yemen, as was mentioned in *al-A'raf* [[See vol. 7, p. 236.]].

**(And He will add to your strength upon your strength.)** It is coordinated with "yursil" (He will send).

**(Strength upon your strength.)** Mujahid said: "Might upon your might." al-Dahhak said: "Fertility upon your fertility." Ali ibn Isa said: "Honour upon your honour." Ikrimah said: "Children upon your children." It was also said: Allah withheld rain from them and made the wombs barren for three years, so no child was born to them. Hud said to them: "If you believe, Allah will revive your lands, and grant you wealth and children; that is the strength." al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "He will add to you strength in blessings."

**(And do not turn away as criminals.)** That is: do not turn away from what I call you to, and persist in disbelief.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof."﴾** That is: a clear argument.

**(We are not going to abandon our gods on your word, and we are not believers in you.)** This is their insistence upon disbelief.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil.﴾** That is: has afflicted you.

**(Some of our gods.)** That is: our idols.

**(With evil.)** That is: with madness, because of your reviling them, according to Ibn Abbas and others. It is said: *'arahu al-amr* and *i'taraha* when a matter befalls him. From this is His saying: ﴿And feed the contented and the beggar﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 47.]] [al-Hajj: 36].

**(He said: "I call Allah to witness.")** That is: against myself.

**(And bear witness.)** That is: and I call you to witness, not because they were people of testimony, but it is an end to affirmation, that is, so that you may know **(that I am free of what)** that is, of worshipping the idols that you worship.

**(So scheme against me all together.)** That is: you and your idols, in your enmity and harm toward me.

**(Then give me no respite.)** That is: do not delay me. This statement, despite the multitude of enemies, indicates complete confidence in the victory of Allah, Exalted is He. It is among the signs of prophethood that the messenger alone should say to his people: "So scheme against me all together." Likewise the Prophet ﷺ said to Quraysh. And Nuh ﷺ said: ﴿So resolve upon your affair and your partners﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 362.]] [Yunus: 71], and so on.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord.﴾** That is: I am content with His judgment, and I trust in His support.

**(There is no creature)** That is: no soul that crawls upon the earth, and it is in the nominative position as a *mubtada'* (subject).

**(But He holds its forelock.)** That is: He directs it as He wills, and restrains it from what He wills, meaning: you cannot reach my harm. Everything that has a spirit is called *dabb* and *dabbah*, and the *ha'* is for emphasis. al-Farra' said: its owner, and the one capable over it. al-Qutabi said: its subduer, because whoever you take by the forelock, you have subdued. al-Dahhak said: He gives it life and then makes it die, and the meanings are close. The forelock is the hair at the front of the head. And *nasawtu al-rajul ansuhu naswan* means I pulled his forelock. Ibn Jurayj said: He specified the forelock only because the Arabs use this when they describe a person as humbled and submissive, and they say: "The forelock of so-and-so is only in the hand of so-and-so," meaning: he is obedient to him and he directs him as he wishes. And when they captured a prisoner and wished to release him as a favour, they would cut his forelock so that he would be known by that, as a mark of pride over him. So He addressed them with what they recognised in their speech.

al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said in *Nawadir al-Usul*, concerning His saying: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾: its meaning, in our view, is that Allah, Exalted is He, decreed the measures of the deeds of the servants, then looked at them, then created His creatures. His sight penetrated all that they would do before He created them. When He created them, He placed the light of that gaze in their forelocks. That light holds their forelocks, directing them toward their deeds that were decreed for them on the Day of Decrees. Allah created the decrees fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. This was related by Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Allah decreed the decrees fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth." For this reason the messengers became strong and became among the *Ulu al-'Azm* (the steadfast messengers), because they perceived the light of the forelocks, and were certain that all of His creation is led by those lights toward the deeds upon which His gaze penetrated. So the one with the greatest share of this perception is the strongest in resolve. For this reason Hud, the Prophet ﷺ, was strengthened, so that he said: "So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite. Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock." The forelock is so named because the deeds have been made explicit (*nussat*) and have emerged from the unseen of the unseen, and so have become explicit in the decrees, the sight of the Creator penetrating with power into all the movements of creation. Then the movements of every living creature that crawls upon the earth were placed on its forehead between its eyes, so that place on it is called the forelock (*nasiyah*), because it makes explicit (*tanuss*) the movements of the servants by what has been decreed. So the forelock is taken from the explicit movements upon which Allah, Exalted is He, looked before He created them. He described the forelock of Abu Jahl, saying: ﴿A lying, sinning forelock﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 124.]] [al-'Alaq: 16]. It informs that the forelocks in it are lying and sinning. According to what they interpreted, it would be impossible for the forelock to be attributed to lying and sinning. [And Allah knows best.]

**(Indeed, my Lord is upon a straight path.)** al-Nahhas said: *al-sirat* in the language is the clear method. The meaning is that Allah, His praise be exalted, although He is capable of everything, does not seize them except with truth. It was also said: its meaning is that there is no defect in His management, and no inconsistency in His creation, glory be to Him.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away…﴾** It is in a position of apocopation (*jazm*), therefore the *nun* is dropped from it; the original is *tatawallaw*, and the *ta'* is dropped because two *ta's* came together.

**(Then I have conveyed to you what I was sent with to you.)** In the sense of: I have made clear to you.

**(And my Lord will replace you with another people.)** That is: He will destroy you and create one who is more obedient to Him than you, who will affirm His oneness and worship Him. "Wa yastakhlifu" is cut off from what precedes it, and therefore it is in the nominative; or it is coordinated with what must follow the *fa'* in His saying: "Then I have conveyed to you." It is narrated from Hafs from Asim: "wa yastakhlif" with apocopation, taking it as a reference to the position of the *fa'* and what follows it, like: ﴿And He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-A'raf: 186] [the reading with *ba'* and sukun on the *ra'* is a reading; see vol. 7, p. 334].

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will not harm Him at all.﴾** That is: by your turning away and your aversion.

**(Indeed, my Lord is over all things a Guardian.)** That is: a Preserver of all things. "'Ala" here has the meaning of "li" (for), so He preserves me from your reaching me with harm.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Our command came…﴾** That is: Our punishment, with the destruction of 'Ad.

**(We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us.)** Because no one is saved except by the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, even if he has good deeds. In the Sahih of Muslim and al-Bukhari and others, from the Prophet ﷺ: "No one among you will be saved by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." It was also said: the meaning of "by mercy from Us" is that We made clear to them the guidance, which is itself a mercy. They were four thousand. It was also said: three thousand.

**(And We saved them from a severe punishment.)** That is: the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: it is the barren wind, as Allah mentioned in *al-Dhariyat* [[See vol. 17, p. 50.]] and elsewhere, and it will come. al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: the punishment with which the Prophet threatens his community, when it arrives, Allah saves the Prophet and the believers with him from it. Yes! It is not far-fetched that Allah tests a prophet and his people, and afflicts them with a calamity that covers them, and that this is a punishment for the disbelievers and a purification for the believers, if it is not what the Prophet threatened them with.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that was 'Ad…﴾** "'Ad" is a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). al-Kisa'i related that among the Arabs there are some who do not inflect "'Ad," making it the name of a tribe.

**(They denied the signs of their Lord.)** That is: they denied the miracles and rejected them.

**(And disobeyed His messengers.)** He means Hud alone, because He did not send any other messenger to them. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 127.]] [al-Mu'minun: 51], meaning the Prophet ﷺ alone, because there was no other messenger in his time. Here the plural is used because whoever denies one messenger has disbelieved in all the messengers. It was also said: they disobeyed Hud and the messengers before him, and they were such that if a thousand messengers had been sent to them, they would have denied all of them.

**(And they followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.)** That is: their lowly ones followed their leaders. *Al-jabbar* is the arrogant one. *Al-'anid* is the transgressor who does not accept the truth and does not submit to it [in one copy: "yanqad" (submit)]. Abu Ubayd said: *al-'anid*, *al-'anud*, *al-'ani*d, and *al-mu'anid* are the one who opposes with dissent, and from this the vein that bursts with blood is called *'anid*. The rajaz poet said:

*"Indeed I am old, I cannot bear the 'unad..."*
[The verse's first half: "When you travel, make me the middle…"]

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾** That is: it was attached to them.

**(And on the Day of Resurrection.)** That is: and on the Day of Resurrection they will be followed by the like of that. So the pause is at His saying: "And on the Day of Resurrection."

**(Unquestionably, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord.)** al-Farra' said: that is, they disbelieved the blessing of their Lord. He said: it is said *kafartuhu* and *kafartu bihi*, like *shakartuhu* and *shakartu lahu*.

**(Unquestionably, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud!)** That is: may they never cease to be far from the mercy of Allah. *Al-bu'd* is destruction, and *al-bu'd* is distance from good. It is said: *ba'uda yab'udu bu'dan* when he delayed and distanced himself, and *ba'ida yab'adu ba'adan* when he perished. He said:

*"Let not my people be far, those who are the poison of enemies and the calamity of the misfortunes..."* [[The verse's explanation was given earlier in vol. 6, p. 14.]]

And al-Nabigha said:

*"So do not let them be far, for death is a watering place, and every man will one day be a passing shade."*

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾**, meaning: and We sent. It is coordinated with "We sent Nuh." It was said that he is called their brother because he was one of them, since the tribe gathered them, as you say, "O brother of Tamim." It was also said that he is called their brother because he is a son of Adam as they are sons of Adam. This was discussed earlier in *al-A'raf* [[See vol. 7, p. 235 onward.]]. They were worshippers of idols. It was said: they are two 'Ads, the first 'Ad and the other 'Ad. Those are the first, and as for the other, it is Shaddad and Luqman, who are mentioned in His saying: ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 44.]] [al-Fajr: 7]. 'Ad was the name of a man, then it continued to be applied to the people who traced their descent to him.

**(You are nothing but fabricators.)** That is: in your taking a god other than Him, you are none but liars against Him, Majestic and Mighty.

**(He will send the sky upon you in abundance.)** It is apocopated (*jazm*) because it is a response, and it carries the sense of a conditional. **"(upon you in abundance)"** is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*), and it carries the sense of profusion, meaning: He will send the sky with rain, successive, one part following another. The Arabs drop the *ha'* in *mif'al* when used as a relative adjective, and *mif'al* mostly comes from *af'ala*, but here it has come from *fa'ala*, because it is from "the sky poured forth (*darrat*) and pours (*tadirru* and *tadurru*), so it is *midrar*." The people of Hud, that is 'Ad, were people of gardens, crops, and cultivation, and their dwellings were the sands between al-Sham and Yemen, as was mentioned in *al-A'raf* [[See vol. 7, p. 236.]].

**(And He will add to your strength upon your strength.)** It is coordinated with "yursil" (He will send).

**(Strength upon your strength.)** Mujahid said: "Might upon your might." al-Dahhak said: "Fertility upon your fertility." Ali ibn Isa said: "Honour upon your honour." Ikrimah said: "Children upon your children." It was also said: Allah withheld rain from them and made the wombs barren for three years, so no child was born to them. Hud said to them: "If you believe, Allah will revive your lands, and grant you wealth and children; that is the strength." al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "He will add to you strength in blessings."

**(And do not turn away as criminals.)** That is: do not turn away from what I call you to, and persist in disbelief.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof."﴾** That is: a clear argument.

**(We are not going to abandon our gods on your word, and we are not believers in you.)** This is their insistence upon disbelief.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil.﴾** That is: has afflicted you.

**(Some of our gods.)** That is: our idols.

**(With evil.)** That is: with madness, because of your reviling them, according to Ibn Abbas and others. It is said: *'arahu al-amr* and *i'taraha* when a matter befalls him. From this is His saying: ﴿And feed the contented and the beggar﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 47.]] [al-Hajj: 36].

**(He said: "I call Allah to witness.")** That is: against myself.

**(And bear witness.)** That is: and I call you to witness, not because they were people of testimony, but it is an end to affirmation, that is, so that you may know **(that I am free of what)** that is, of worshipping the idols that you worship.

**(So scheme against me all together.)** That is: you and your idols, in your enmity and harm toward me.

**(Then give me no respite.)** That is: do not delay me. This statement, despite the multitude of enemies, indicates complete confidence in the victory of Allah, Exalted is He. It is among the signs of prophethood that the messenger alone should say to his people: "So scheme against me all together." Likewise the Prophet ﷺ said to Quraysh. And Nuh ﷺ said: ﴿So resolve upon your affair and your partners﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 362.]] [Yunus: 71], and so on.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord.﴾** That is: I am content with His judgment, and I trust in His support.

**(There is no creature)** That is: no soul that crawls upon the earth, and it is in the nominative position as a *mubtada'* (subject).

**(But He holds its forelock.)** That is: He directs it as He wills, and restrains it from what He wills, meaning: you cannot reach my harm. Everything that has a spirit is called *dabb* and *dabbah*, and the *ha'* is for emphasis. al-Farra' said: its owner, and the one capable over it. al-Qutabi said: its subduer, because whoever you take by the forelock, you have subdued. al-Dahhak said: He gives it life and then makes it die, and the meanings are close. The forelock is the hair at the front of the head. And *nasawtu al-rajul ansuhu naswan* means I pulled his forelock. Ibn Jurayj said: He specified the forelock only because the Arabs use this when they describe a person as humbled and submissive, and they say: "The forelock of so-and-so is only in the hand of so-and-so," meaning: he is obedient to him and he directs him as he wishes. And when they captured a prisoner and wished to release him as a favour, they would cut his forelock so that he would be known by that, as a mark of pride over him. So He addressed them with what they recognised in their speech.

al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said in *Nawadir al-Usul*, concerning His saying: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾: its meaning, in our view, is that Allah, Exalted is He, decreed the measures of the deeds of the servants, then looked at them, then created His creatures. His sight penetrated all that they would do before He created them. When He created them, He placed the light of that gaze in their forelocks. That light holds their forelocks, directing them toward their deeds that were decreed for them on the Day of Decrees. Allah created the decrees fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. This was related by Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Allah decreed the decrees fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth." For this reason the messengers became strong and became among the *Ulu al-'Azm* (the steadfast messengers), because they perceived the light of the forelocks, and were certain that all of His creation is led by those lights toward the deeds upon which His gaze penetrated. So the one with the greatest share of this perception is the strongest in resolve. For this reason Hud, the Prophet ﷺ, was strengthened, so that he said: "So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite. Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock." The forelock is so named because the deeds have been made explicit (*nussat*) and have emerged from the unseen of the unseen, and so have become explicit in the decrees, the sight of the Creator penetrating with power into all the movements of creation. Then the movements of every living creature that crawls upon the earth were placed on its forehead between its eyes, so that place on it is called the forelock (*nasiyah*), because it makes explicit (*tanuss*) the movements of the servants by what has been decreed. So the forelock is taken from the explicit movements upon which Allah, Exalted is He, looked before He created them. He described the forelock of Abu Jahl, saying: ﴿A lying, sinning forelock﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 124.]] [al-'Alaq: 16]. It informs that the forelocks in it are lying and sinning. According to what they interpreted, it would be impossible for the forelock to be attributed to lying and sinning. [And Allah knows best.]

**(Indeed, my Lord is upon a straight path.)** al-Nahhas said: *al-sirat* in the language is the clear method. The meaning is that Allah, His praise be exalted, although He is capable of everything, does not seize them except with truth. It was also said: its meaning is that there is no defect in His management, and no inconsistency in His creation, glory be to Him.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away…﴾** It is in a position of apocopation (*jazm*), therefore the *nun* is dropped from it; the original is *tatawallaw*, and the *ta'* is dropped because two *ta's* came together.

**(Then I have conveyed to you what I was sent with to you.)** In the sense of: I have made clear to you.

**(And my Lord will replace you with another people.)** That is: He will destroy you and create one who is more obedient to Him than you, who will affirm His oneness and worship Him. "Wa yastakhlifu" is cut off from what precedes it, and therefore it is in the nominative; or it is coordinated with what must follow the *fa'* in His saying: "Then I have conveyed to you." It is narrated from Hafs from Asim: "wa yastakhlif" with apocopation, taking it as a reference to the position of the *fa'* and what follows it, like: ﴿And He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-A'raf: 186] [the reading with *ba'* and sukun on the *ra'* is a reading; see vol. 7, p. 334].

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will not harm Him at all.﴾** That is: by your turning away and your aversion.

**(Indeed, my Lord is over all things a Guardian.)** That is: a Preserver of all things. "'Ala" here has the meaning of "li" (for), so He preserves me from your reaching me with harm.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Our command came…﴾** That is: Our punishment, with the destruction of 'Ad.

**(We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us.)** Because no one is saved except by the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, even if he has good deeds. In the Sahih of Muslim and al-Bukhari and others, from the Prophet ﷺ: "No one among you will be saved by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." It was also said: the meaning of "by mercy from Us" is that We made clear to them the guidance, which is itself a mercy. They were four thousand. It was also said: three thousand.

**(And We saved them from a severe punishment.)** That is: the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: it is the barren wind, as Allah mentioned in *al-Dhariyat* [[See vol. 17, p. 50.]] and elsewhere, and it will come. al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: the punishment with which the Prophet threatens his community, when it arrives, Allah saves the Prophet and the believers with him from it. Yes! It is not far-fetched that Allah tests a prophet and his people, and afflicts them with a calamity that covers them, and that this is a punishment for the disbelievers and a purification for the believers, if it is not what the Prophet threatened them with.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that was 'Ad…﴾** "'Ad" is a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). al-Kisa'i related that among the Arabs there are some who do not inflect "'Ad," making it the name of a tribe.

**(They denied the signs of their Lord.)** That is: they denied the miracles and rejected them.

**(And disobeyed His messengers.)** He means Hud alone, because He did not send any other messenger to them. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 127.]] [al-Mu'minun: 51], meaning the Prophet ﷺ alone, because there was no other messenger in his time. Here the plural is used because whoever denies one messenger has disbelieved in all the messengers. It was also said: they disobeyed Hud and the messengers before him, and they were such that if a thousand messengers had been sent to them, they would have denied all of them.

**(And they followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.)** That is: their lowly ones followed their leaders. *Al-jabbar* is the arrogant one. *Al-'anid* is the transgressor who does not accept the truth and does not submit to it [in one copy: "yanqad" (submit)]. Abu Ubayd said: *al-'anid*, *al-'anud*, *al-'ani*d, and *al-mu'anid* are the one who opposes with dissent, and from this the vein that bursts with blood is called *'anid*. The rajaz poet said:

*"Indeed I am old, I cannot bear the 'unad..."*
[The verse's first half: "When you travel, make me the middle…"]

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾** That is: it was attached to them.

**(And on the Day of Resurrection.)** That is: and on the Day of Resurrection they will be followed by the like of that. So the pause is at His saying: "And on the Day of Resurrection."

**(Unquestionably, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord.)** al-Farra' said: that is, they disbelieved the blessing of their Lord. He said: it is said *kafartuhu* and *kafartu bihi*, like *shakartuhu* and *shakartu lahu*.

**(Unquestionably, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud!)** That is: may they never cease to be far from the mercy of Allah. *Al-bu'd* is destruction, and *al-bu'd* is distance from good. It is said: *ba'uda yab'udu bu'dan* when he delayed and distanced himself, and *ba'ida yab'adu ba'adan* when he perished. He said:

*"Let not my people be far, those who are the poison of enemies and the calamity of the misfortunes..."* [[The verse's explanation was given earlier in vol. 6, p. 14.]]

And al-Nabigha said:

*"So do not let them be far, for death is a watering place, and every man will one day be a passing shade."*

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾**, meaning: and We sent. It is coordinated with "We sent Nuh." It was said that he is called their brother because he was one of them, since the tribe gathered them, as you say, "O brother of Tamim." It was also said that he is called their brother because he is a son of Adam as they are sons of Adam. This was discussed earlier in *al-A'raf* [[See vol. 7, p. 235 onward.]]. They were worshippers of idols. It was said: they are two 'Ads, the first 'Ad and the other 'Ad. Those are the first, and as for the other, it is Shaddad and Luqman, who are mentioned in His saying: ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 44.]] [al-Fajr: 7]. 'Ad was the name of a man, then it continued to be applied to the people who traced their descent to him.

Five issues arise from this verse.

The first concerns the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And to Thamud﴾, meaning: We sent to Thamud ﴿their brother﴾, meaning by lineage, ﴿Salih﴾.

Yahya ibn Wathhab recited "wa-ila Thamudin" with tanwin (nunation) throughout the Qur'an, and this is also related from al-Hasan. The other reciters differed on it: they left it unexpanded (without tanwin) in one place and expanded it in another. Abu 'Ubayda claimed that, were it not for its conflict with the written consonantal text (al-sawad), the proper reading would be to omit tanwin, since the word is predominantly feminine. Al-Nahhas said: what Abu 'Ubayda, may Allah have mercy on him, said, that the word is predominantly feminine, is a rejected statement. Thamud is described as a tribe (hayy) and as a qabila (tribe), and the predominant sense is not that of a qabila. Rather, the matter is the opposite of what he said, according to Sibawayh. According to Sibawayh, the preferred form for names not preceded by "banu fulan" (sons of so-and-so) is to take tanwin, as with Quraysh, Thaqif and similar names, and Thamud is likewise. The reason is that since the masculine is the basic form, and the word occurs in both masculine and feminine usage, the lighter, basic form takes precedence. The feminine usage is also good, eloquent and fine. Sibawayh recited, as evidence for the feminine:

*"The Walid overcame the generous through his generosity, and Quraysh's difficulties were sufficient for its chief."*

(The verse is by 'Adi ibn al-Raqa', praising al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik. The evidence lies in the omission of tanwin on "Quraysh", treating it according to the sense of "tribe". Tanwin is more common and better known for it, since they intended it in the sense of a clan, and that sense predominated over it.)

The second issue concerns the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾. This has already been discussed.

﴿He brought you into being from the earth﴾, meaning He originated your creation from the earth. This is because Adam was created from the earth, as has been mentioned in al-Baqarah and al-An'am, and they are from him. It has also been said: "He brought you into being in the earth." The "ha'" of "ghayruhu" may not be assimilated into the "ha'" of "huwa" except according to the dialect of those who drop the waw in continuous recitation.

﴿And He made you settle it﴾, meaning He made you its inhabitants and dwellers. Mujahid said: the meaning of "istamarakum" is "a'marakum", from the saying: "So-and-so granted so-and-so his house, and it is his for his lifetime (umra)." Qatadah said: He made you dwell in it. On these two views, "istaf'ala" carries the sense of "af'ala", like "istajaba" in the sense of "ajaba". Al-Dahhak said: He lengthened your lives, and their lives ranged from three hundred to a thousand years. Ibn 'Abbas said: He let you live in it. Zayd ibn Aslam said: He commanded you to develop what you need in it, by building dwellings and planting trees. It has also been said: the meaning is that He inspired you to develop it through tillage, planting, digging rivers and other means.

The third issue: Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some Shafi'i scholars said: "al-istimar" means seeking development (al-'imarah), and the unrestricted demand from God is obligatory. The judge Abu Bakr said: The form "istaf'ala" comes in the Arabic language with several meanings. Among them: "istaf'ala" in the sense of seeking the act, as in "istahmaltuhu", meaning I asked him for a load. And in the sense of believing, as in the saying "istashhaltu hadha al-amr", meaning I believed this matter to be easy, or found it easy, and "ista'zamtuhu", meaning I believed it to be great or found it great. From this also comes "istaf'altu" in the sense of "asabtu", as in "istajadtuhu", meaning I found it good. Among its meanings is also the sense of "fa'ala", as in "qarra fi al-makan" and "istaqarra". And the words of God "yastahziu" (they mock) and "yastaskhiruna" (they scoff) are of this kind. So the words of God, "istamarakum fiha" (He made you settle it), mean "khalaqakum li-'imaratiha" (He created you for its development). There is no sense here of finding something good or easy, that is, of finding it good and easy, and this is impossible for the Creator. So it reverts to the meaning that He created, since that is the purpose, and a thing may be designated by its purpose metaphorically. It is not correct to say that He sought from God its development, since this expression is not permitted with respect to Him. But it is correct to say that He requested its development, for He used the form "istaf'ala", which means requesting an act by speech from one who is lower, when it is a command, and seeking an act when it comes from a lower party to a higher one [out of desire]. [The addition is from Ibn al-'Arabi.]

I say: The form "istaf'ala" in the sense of "af'ala" is not mentioned, as in the words "istawqada" in the sense of "awqada" (to kindle), and I have already mentioned it.

The fourth issue: There is in this verse evidence for habitation (iskan) and for the 'umra (the grant of use for life). The discussion of habitation (sukna) and ruqba (grant of use until one of the parties dies) has already passed in al-Baqarah. As for 'umra, the scholars differed on it in three views.

The first: It is a grant of ownership of the usufruct of the property for the lifetime of the grantee. If the grantee does not specify heirs and dies, the property returns to the one who gave it or to his heirs. This is the view of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Yazid ibn Qusayt and al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and it is the well-known position of Malik and one of al-Shafi'i's views. The proof for this view has already been given in al-Baqarah.

The second: It is the transfer of ownership of the property and its usufruct, and it is an irrevocable gift (hiba mabtula, meaning one cut off and not returning to the donor; from batala, to sever and separate). This is the view of Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and their companions, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn Shubrumah and Abu 'Ubayd. They said: Whoever grants a man something for his lifetime, it is his for his life, and after his death it belongs to his heirs, because he has come to own its substance. The condition of the giver that it be for life and for the grantee's lifetime is void, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The 'umra is permitted," and "the 'umra belongs to the one to whom it is given."

The third: If he says "for your lifetime" and does not mention the descendants, it is like the first view. If he says "for you and your descendants," it is like the second view. This is the view of al-Zuhri, Abu Thawr, Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and Ibn Abi Dhi'b. It has also been related from Malik, and it is the apparent meaning of his statement in the Muwatta' (a collection of Hadith compiled by Malik). The well-known position of Malik and his companions is that it returns to the grantor when the descendants of the grantee die out, if the grantor is alive; otherwise it goes to whoever of his heirs is alive, and the people most entitled to inherit from him. According to Malik, the grantee does not acquire ownership by the wording of 'umra, and likewise in the case of habs (waqf, endowment). If it is endowed for a man and his descendants, it does not return to him. If it is endowed for a specific man for his lifetime, it returns to him. The 'umra is likewise by analogy, and this is the apparent meaning of the Muwatta'.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever grants a man an 'umra for him and his descendants, saying: 'I have given it to you and your descendants,' and no one of you remains alive, it belongs to the one to whom it was given, and it does not return to its owner, because he gave a gift in which inheritance has taken effect." And from him (Jabir) he said: The 'umra which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted is that one says: "It is yours and your descendants'." As for when he says: "It is yours for as long as you live," then it returns to its owner. Ma'mar said: And this was the fatwa of al-Zuhri.

I say: The meaning of the Qur'an accords with the people of the second view, because Allah, the Exalted, said: "And He made you settle it" (istamarakum), in the sense of "a'marakum" (granted you its use). So He granted the righteous man the use of it for the duration of his life through righteous deeds, and after his death through a good remembrance and fine praise. The reverse applies to the wicked man. So the world is a vessel for both, in life and in death. It may be said that good praise takes the place of descendants. In the revelation: "And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations," meaning a good praise. It has also been said that this refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). And He said: "And We made his descendants the survivors." And He said: "And We blessed him and Isaac, and of their descendants are the good-doers and those who wrong themselves clearly."

The fifth issue: The words of God, the Exalted: ﴿So seek His forgiveness﴾, meaning ask Him for forgiveness from worshipping idols.

﴿Then turn to Him in repentance﴾, meaning return to His worship.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive﴾, meaning near in answering those who call upon Him. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, at His words: "Indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 62–68:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this."﴾ That is, we used to hope that you would become a leader among us before this, meaning before your call to prophethood. It was also said: Salih used to criticize their gods and denounce them, and they hoped he would return to their religion. So when he called them to Allah, they said, "Our hope in you has ended."

(Atanhana) is an interrogative whose meaning is denial.

(An na'bud) means "against our worshipping."

(Ma ya'budu aba'una) here "an" is in a position of nasb (accusative) by the removal of the preposition.

(Wa innana lafi shakkin) In Surat Ibrahim it is "wa inna" and the original is "wa innana." Three nuns were considered heavy, so the third was dropped.

(Mimma tad'unana) The address is to Salih. In Surat Ibrahim it is "tad'unana" (see p. 344 of this part), because the address is to the Messengers (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them).

(Ilayhi murib) From "arabtuhu," so "uribuhu" when I do to him an act that causes him suspicion. The Hudhali said:

"Whenever I came to him from his absence... he sniffs at my side and tugs at my garment..." (yabuzzu thawbi: he pulls it toward himself), "as if I had aroused him with suspicion."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself..."﴾ Its meaning has been explained previously in the discussion of Nuh.

(Fa man yansuruni min Allahi in 'asaytuhu) is an interrogative whose meaning is negation: no one can help me against Him if I disobey Him.

(Fa ma tazidunani ghayra takhsir) That is, misguidance and distance from good, as said by al-Farra'.

The loss (takhsir) is for them, not for him ﷺ. It is as if he said: "a loss for you, not for me." It was also said: the meaning is, "You do not increase me, by your argument with the religion of your fathers, except in unawareness of your own loss," on the authority of Ibn Abbas.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah﴾: an inchoative subject and predicate.

(Lakum ayah) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and the governing element is the meaning of pointing or alerting in "hadhihi." It was said "the she-camel of Allah" because He brought it out from a mountain, as they had requested, on condition that they would believe. It was also said: He brought it out from a solid, isolated rock in a region of al-Hijr called al-Kathiba. When the she-camel came out, as they had requested, the Prophet of Allah Salih said to them: "This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you."

(Fa dharuha ta'kul) is a command and its answer. The nun was dropped from "fadharuha" because it is a command. "Wadhara" and "wadhir" are not said except rarely. Grammarians have two opinions on this. Sibawayh said: they dispensed with it by using "taraka" (to leave). Others said: since the waw was heavy, and there was in the language a verb with the same meaning that has no waw, they dropped it. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "ta'kul" in the nominative as a circumstantial clause or a resumed statement.

(Wa la tamassuha) is a jussive in prohibition.

(Bi su') al-Farra' said: "by slaughtering."

(Fa ya'khudhakum) is the answer to the prohibition.

(Adhabun qarib): that is, near to its slaughter.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But they hamstrung her, so he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days."﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: the words ﴿they hamstrung her﴾. Only some of them hamstrung her, but it is attributed to all because it was with the approval of the rest. The discussion of her slaughter has already been given in "al-A'raf," and it will also come again.

(Fa qala tamatta'u) That is, Salih said to them: "Enjoy" the blessings of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, before the punishment.

(Fi darikum) That is, in your land. Had he meant the dwelling, he would have said "fi duurikum." It was also said: each one of you enjoys in his own house and dwelling, like His saying: "He brings you out as a child" (see vol. 12 p. 11 and p. 330 of vol. 15), meaning each one as a child. Enjoyment is expressed by "life," because the dead do not delight in or enjoy anything. She was hamstrung on Wednesday, and they remained on Thursday, Friday and Saturday, and the punishment came to them on Sunday. They remained three days because the young camel cried out three times, as mentioned previously in "al-A'raf." On the first day their faces turned yellow, on the second day they turned red, on the third day they turned black, and they perished on the fourth day, as was mentioned in "al-A'raf."

The second: Our scholars have taken as evidence the postponement of the punishment from the people of Salih for three days, that a traveler who has not resolved to stay four nights shortens the prayer, because the three days are outside the ruling of residence. What the scholars have said on this has been mentioned previously in "al-Nisa'" (vol. 5 p. 357).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾: that is, not a lie. It was also said: not a lie in it.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when Our command came﴾: that is, Our punishment.

(We saved Salih and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us) has already been explained.

(And from the disgrace of that day) That is, and We saved them from the disgrace of that day, meaning from its humiliation and abasement. It was also said the waw is extra, meaning, "We saved them from the disgrace of that day." According to Sibawayh and the people of Basra, it is not permissible for it to be extra; according to the Kufans, it is permissible for it to be extra only with "lamma" and "hatta." Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "yawmi'idhin" with fatha. The rest read it with kasra, as an idafa of "yawm" to "idh." Abu Hatim said: Abu Zayd related to us from Abu 'Amr that he read "wa min khizyi yawmi'idhin," assimilating the ya into the ya and making an idafa, and vowelling the mim in "yawmi'idhin" with kasra. Al-Nahhas said: What the grammarians transmit, like Sibawayh and those close to him, from Abu 'Amr in such a case is ikhfa' (partial assimilation). As for full idgham, it is not permissible, because two sakins would meet, and the zay cannot be vowelled with kasra.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾: that is, on the fourth day they were struck with a cry and died. It is masculine because "al-sayha" and "al-siyah" are the same. It was said: it was the cry of Jibril. It was also said: a cry from the sky containing the sound of every thunderbolt and the sound of everything on earth, so their hearts were torn and they died. Here it says "the cry seized those who did wrong," while in "al-A'raf" it says "the earthquake seized them," and its explanation has already been given there (vol. 7 p. 242). In the tafsir it is related that when they were certain of the punishment, some of them said to others: "Why do we stay here, lest the command come upon us suddenly?" They said: "What shall we do?" So they took their swords, spears and weapons. They were, it is said, twelve thousand tribes, with twelve thousand fighters in each tribe. They stood on the roads and in the passes, claiming they would meet the punishment. Then Allah the Exalted revealed to the angel in charge of the sun that he should punish them with its heat, so he brought it near their heads, their hands were roasted, and their tongues hung out over their chests from thirst. All the animals they had died. The water began to bubble from those springs from its boiling, rising until it reached the sky, and it would not fall upon anything without destroying it because of its intense heat. They remained in this state. Allah revealed to the Angel of Death that he should not take their souls, as a torment for them, until the sun set. Then a cry came upon them and they were destroyed.

(So they were found in their homes, lying prostrate) That is, fallen on their faces, clinging to the dust like birds when they crouch.

(Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!) Its meaning has been previously explained.
