They stood on the roads and in the passes, claiming they would meet the punishment. Then Allah the Exalted revealed to the angel in charge of the sun that he should punish them with its heat, so he brought it near their heads, their hands were roasted, and their tongues hung out over their chests from thirst. All the animals they had died. The water began to bubble from those springs from its boiling, rising until it reached the sky, and it would not fall upon anything without destroying it because of its intense heat. They remained in this state. Allah revealed to the Angel of Death that he should not take their souls, as a torment for them, until the sun set. Then a cry came upon them and they were destroyed.

(So they were found in their homes, lying prostrate) That is, fallen on their faces, clinging to the dust like birds when they crouch.

(Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!) Its meaning has been previously explained.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 62–68:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this."﴾ That is, we used to hope that you would become a leader among us before this, meaning before your call to prophethood. It was also said: Salih used to criticize their gods and denounce them, and they hoped he would return to their religion. So when he called them to Allah, they said, "Our hope in you has ended."

(Atanhana) is an interrogative whose meaning is denial.

(An na'bud) means "against our worshipping."

(Ma ya'budu aba'una) here "an" is in a position of nasb (accusative) by the removal of the preposition.

(Wa innana lafi shakkin) In Surat Ibrahim it is "wa inna" and the original is "wa innana." Three nuns were considered heavy, so the third was dropped.

(Mimma tad'unana) The address is to Salih. In Surat Ibrahim it is "tad'unana" (see p. 344 of this part), because the address is to the Messengers (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them).

(Ilayhi murib) From "arabtuhu," so "uribuhu" when I do to him an act that causes him suspicion. The Hudhali said:

"Whenever I came to him from his absence... he sniffs at my side and tugs at my garment..." (yabuzzu thawbi: he pulls it toward himself), "as if I had aroused him with suspicion."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself..."﴾ Its meaning has been explained previously in the discussion of Nuh.

(Fa man yansuruni min Allahi in 'asaytuhu) is an interrogative whose meaning is negation: no one can help me against Him if I disobey Him.

(Fa ma tazidunani ghayra takhsir) That is, misguidance and distance from good, as said by al-Farra'.

The loss (takhsir) is for them, not for him ﷺ. It is as if he said: "a loss for you, not for me." It was also said: the meaning is, "You do not increase me, by your argument with the religion of your fathers, except in unawareness of your own loss," on the authority of Ibn Abbas.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah﴾: an inchoative subject and predicate.

(Lakum ayah) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and the governing element is the meaning of pointing or alerting in "hadhihi." It was said "the she-camel of Allah" because He brought it out from a mountain, as they had requested, on condition that they would believe. It was also said: He brought it out from a solid, isolated rock in a region of al-Hijr called al-Kathiba. When the she-camel came out, as they had requested, the Prophet of Allah Salih said to them: "This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you."

(Fa dharuha ta'kul) is a command and its answer. The nun was dropped from "fadharuha" because it is a command. "Wadhara" and "wadhir" are not said except rarely. Grammarians have two opinions on this. Sibawayh said: they dispensed with it by using "taraka" (to leave). Others said: since the waw was heavy, and there was in the language a verb with the same meaning that has no waw, they dropped it. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "ta'kul" in the nominative as a circumstantial clause or a resumed statement.

(Wa la tamassuha) is a jussive in prohibition.

(Bi su') al-Farra' said: "by slaughtering."

(Fa ya'khudhakum) is the answer to the prohibition.

(Adhabun qarib): that is, near to its slaughter.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But they hamstrung her, so he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days."﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: the words ﴿they hamstrung her﴾. Only some of them hamstrung her, but it is attributed to all because it was with the approval of the rest. The discussion of her slaughter has already been given in "al-A'raf," and it will also come again.

(Fa qala tamatta'u) That is, Salih said to them: "Enjoy" the blessings of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, before the punishment.

(Fi darikum) That is, in your land. Had he meant the dwelling, he would have said "fi duurikum." It was also said: each one of you enjoys in his own house and dwelling, like His saying: "He brings you out as a child" (see vol. 12 p. 11 and p. 330 of vol. 15), meaning each one as a child. Enjoyment is expressed by "life," because the dead do not delight in or enjoy anything. She was hamstrung on Wednesday, and they remained on Thursday, Friday and Saturday, and the punishment came to them on Sunday. They remained three days because the young camel cried out three times, as mentioned previously in "al-A'raf." On the first day their faces turned yellow, on the second day they turned red, on the third day they turned black, and they perished on the fourth day, as was mentioned in "al-A'raf."

The second: Our scholars have taken as evidence the postponement of the punishment from the people of Salih for three days, that a traveler who has not resolved to stay four nights shortens the prayer, because the three days are outside the ruling of residence. What the scholars have said on this has been mentioned previously in "al-Nisa'" (vol. 5 p. 357).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾: that is, not a lie. It was also said: not a lie in it.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when Our command came﴾: that is, Our punishment.

(We saved Salih and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us) has already been explained.

(And from the disgrace of that day) That is, and We saved them from the disgrace of that day, meaning from its humiliation and abasement. It was also said the waw is extra, meaning, "We saved them from the disgrace of that day." According to Sibawayh and the people of Basra, it is not permissible for it to be extra; according to the Kufans, it is permissible for it to be extra only with "lamma" and "hatta." Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "yawmi'idhin" with fatha. The rest read it with kasra, as an idafa of "yawm" to "idh." Abu Hatim said: Abu Zayd related to us from Abu 'Amr that he read "wa min khizyi yawmi'idhin," assimilating the ya into the ya and making an idafa, and vowelling the mim in "yawmi'idhin" with kasra. Al-Nahhas said: What the grammarians transmit, like Sibawayh and those close to him, from Abu 'Amr in such a case is ikhfa' (partial assimilation). As for full idgham, it is not permissible, because two sakins would meet, and the zay cannot be vowelled with kasra.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾: that is, on the fourth day they were struck with a cry and died. It is masculine because "al-sayha" and "al-siyah" are the same. It was said: it was the cry of Jibril. It was also said: a cry from the sky containing the sound of every thunderbolt and the sound of everything on earth, so their hearts were torn and they died. Here it says "the cry seized those who did wrong," while in "al-A'raf" it says "the earthquake seized them," and its explanation has already been given there (vol. 7 p. 242). In the tafsir it is related that when they were certain of the punishment, some of them said to others: "Why do we stay here, lest the command come upon us suddenly?" They said: "What shall we do?" So they took their swords, spears and weapons. They were, it is said, twelve thousand tribes, with twelve thousand fighters in each tribe. They stood on the roads and in the passes, claiming they would meet the punishment. Then Allah the Exalted revealed to the angel in charge of the sun that he should punish them with its heat, so he brought it near their heads, their hands were roasted, and their tongues hung out over their chests from thirst. All the animals they had died. The water began to bubble from those springs from its boiling, rising until it reached the sky, and it would not fall upon anything without destroying it because of its intense heat. They remained in this state. Allah revealed to the Angel of Death that he should not take their souls, as a torment for them, until the sun set. Then a cry came upon them and they were destroyed.

(So they were found in their homes, lying prostrate) That is, fallen on their faces, clinging to the dust like birds when they crouch.

(Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!) Its meaning has been previously explained.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 69–71 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And certainly Our messengers came to Ibrahim with the good tidings﴾. This is the story of Lut, peace be upon him, who was the nephew of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, being closely related to him by lineage [[i.e., connected to him by kinship.]]. The villages of Lut were in the regions of al-Sham, while Ibrahim was in the lands of Palestine. When Allah sent the angels with the punishment of the people of Lut, they passed by Ibrahim and stayed with him. Everyone who stayed with him was generously hospitable to them, and they had passed by with the good tidings for Ibrahim, so he took them to be guests. They were Jibril, Mika'il and Isra'il, peace be upon them; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Dahhak said they were nine. Al-Suddi said they were eleven angels in the form of handsome youths, of radiant faces and surpassing beauty. "With the good tidings": it was said, with the news of a son. It was said, with the news of the destruction of the people of Lut. It was said, they gave him the good news that they were messengers of Allah, mighty and majestic, and that there was no fear for him.

(They said, "Peace!") It is in the accusative because the verb falls upon it, as you say, "They said good." This is the preference of al-Tabari. As for His saying, "Three will say [they were three]" [[See vol. 10, p. 382.]], "three" is a noun, not a [speech] [[From ʿ.]] that is said. If both were in the nominative or both in the accusative, "They said, 'Peace,' he said, 'Peace'" would be permissible in Arabic. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). It was said: "They said, 'Peace'" means they opened the conversation with a correct word, as He said: "And when the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'" [[See vol. 13, p. 67.]], meaning, "Correct." So "peace" is the meaning of their words, not their wording. Ibn al-'Arabi said this and preferred it. He said: Do you not see that when Allah wished to mention the wording, He said it exactly, reporting about the angels: "Peace be upon you, for what you have endured patiently" [[See p. 312 of this volume.]] and "Peace be upon you, you are good" [[See vol. 15, p. 284 onward.]]. It was also said that they prayed for him, and the meaning is "may you be safe with a safety."

(He said, "Peace.") In its nominative form there are two possibilities. The first: by supposing an omitted subject, meaning "he is peace," or "my matter is peace." The second: it means "Peace be upon you," if it is taken as a greeting, with the predicate omitted. "Peace" was permitted as an indefinite noun because it is used so frequently, so the alif and lam were dropped, as they are dropped from "lahumma" in your saying "allahumma." It is also read "silm." Al-Farra' said: "al-silm" and "al-salam" have the same meaning, like "al-hil" and "al-halal."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But he did not delay to bring a roasted calf﴾. In this there are fourteen issues [[So it stands in the original; the issues mentioned also relate to verses 70 and 71, not to this verse alone.]]:

The first: His saying, "fa-ma labitha an ja'" ("he did not delay to come"). "An" here means "until." This is said by the greater grammarians, related by Ibn al-'Arabi. The sense is: "he did not delay until he came." It was also said: "an" is in the position of the accusative after the removal of the preposition, the sense being "he did not delay from his coming," that is, he was not slow in bringing a calf; when the preposition is removed, "an" remains in the accusative position. In "labitha" there is a pronoun referring to Ibrahim. And "salaman" is negating, said Sibawayh. Al-Farra' said: "fa-ma labitha majiuhu," meaning "his coming was not delayed," so "an" is in the nominative position, and there is no pronoun in "labitha," and "salaman" is negating. It is also permissible for "salaman" to mean "the one who," with a pronoun for Ibrahim in "labitha," and "an ja'" as the predicate of "salaman," meaning: what Ibrahim delayed was his bringing of a roasted calf. "Haneedh" means roasted. It was said it is roasted by the heat of stones without the fire touching it. One says "hanadhtu al-shah uhnidhuha hanadhan," meaning "I roasted it," and I placed heated stones above it so they would cook it, and so it is haneedh. "Hanadhtu al-faras uhnidhuhu hanadhan" means you make the horse run a course or two and then spread a blanket over it in the sun so that it sweats; it is then mahnudh and haneedh. If it does not sweat, it is said "kaba." "Hanadh" is also a place near Madina [[And Haneedh is also a place near Makka.]]. It was said: al-haneedh is the skinned one. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: haneedh is well-cooked. "Haneedh" has the meaning of "mahnudh." He brought a calf because cattle were the greater part of his wealth.

The second: In this verse, part of the etiquette of the guest is that the host hastens his hospitality, offering what is available and easy at once, then following it with other things if he has the means, without burdening himself with what would harm him. Hospitality is among the noble qualities, among the etiquettes of Islam, and among the character of the prophets and the righteous. Ibrahim was the first to host guests, as mentioned in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 98.]]. It is not obligatory according to the general body of scholars, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Hospitality is three days, and its generous gift [jaizah] is one day and night; whatever is beyond that is charity." "Jaizah" is the gift and the kindness whose basis is recommended. The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour; and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest." Honouring the neighbour is not obligatory by consensus, so hospitality is similar to it. And Allah knows best. Al-Layth held that it is obligatory, relying on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The night of the guest is a right," among other hadiths. What we have pointed to is sufficient, and Allah is the One who grants success in guidance. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some people said that the obligation of hospitality was in the early period of Islam and was then abrogated (naskh), but this is weak, for the obligation was never established, and no abrogating text came. He mentioned the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, related by the imams, in which: "We asked them for hospitality, but they refused to host us, so the chief of that tribe was stung..." the hadith. He said: This shows clearly that if hospitality were a right, the Prophet ﷺ would have rebuked the people who refused, and would have made it clear to them.

The third: The scholars differed about to whom it is addressed. Al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hakam held that it is addressed to the people of towns and of the desert. Malik said: there is no hospitality obligation on the people of towns. Sahnun said: hospitality is only upon the people of villages; as for towns, the inn (funduq) is where the traveller stays [Sahib al-'Ayn and others related both dialects [[From w; consider this.]]]. They argued from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, who said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hospitality is for the people of the wabar [tents] and not for the people of the madar [towns]." This hadith is not authentic; Ibrahim, the nephew of 'Abd al-Razzaq, is a discarded narrator, accused of lying, and this is among what he alone related, and he was accused of fabricating it, as said by Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Hospitality is in reality a collective obligation (fard kifayah). Some people said it is obligatory in villages where there is no food or shelter, unlike cities, which are full of lodging and provisions. There is no doubt that the guest is honoured and hospitality is a mark of honour; if he is a stranger, it is an obligation.

The fourth: Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some of our scholars said: Ibrahim's hospitality was meagre, and so the Beloved thanked the Beloved for it. This is a judgment by conjecture where certainty is required, and by analogy where transmission is required. From where was it known that it was meagre?! Indeed, the exegetes have related that the angels were three, Jibril, Mika'il and Isra'il, peace be upon them, and a calf for three is large. So how is this interpretation of the Book of Allah by opinion?! By the trust of Allah, this is the blameworthy interpretation, so avoid it, for you know it.

The fifth: The Sunnah is that when food is brought to a guest, the one who brought it should hasten to eat, for the honour of the guest is quick service, and the honour of the host is prompt acceptance. When they withheld their hands, Ibrahim disliked it, because they had departed from custom and opposed the Sunnah, and he feared that behind them was some harm they intended. It is related that they were pricking with arrows (qidah) [[qidah (plural qidah): an arrow before it is fitted with its head and feathers.]] that were in their hands into the meat, and their hands did not reach the meat. When he saw that from them...

(He disliked them and conceived fear of them.) That is, he concealed it. It was said: he perceived. "Al-wujus" means entering. The poet said:
"The courier came with a paper he hurried with, so the heart conceived fear of its paper."
"Khifatan" means fear, that is, dread. When they saw that the guest did not eat, they thought evil of him, so the angels said: ﴿Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut﴾.

The sixth: Among the etiquettes of food is that the host may look at his guest to see whether he eats or not, and this should be done with glancing and stealth, not by fixing the gaze. It is related that a Bedouin ate with Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, and Sulayman saw a hair in the Bedouin's morsel and said to him: "Remove the hair from your morsel." He said: "Do you look at me as one who sees a hair in my morsel?! By Allah, I will not eat with you again." I say: It has been mentioned that this anecdote was actually with Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, not with Sulayman, and that the Bedouin left his presence saying:
"Death is better than the visit of a stingy man who watches the edges of the eater with deliberate intent."

The seventh: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when he saw their hands not reaching it, he disliked them﴾. It means he denied them; one says "nakirtuka" and "istankartuka" when you find someone other than as you knew him. The poet said:
"She disowned me, and what she disowned of the events was nothing but grey hair and baldness."
So he combined the two usages. It is said: "nakirtu" for what you see with your eye, and "ankartu" for what you see with your heart.

The eighth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And his wife was standing﴾. It is a subject and predicate, meaning she was standing in a place where she could see the angels. It was said she was behind the screen. It was said she was serving the angels while he was seated. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: she was standing and praying. In the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is: "and his wife was standing, and he was seated."

The ninth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So she laughed﴾. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: she menstruated, and she was past menopause, confirming the good tidings. The lexicographers cited in support of this:
"Indeed I come to the wife when she is pure, and I abandon her one day when she laughs."
And another said:
"The laughing of the hares upon the rock is like the blood of the belly on the day of the encounter."
The Arabs say "the hare laughed" when she menstruates. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and 'Ikrimah, that it is taken from their saying: "the kafurah laughed," meaning the sheath of the spathe split open. Some lexicographers denied that "dahakat" in the speech of the Arabs means "haidat" (menstruated). The majority said: it is the well-known laughter, and they differed about it. It was said: it is the laughter of wonder. Abu Dhu'ayb said: "Then came a honey-drink such as people had not seen the like of; it is the laughter, except that it is the work of the bees."

Mujahid said: she laughed out of fear of Abraham, and his trembling before three men, while Abraham was surrounded by his retinue and servants, and Abraham would stand up alone against a hundred men. He said: "Laughing is not the correct meaning of al-ḥayḍ (menstruation) in the language." Abu 'Ubayd and al-Farra' rejected this. Al-Farra' said: "I have not heard it from a trustworthy source; it is rather a metaphor (kināya)." It is narrated that the angels wiped the calf, so it rose from its place and joined its mother, and Sarah laughed at that moment, so they gave her the good news of Isaac. It is said: when Abraham wished to honour his guests, he would have Sarah serve them, and this is the meaning of His saying: "and his wife was standing," i.e., standing in their service. It is also said: "standing" refers to Abraham's fright, and "she laughed" at their saying "Do not fear," out of joy at safety. Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in it; the meaning is: "So We gave her the good news of Isaac, and she laughed," i.e., she laughed in joy at the child, though she had grown old. And God knows best which of these it was. Al-Nahhas said: there are several views on it, the best of which is: when they did not eat, he became wary of them and feared them; when they said "Do not fear" and informed him that they were messengers of [God], he rejoiced, so his wife laughed out of joy at his happiness. It was also said: she had told him, "I think these people will be struck by a punishment, so bring Lot to you," and when the messengers came with what she had said, she was delighted and laughed. Al-Nahhas said: if this chain of transmission is sound, it is good. Laughter is the baring of the teeth. It is also possible that laughter means the brightening of the face; one says: "I saw so-and-so laughing," i.e., radiant. "I came upon a meadow that laughs," i.e., bright. In the hadith: "God, glory be to Him, [sends] the clouds and they laugh with the best laughter," making the clearing of the lightning a laugh, and this is a figurative expression. It is related from a man of the Qur'an readers of Mecca called Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-A'rabi, that he read "ḍaḥikat" with a fatḥa on the ḥā'. Al-Mahdawi said: opening the ḥā' in "fa-ḍaḥikat" is not known. "Ḍaḥika yaḍḥaku ḍaḥkan, ḍiḥkan, ḍiḥikan" are four dialectal forms. "Ḍaḥkah" means a single occurrence of laughing, and from it is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"Their necks were bound by his laughter, the wealth's necks" [the verse's first half: "Enveloped in his cloak when he smiles laughing"]

Said by al-Jawhari.

The tenth: Muslim related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: Abu Usayd al-Sa'idi invited the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to his wedding feast, and his wife was serving them that day, and she was the bride. Sahl said: Do you know what she gave the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to drink? She soaked some dates for him during the night in a tawr (a vessel from which the Arabs drink and perform wudu, made of brass or stone), and when he had eaten, she gave it to him to drink. Al-Bukhari also narrated it and titled a chapter for it: "The chapter on a woman standing over men at a wedding and serving them personally." Our scholars said: in it is the permissibility of the bride serving her husband and his companions at her wedding. It also shows there is no harm in a man presenting his womenfolk to his righteous brothers and having them serve them. It is possible that this was before the revelation of the veil, and God knows best.

The eleventh: al-Tabari mentioned that when Abraham, peace be upon him, brought forward the calf, they said: "We do not eat food except for a price." He said to them: "Its price is that you mention God at its beginning and praise Him at its end." Then Gabriel said to his companions: "Truly, God has taken this man as a friend (khalīl)." Our scholars said: they did not eat because angels do not eat. Although it was permissible that, just as God made it easy for the angels to take on human form in body and appearance, He could make it easy for them to eat food, yet according to the scholars' view He sent them in human form, and Abraham, peace be upon him, undertook the hospitality, [until when he saw their hesitation and feared, the good news came to him suddenly].

The twelfth: This shows that mentioning God's name at the beginning of a meal and praising Him at its end is prescribed in the nations before us. It has come in the Isra'iliyyat that Abraham would not eat alone; when his food was ready he would send to seek someone to eat with him. One day he met a man, and when he sat with him at the meal, Abraham said to him: "Say the name of God." The man said: "I do not know what God is." He said to him: "Then leave my food." When he left, Gabriel descended to him and said: "God says: He provides for him throughout his life despite his disbelief, and you begrudged him a morsel." Abraham went out in alarm, dragging his cloak, and said: "Return!" The man said: "I will not return until you tell me why you turned me away for no reason." He informed him of the matter, and he said: "This is a generous Lord; I have believed," and he entered, mentioned God's name, and ate as a believer. [In another version: as one who enjoys it.]

The thirteenth: His saying, exalted is He: "So We gave her the good news of Isaac." When Ishmael was born to Abraham from Hagar, Sarah wished that she might have a son, but she despaired because of her advanced age, so she was given the good news of a son who would be a prophet and would father a prophet. This was a good news to her that she would see her son's son.

The fourteenth: His saying, exalted is He: "And after Isaac, Jacob." Hamza, Ibn 'Amir and 'Abd Allah read "Ya'qub" in the accusative (naṣb). The rest read it in the nominative (raf'). The nominative is according to the meaning: "and there will be produced for her, after Isaac, Jacob." It may also be governed by the verb that operates on "min": as if the meaning is "and there was established for her, after Isaac, Jacob." It may also be in the nominative as a subject, and be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), i.e., "they gave her the good news of Isaac, with Jacob following him." The accusative is according to the meaning: "and We granted her, after Isaac, Jacob." Al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim permitted that "Ya'qub" be in the genitive position, according to the meaning: "and We gave her the good news of Isaac and after Isaac, Jacob." Al-Farra' said: the genitive is not permitted except by repeating the governing preposition. Sibawayh said: if you said, "I passed by Zayd before yesterday and yesterday of 'Amr" [the preferred form being "and yesterday with 'Amr"], it would be ugly, because you have separated the genitive noun from what it is conjoined with, which is the conjunction "wa," just as you separate the preposition from the genitive, since a preposition may not be separated from its genitive noun, nor from the conjunction.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 69–71 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And certainly Our messengers came to Ibrahim with the good tidings﴾. This is the story of Lut, peace be upon him, who was the nephew of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, being closely related to him by lineage [[i.e., connected to him by kinship.]]. The villages of Lut were in the regions of al-Sham, while Ibrahim was in the lands of Palestine. When Allah sent the angels with the punishment of the people of Lut, they passed by Ibrahim and stayed with him. Everyone who stayed with him was generously hospitable to them, and they had passed by with the good tidings for Ibrahim, so he took them to be guests. They were Jibril, Mika'il and Isra'il, peace be upon them; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Dahhak said they were nine. Al-Suddi said they were eleven angels in the form of handsome youths, of radiant faces and surpassing beauty. "With the good tidings": it was said, with the news of a son. It was said, with the news of the destruction of the people of Lut. It was said, they gave him the good news that they were messengers of Allah, mighty and majestic, and that there was no fear for him.

(They said, "Peace!") It is in the accusative because the verb falls upon it, as you say, "They said good." This is the preference of al-Tabari. As for His saying, "Three will say [they were three]" [[See vol. 10, p. 382.]], "three" is a noun, not a [speech] [[From ʿ.]] that is said. If both were in the nominative or both in the accusative, "They said, 'Peace,' he said, 'Peace'" would be permissible in Arabic. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). It was said: "They said, 'Peace'" means they opened the conversation with a correct word, as He said: "And when the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'" [[See vol. 13, p. 67.]], meaning, "Correct." So "peace" is the meaning of their words, not their wording. Ibn al-'Arabi said this and preferred it. He said: Do you not see that when Allah wished to mention the wording, He said it exactly, reporting about the angels: "Peace be upon you, for what you have endured patiently" [[See p. 312 of this volume.]] and "Peace be upon you, you are good" [[See vol. 15, p. 284 onward.]]. It was also said that they prayed for him, and the meaning is "may you be safe with a safety."

(He said, "Peace.") In its nominative form there are two possibilities. The first: by supposing an omitted subject, meaning "he is peace," or "my matter is peace." The second: it means "Peace be upon you," if it is taken as a greeting, with the predicate omitted. "Peace" was permitted as an indefinite noun because it is used so frequently, so the alif and lam were dropped, as they are dropped from "lahumma" in your saying "allahumma." It is also read "silm." Al-Farra' said: "al-silm" and "al-salam" have the same meaning, like "al-hil" and "al-halal."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But he did not delay to bring a roasted calf﴾. In this there are fourteen issues [[So it stands in the original; the issues mentioned also relate to verses 70 and 71, not to this verse alone.]]:

The first: His saying, "fa-ma labitha an ja'" ("he did not delay to come"). "An" here means "until." This is said by the greater grammarians, related by Ibn al-'Arabi. The sense is: "he did not delay until he came." It was also said: "an" is in the position of the accusative after the removal of the preposition, the sense being "he did not delay from his coming," that is, he was not slow in bringing a calf; when the preposition is removed, "an" remains in the accusative position. In "labitha" there is a pronoun referring to Ibrahim. And "salaman" is negating, said Sibawayh. Al-Farra' said: "fa-ma labitha majiuhu," meaning "his coming was not delayed," so "an" is in the nominative position, and there is no pronoun in "labitha," and "salaman" is negating. It is also permissible for "salaman" to mean "the one who," with a pronoun for Ibrahim in "labitha," and "an ja'" as the predicate of "salaman," meaning: what Ibrahim delayed was his bringing of a roasted calf. "Haneedh" means roasted. It was said it is roasted by the heat of stones without the fire touching it. One says "hanadhtu al-shah uhnidhuha hanadhan," meaning "I roasted it," and I placed heated stones above it so they would cook it, and so it is haneedh. "Hanadhtu al-faras uhnidhuhu hanadhan" means you make the horse run a course or two and then spread a blanket over it in the sun so that it sweats; it is then mahnudh and haneedh. If it does not sweat, it is said "kaba." "Hanadh" is also a place near Madina [[And Haneedh is also a place near Makka.]]. It was said: al-haneedh is the skinned one. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: haneedh is well-cooked. "Haneedh" has the meaning of "mahnudh." He brought a calf because cattle were the greater part of his wealth.

The second: In this verse, part of the etiquette of the guest is that the host hastens his hospitality, offering what is available and easy at once, then following it with other things if he has the means, without burdening himself with what would harm him. Hospitality is among the noble qualities, among the etiquettes of Islam, and among the character of the prophets and the righteous. Ibrahim was the first to host guests, as mentioned in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 98.]]. It is not obligatory according to the general body of scholars, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Hospitality is three days, and its generous gift [jaizah] is one day and night; whatever is beyond that is charity." "Jaizah" is the gift and the kindness whose basis is recommended. The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour; and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest." Honouring the neighbour is not obligatory by consensus, so hospitality is similar to it. And Allah knows best. Al-Layth held that it is obligatory, relying on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The night of the guest is a right," among other hadiths. What we have pointed to is sufficient, and Allah is the One who grants success in guidance. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some people said that the obligation of hospitality was in the early period of Islam and was then abrogated (naskh), but this is weak, for the obligation was never established, and no abrogating text came. He mentioned the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, related by the imams, in which: "We asked them for hospitality, but they refused to host us, so the chief of that tribe was stung..." the hadith. He said: This shows clearly that if hospitality were a right, the Prophet ﷺ would have rebuked the people who refused, and would have made it clear to them.

The third: The scholars differed about to whom it is addressed. Al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hakam held that it is addressed to the people of towns and of the desert. Malik said: there is no hospitality obligation on the people of towns. Sahnun said: hospitality is only upon the people of villages; as for towns, the inn (funduq) is where the traveller stays [Sahib al-'Ayn and others related both dialects [[From w; consider this.]]]. They argued from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, who said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hospitality is for the people of the wabar [tents] and not for the people of the madar [towns]." This hadith is not authentic; Ibrahim, the nephew of 'Abd al-Razzaq, is a discarded narrator, accused of lying, and this is among what he alone related, and he was accused of fabricating it, as said by Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Hospitality is in reality a collective obligation (fard kifayah). Some people said it is obligatory in villages where there is no food or shelter, unlike cities, which are full of lodging and provisions. There is no doubt that the guest is honoured and hospitality is a mark of honour; if he is a stranger, it is an obligation.

The fourth: Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some of our scholars said: Ibrahim's hospitality was meagre, and so the Beloved thanked the Beloved for it. This is a judgment by conjecture where certainty is required, and by analogy where transmission is required. From where was it known that it was meagre?! Indeed, the exegetes have related that the angels were three, Jibril, Mika'il and Isra'il, peace be upon them, and a calf for three is large. So how is this interpretation of the Book of Allah by opinion?! By the trust of Allah, this is the blameworthy interpretation, so avoid it, for you know it.

The fifth: The Sunnah is that when food is brought to a guest, the one who brought it should hasten to eat, for the honour of the guest is quick service, and the honour of the host is prompt acceptance. When they withheld their hands, Ibrahim disliked it, because they had departed from custom and opposed the Sunnah, and he feared that behind them was some harm they intended. It is related that they were pricking with arrows (qidah) [[qidah (plural qidah): an arrow before it is fitted with its head and feathers.]] that were in their hands into the meat, and their hands did not reach the meat. When he saw that from them...

(He disliked them and conceived fear of them.) That is, he concealed it. It was said: he perceived. "Al-wujus" means entering. The poet said:
"The courier came with a paper he hurried with, so the heart conceived fear of its paper."
"Khifatan" means fear, that is, dread. When they saw that the guest did not eat, they thought evil of him, so the angels said: ﴿Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut﴾.

The sixth: Among the etiquettes of food is that the host may look at his guest to see whether he eats or not, and this should be done with glancing and stealth, not by fixing the gaze. It is related that a Bedouin ate with Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, and Sulayman saw a hair in the Bedouin's morsel and said to him: "Remove the hair from your morsel." He said: "Do you look at me as one who sees a hair in my morsel?! By Allah, I will not eat with you again." I say: It has been mentioned that this anecdote was actually with Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, not with Sulayman, and that the Bedouin left his presence saying:
"Death is better than the visit of a stingy man who watches the edges of the eater with deliberate intent."

The seventh: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when he saw their hands not reaching it, he disliked them﴾. It means he denied them; one says "nakirtuka" and "istankartuka" when you find someone other than as you knew him. The poet said:
"She disowned me, and what she disowned of the events was nothing but grey hair and baldness."
So he combined the two usages. It is said: "nakirtu" for what you see with your eye, and "ankartu" for what you see with your heart.

The eighth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And his wife was standing﴾. It is a subject and predicate, meaning she was standing in a place where she could see the angels. It was said she was behind the screen. It was said she was serving the angels while he was seated. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: she was standing and praying. In the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is: "and his wife was standing, and he was seated."

The ninth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So she laughed﴾. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: she menstruated, and she was past menopause, confirming the good tidings. The lexicographers cited in support of this:
"Indeed I come to the wife when she is pure, and I abandon her one day when she laughs."
And another said:
"The laughing of the hares upon the rock is like the blood of the belly on the day of the encounter."
The Arabs say "the hare laughed" when she menstruates. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and 'Ikrimah, that it is taken from their saying: "the kafurah laughed," meaning the sheath of the spathe split open. Some lexicographers denied that "dahakat" in the speech of the Arabs means "haidat" (menstruated). The majority said: it is the well-known laughter, and they differed about it. It was said: it is the laughter of wonder. Abu Dhu'ayb said: "Then came a honey-drink such as people had not seen the like of; it is the laughter, except that it is the work of the bees."

Mujahid said: she laughed out of fear of Abraham, and his trembling before three men, while Abraham was surrounded by his retinue and servants, and Abraham would stand up alone against a hundred men. He said: "Laughing is not the correct meaning of al-ḥayḍ (menstruation) in the language." Abu 'Ubayd and al-Farra' rejected this. Al-Farra' said: "I have not heard it from a trustworthy source; it is rather a metaphor (kināya)." It is narrated that the angels wiped the calf, so it rose from its place and joined its mother, and Sarah laughed at that moment, so they gave her the good news of Isaac. It is said: when Abraham wished to honour his guests, he would have Sarah serve them, and this is the meaning of His saying: "and his wife was standing," i.e., standing in their service. It is also said: "standing" refers to Abraham's fright, and "she laughed" at their saying "Do not fear," out of joy at safety. Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in it; the meaning is: "So We gave her the good news of Isaac, and she laughed," i.e., she laughed in joy at the child, though she had grown old. And God knows best which of these it was. Al-Nahhas said: there are several views on it, the best of which is: when they did not eat, he became wary of them and feared them; when they said "Do not fear" and informed him that they were messengers of [God], he rejoiced, so his wife laughed out of joy at his happiness. It was also said: she had told him, "I think these people will be struck by a punishment, so bring Lot to you," and when the messengers came with what she had said, she was delighted and laughed. Al-Nahhas said: if this chain of transmission is sound, it is good. Laughter is the baring of the teeth. It is also possible that laughter means the brightening of the face; one says: "I saw so-and-so laughing," i.e., radiant. "I came upon a meadow that laughs," i.e., bright. In the hadith: "God, glory be to Him, [sends] the clouds and they laugh with the best laughter," making the clearing of the lightning a laugh, and this is a figurative expression. It is related from a man of the Qur'an readers of Mecca called Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-A'rabi, that he read "ḍaḥikat" with a fatḥa on the ḥā'. Al-Mahdawi said: opening the ḥā' in "fa-ḍaḥikat" is not known. "Ḍaḥika yaḍḥaku ḍaḥkan, ḍiḥkan, ḍiḥikan" are four dialectal forms. "Ḍaḥkah" means a single occurrence of laughing, and from it is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"Their necks were bound by his laughter, the wealth's necks" [the verse's first half: "Enveloped in his cloak when he smiles laughing"]

Said by al-Jawhari.

The tenth: Muslim related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: Abu Usayd al-Sa'idi invited the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to his wedding feast, and his wife was serving them that day, and she was the bride. Sahl said: Do you know what she gave the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to drink? She soaked some dates for him during the night in a tawr (a vessel from which the Arabs drink and perform wudu, made of brass or stone), and when he had eaten, she gave it to him to drink. Al-Bukhari also narrated it and titled a chapter for it: "The chapter on a woman standing over men at a wedding and serving them personally." Our scholars said: in it is the permissibility of the bride serving her husband and his companions at her wedding. It also shows there is no harm in a man presenting his womenfolk to his righteous brothers and having them serve them. It is possible that this was before the revelation of the veil, and God knows best.

The eleventh: al-Tabari mentioned that when Abraham, peace be upon him, brought forward the calf, they said: "We do not eat food except for a price." He said to them: "Its price is that you mention God at its beginning and praise Him at its end." Then Gabriel said to his companions: "Truly, God has taken this man as a friend (khalīl)." Our scholars said: they did not eat because angels do not eat. Although it was permissible that, just as God made it easy for the angels to take on human form in body and appearance, He could make it easy for them to eat food, yet according to the scholars' view He sent them in human form, and Abraham, peace be upon him, undertook the hospitality, [until when he saw their hesitation and feared, the good news came to him suddenly].

The twelfth: This shows that mentioning God's name at the beginning of a meal and praising Him at its end is prescribed in the nations before us. It has come in the Isra'iliyyat that Abraham would not eat alone; when his food was ready he would send to seek someone to eat with him. One day he met a man, and when he sat with him at the meal, Abraham said to him: "Say the name of God." The man said: "I do not know what God is." He said to him: "Then leave my food." When he left, Gabriel descended to him and said: "God says: He provides for him throughout his life despite his disbelief, and you begrudged him a morsel." Abraham went out in alarm, dragging his cloak, and said: "Return!" The man said: "I will not return until you tell me why you turned me away for no reason." He informed him of the matter, and he said: "This is a generous Lord; I have believed," and he entered, mentioned God's name, and ate as a believer. [In another version: as one who enjoys it.]

The thirteenth: His saying, exalted is He: "So We gave her the good news of Isaac." When Ishmael was born to Abraham from Hagar, Sarah wished that she might have a son, but she despaired because of her advanced age, so she was given the good news of a son who would be a prophet and would father a prophet. This was a good news to her that she would see her son's son.

The fourteenth: His saying, exalted is He: "And after Isaac, Jacob." Hamza, Ibn 'Amir and 'Abd Allah read "Ya'qub" in the accusative (naṣb). The rest read it in the nominative (raf'). The nominative is according to the meaning: "and there will be produced for her, after Isaac, Jacob." It may also be governed by the verb that operates on "min": as if the meaning is "and there was established for her, after Isaac, Jacob." It may also be in the nominative as a subject, and be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), i.e., "they gave her the good news of Isaac, with Jacob following him." The accusative is according to the meaning: "and We granted her, after Isaac, Jacob." Al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim permitted that "Ya'qub" be in the genitive position, according to the meaning: "and We gave her the good news of Isaac and after Isaac, Jacob." Al-Farra' said: the genitive is not permitted except by repeating the governing preposition. Sibawayh said: if you said, "I passed by Zayd before yesterday and yesterday of 'Amr" [the preferred form being "and yesterday with 'Amr"], it would be ugly, because you have separated the genitive noun from what it is conjoined with, which is the conjunction "wa," just as you separate the preposition from the genitive, since a preposition may not be separated from its genitive noun, nor from the conjunction.

I say: It has been mentioned that this anecdote was actually with Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, not with Sulayman, and that the Bedouin left his presence saying:
"Death is better than the visit of a stingy man who watches the edges of the eater with deliberate intent."

The seventh: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when he saw their hands not reaching it, he disliked them﴾. It means he denied them; one says "nakirtuka" and "istankartuka" when you find someone other than as you knew him. The poet said:
"She disowned me, and what she disowned of the events was nothing but grey hair and baldness."
So he combined the two usages. It is said: "nakirtu" for what you see with your eye, and "ankartu" for what you see with your heart.

The eighth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And his wife was standing﴾. It is a subject and predicate, meaning she was standing in a place where she could see the angels. It was said she was behind the screen. It was said she was serving the angels while he was seated. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: she was standing and praying. In the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is: "and his wife was standing, and he was seated."

The ninth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So she laughed﴾. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: she menstruated, and she was past menopause, confirming the good tidings. The lexicographers cited in support of this:
"Indeed I come to the wife when she is pure, and I abandon her one day when she laughs."
And another said:
"The laughing of the hares upon the rock is like the blood of the belly on the day of the encounter."
The Arabs say "the hare laughed" when she menstruates. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and 'Ikrimah, that it is taken from their saying: "the kafurah laughed," meaning the sheath of the spathe split open. Some lexicographers denied that "dahakat" in the speech of the Arabs means "haidat" (menstruated). The majority said: it is the well-known laughter, and they differed about it. It was said: it is the laughter of wonder. Abu Dhu'ayb said: "Then came a honey-drink such as people had not seen the like of; it is the laughter, except that it is the work of the bees."

Mujahid said: she laughed out of fear of Abraham, and his trembling before three men, while Abraham was surrounded by his retinue and servants, and Abraham would stand up alone against a hundred men. He said: "Laughing is not the correct meaning of al-ḥayḍ (menstruation) in the language." Abu 'Ubayd and al-Farra' rejected this. Al-Farra' said: "I have not heard it from a trustworthy source; it is rather a metaphor (kināya)." It is narrated that the angels wiped the calf, so it rose from its place and joined its mother, and Sarah laughed at that moment, so they gave her the good news of Isaac. It is said: when Abraham wished to honour his guests, he would have Sarah serve them, and this is the meaning of His saying: "and his wife was standing," i.e., standing in their service. It is also said: "standing" refers to Abraham's fright, and "she laughed" at their saying "Do not fear," out of joy at safety. Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in it; the meaning is: "So We gave her the good news of Isaac, and she laughed," i.e., she laughed in joy at the child, though she had grown old. And God knows best which of these it was. Al-Nahhas said: there are several views on it, the best of which is: when they did not eat, he became wary of them and feared them; when they said "Do not fear" and informed him that they were messengers of [God], he rejoiced, so his wife laughed out of joy at his happiness. It was also said: she had told him, "I think these people will be struck by a punishment, so bring Lot to you," and when the messengers came with what she had said, she was delighted and laughed. Al-Nahhas said: if this chain of transmission is sound, it is good. Laughter is the baring of the teeth. It is also possible that laughter means the brightening of the face; one says: "I saw so-and-so laughing," i.e., radiant. "I came upon a meadow that laughs," i.e., bright. In the hadith: "God, glory be to Him, [sends] the clouds and they laugh with the best laughter," making the clearing of the lightning a laugh, and this is a figurative expression. It is related from a man of the Qur'an readers of Mecca called Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-A'rabi, that he read "ḍaḥikat" with a fatḥa on the ḥā'. Al-Mahdawi said: opening the ḥā' in "fa-ḍaḥikat" is not known. "Ḍaḥika yaḍḥaku ḍaḥkan, ḍiḥkan, ḍiḥikan" are four dialectal forms. "Ḍaḥkah" means a single occurrence of laughing, and from it is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"Their necks were bound by his laughter, the wealth's necks" [the verse's first half: "Enveloped in his cloak when he smiles laughing"]

Said by al-Jawhari.

The tenth: Muslim related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: Abu Usayd al-Sa'idi invited the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to his wedding feast, and his wife was serving them that day, and she was the bride. Sahl said: Do you know what she gave the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to drink? She soaked some dates for him during the night in a tawr (a vessel from which the Arabs drink and perform wudu, made of brass or stone), and when he had eaten, she gave it to him to drink. Al-Bukhari also narrated it and titled a chapter for it: "The chapter on a woman standing over men at a wedding and serving them personally." Our scholars said: in it is the permissibility of the bride serving her husband and his companions at her wedding. It also shows there is no harm in a man presenting his womenfolk to his righteous brothers and having them serve them. It is possible that this was before the revelation of the veil, and God knows best.

The eleventh: al-Tabari mentioned that when Abraham, peace be upon him, brought forward the calf, they said: "We do not eat food except for a price." He said to them: "Its price is that you mention God at its beginning and praise Him at its end." Then Gabriel said to his companions: "Truly, God has taken this man as a friend (khalīl)." Our scholars said: they did not eat because angels do not eat. Although it was permissible that, just as God made it easy for the angels to take on human form in body and appearance, He could make it easy for them to eat food, yet according to the scholars' view He sent them in human form, and Abraham, peace be upon him, undertook the hospitality, [until when he saw their hesitation and feared, the good news came to him suddenly].

The twelfth: This shows that mentioning God's name at the beginning of a meal and praising Him at its end is prescribed in the nations before us. It has come in the Isra'iliyyat that Abraham would not eat alone; when his food was ready he would send to seek someone to eat with him. One day he met a man, and when he sat with him at the meal, Abraham said to him: "Say the name of God." The man said: "I do not know what God is." He said to him: "Then leave my food." When he left, Gabriel descended to him and said: "God says: He provides for him throughout his life despite his disbelief, and you begrudged him a morsel." Abraham went out in alarm, dragging his cloak, and said: "Return!" The man said: "I will not return until you tell me why you turned me away for no reason." He informed him of the matter, and he said: "This is a generous Lord; I have believed," and he entered, mentioned God's name, and ate as a believer. [In another version: as one who enjoys it.]

The thirteenth: His saying, exalted is He: "So We gave her the good news of Isaac." When Ishmael was born to Abraham from Hagar, Sarah wished that she might have a son, but she despaired because of her advanced age, so she was given the good news of a son who would be a prophet and would father a prophet. This was a good news to her that she would see her son's son.

The fourteenth: His saying, exalted is He: "And after Isaac, Jacob." Hamza, Ibn 'Amir and 'Abd Allah read "Ya'qub" in the accusative (naṣb). The rest read it in the nominative (raf'). The nominative is according to the meaning: "and there will be produced for her, after Isaac, Jacob." It may also be governed by the verb that operates on "min": as if the meaning is "and there was established for her, after Isaac, Jacob." It may also be in the nominative as a subject, and be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), i.e., "they gave her the good news of Isaac, with Jacob following him." The accusative is according to the meaning: "and We granted her, after Isaac, Jacob." Al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim permitted that "Ya'qub" be in the genitive position, according to the meaning: "and We gave her the good news of Isaac and after Isaac, Jacob." Al-Farra' said: the genitive is not permitted except by repeating the governing preposition. Sibawayh said: if you said, "I passed by Zayd before yesterday and yesterday of 'Amr" [the preferred form being "and yesterday with 'Amr"], it would be ugly, because you have separated the genitive noun from what it is conjoined with, which is the conjunction "wa," just as you separate the preposition from the genitive, since a preposition may not be separated from its genitive noun, nor from the conjunction.

**Second question on this verse.** Its first issue concerns His words, Exalted is He: (O woe is me!) Al-Zajjaj said: Its original form is *yā wayletī*, and the *yā* (ي) was replaced by an *alif*, because it is lighter than the *yā* and the *kasra*. She did not intend to call down woe upon herself, but it is a word that comes easily to women's mouths when something befalls them that makes them wonder at it. She was astonished at giving birth, [and] [[من ع.]] at her husband being an old man, because this was outside the normal course, and what falls outside the normal course is strange and reprehensible. **﴿أَأَلِدُ﴾** (*a-alidu*, "Shall I indeed give birth?") is an interrogative, meaning amazement.

**(And I am an old woman)**: that is, *shaykhah* (an elderly woman). One says *ʿajuza taʿjuzu ʿajzan* and *ʿajjazat taʿjīzan*, meaning she advanced in years. It is also said *ʿajūzah*. The woman *ʿajizat* (with *kasra* on the *jīm*) means her buttocks became large, *ʿujzan* and *ʿajazan* (with *ḍamma* and *fatḥa* on the *ʿayn*). Mujahid said: she was ninety-nine years old. Ibn Ishaq said: she was ninety [years old [[من ع.]]]. Other views have also been stated.

**The second issue** concerns His words, Exalted is He: **﴿And this is my husband﴾**, that is, my spouse.

**(Old)**, *shaykhan*, is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier), and its governing element is the attention-drawing particle or the demonstrative. **"And this is my husband"** is a subject and predicate (*mubtadaʾ wa khabar*). Al-Akhfash said: in the recitation of Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy, it reads "**And this is my husband, old**" (*wa hādhā baʿlī shaykhan*). Al-Nahhas said: just as you say *hādhā Zaydun qāʾimun*, where *Zaydun* is an appositive (*badal*) of *hādhā* and *qāʾimun* is the predicate of the subject. It is also permissible for *hādhā* to be the subject, with *Zaydun qāʾimun* as two predicates. Sibawayh related: *hādhā ḥulwun ḥāmiḍun* (this is sweet and sour).

It was said that Ibrahim was one hundred and twenty years old. It was also said he was one hundred, and according to Mujahid he was one year more than that. It was said that she was hinting, by her words "And this is my husband, old," that he had stopped approaching her.

This Sarah was the wife of Ibrahim, the daughter of Haran ibn Nahur ibn Sarugh ibn Arghu ibn Falikh, and she was the daughter of Ibrahim's paternal uncle.

**(Indeed, this is a wondrous thing)**: that is, what you have given me good news of is indeed a wondrous thing.

**First issue: the Almighty's command and the angels' reply.** When she said, "And I am an old woman, and this is my husband, an old man," and expressed wonder, the angels rebuked her for her wonder at the command of Allah, i.e., at His decree and His determination. That is, there is no cause for wonder that Allah should grant you both a child, namely Isaac. Many scholars have used this verse to argue that the one who was sacrificed was Ishmael, and that he was older than Isaac, because she was given the good news that Isaac would live until Jacob was born to him. The discussion of this, and its explanation, will come in *al-Saffat* [[See vol. 15, p. 98 onward.]], if Allah the Exalted wills.

**Second issue: the grammar of "Mercy of Allah and His blessings."** The phrase ﴿rahmatu Allahi wa barakatuhu﴾ is a *mubtada'* (subject), and the *khabar* (predicate) is "upon you" ('alaykum). Sibawayh (d. c. 180 AH) transmitted "'alaykum" with a kasra on the kaf because it is adjacent to the ya'. The question is whether this is a *khabar* (statement) or a *du'a'* (supplication). Taking it as a statement is more excellent, because it implies that mercy and blessing have actually reached them. The meaning is: Allah has delivered to you His mercy and His blessings, O people of the house. Taking it as a supplication implies only that it is something hoped for and has not yet occurred. "Ahla al-bayt" is in the accusative by way of *ikhtisas* (specification), and this is the view of Sibawayh. It was also said that it is in the accusative by way of address (*nida'*).

**Third issue: wives among the People of the House.** This verse indicates that a man's wife is among the People of the House. From this it follows that the wives of the prophets are among the People of the House. Thus 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and others are among the People of the House of the Prophet ﷺ, concerning whom Allah said: ﴿and purify you with thorough purification﴾ [33:33]. This will come later [[See vol. 14, p. 178.]].

**Fourth issue: the end of the greeting is "and His blessings."** The verse also indicates that the endpoint of the greeting is "and His blessings," as Allah reported of His righteous servants: "Mercy of Allah and His blessings upon you, O people of the house." *Al-barakah* means growth and increase. Among those blessings is that all the prophets and messengers were from the offspring of Abraham and Sarah.

Malik narrated from Wahb ibn Kaysan Abu Nu'aym, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn 'Ata', who said: I was sitting with 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas when a man from Yemen entered upon him and said, "Al-salamu 'alayka wa rahmatu Allahi wa barakatuh," and then he added something to that. Ibn 'Abbas, who had by then lost his sight, said, "Who is this?" They said, "The Yemeni who visits you." They described him to him, and he said, "Indeed the greeting has ended at the blessing."

It is also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: I entered the mosque and found the Prophet ﷺ in a group of his companions. I said, "Al-salamu 'alaykum." He said, "Wa 'alayka al-salam wa rahmatu Allah: twenty for me and ten for you." He said: I entered a second time and said, "Al-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatu Allah," and he said, "Wa 'alayka al-salam wa rahmatu Allahi wa barakatuh: thirty for me and twenty for you." Then I entered a third time and said, "Al-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatu Allahi wa barakatuh," and he said, "Wa 'alayka al-salam wa rahmatu Allahi wa barakatuh: thirty for me and thirty for you. You and I are equal in the greeting."

﴿Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, Glorious﴾: that is, *mahmud* (praised) and *majid* (glorious). We have explained both in "al-Asma' al-Husna" (the Beautiful Names).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 74–76:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the fear had left Ibrahim﴾, i.e. the fear (al-raw'). It is said: "irtaa'a min kadha" when he feared it. The poet al-Nabigha said:

fa-ir-taa'a min sawti kallabin [[al-Kallab: the owner of the dogs. The poet describes a wild bull who spent the night in the fear that overtook him and the cold that afflicted him, a wretched night; his remaining in that state gladdens his enemies.]] fa-baata lahu ... ṭawa'a al-shawamit min khawfin wa-min ṣarad

(﴿And the good tidings came to him﴾), i.e. of Isaac and Jacob. Qatadah said: they gave him the good news that they had only come with the punishment for the people of Lut, and that he had nothing to fear.

(﴿He argued with Us﴾), i.e. he argued with Our messengers, and He attributed it to Himself because they had descended by His command. This argument was related by Humayd ibn Hilal from Jundub from Hudhayfah: when they said, "Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town" [[See vol. 13, p. 341 onward.]], he said to them: "Tell me, if there are fifty Muslims in it, will you destroy them?" They said: "No." He said: "Forty?" They said: "No." He said: "Thirty?" They said: "No." He said: "Twenty?" They said: "No." He said: "If there are ten in it — or five, Humayd is uncertain —" They said: "No." Qatadah said: "Something similar to it." He said — meaning Ibrahim — "A people among whom there are not ten Muslims has no good in it." It is also said that Ibrahim said: "Tell me, if there is one Muslim man in it, will you destroy it?" They said: "No." Then Ibrahim said at that point: "Indeed, Lut is in it." They said: "We know best who is in it; we will surely save him and his family, except his wife, who was among those who remained behind." Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah said: they were four hundred thousand. Ibn Jurayj said: there were in the villages of the people of Lut four thousand thousand.

The view of al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i is that "yujadiluna" is in the place of "jadalana." Al-Nahhas said: since the response to "falamma" must be in the past tense, the present tense has been put in its place, just as the condition must be in the present tense, so the past tense has been put in its place. There is also another answer: that "yujadiluna" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "he came arguing with us," and this is the view of al-Farra'.

(﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing, tender-hearted, and turning back in repentance﴾). The meaning of "la-awwah halim" has already been discussed in "Bara'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 274.]]. And al-Munib is the one who returns; it is said: "anaba" when he returned. Ibrahim (ﷺ) was returning to Allah in all his affairs. It is also said: al-Awwah is the one who sighs in grief over what the people of Lut had lost of faith.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Ibrahim, turn away from this﴾, i.e. leave off the argument concerning the people of Lut.

(﴿Indeed, the command of your Lord has come﴾), i.e. His punishment upon them.

(﴿And indeed, there will reach them a punishment that cannot be turned back﴾), i.e. one that will descend upon them and will not be averted from them nor repelled.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verses 77–83 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them.﴾ When the angels left Abraham, and the distance between Abraham and the town of Lot was four farsakh, two daughters of Lot, who were drawing water, saw the angels and noticed their handsome appearance. They said: "What is your business, and where have you come from?" The angels said: "From such-and-such a place. We want this town." The two girls said: "Its people are men of immorality." The angels said: "Is there anyone in it who will host us?" The two girls said: "Yes, this old man," and they pointed to Lot. When Lot saw their appearance, he feared for them on account of his people.

(*sā'a bihim*) means that their coming distressed him. It is said: *sā'a yasū'u*, which is intransitive, and *sā'ahu yasū'uhu*, which is also transitive. If you wish, you may vowel the *sīn* with a *ḍamma*, because its original vowel is *ḍamma*. The original form is *sūi'a bihim*, from *al-sū'*. The vowel of the *wāw* was transferred to the *sīn*, and so it became a *yā'*. If the *hamza* is lightened, its vowel is placed on the *yā'*, and you say *sī bihim* with a light pronunciation. There is also an irregular dialect with doubling (*shaddah*).

(*wa-ḍāqa bihim dharʿan*) means that his chest was constrained by their coming and he disliked it. It has also been said: his capacity and power were constrained. Its original sense is that a camel stretches its forelegs during its walk, each stride measured by the breadth of its step. When it is loaded beyond its capacity, it is constrained in that, weakens, and stretches out its neck. So "narrowness of the forelegs" is an expression for narrowness of capacity. It has also been said: it comes from *dhara'ahu al-qay'*, meaning that vomiting overcame him, that is, he could not contain the disagreeable matter within himself. His chest was constrained because of them, because of what he saw of their beauty and because of what he knew of the wickedness of his people.

(*wa-qāla hādhā yawmun ʿaṣīb*) means a severe day of evil. The poet said:
"And if you do not satisfy Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will be a grievous day for you in Iraq."
Another said:
"A grievous day that binds the champions, binding them as the strong binds the tall, slender ones."
It is said: *ʿaṣīb* and *ʿaṣʿaṣ* with intensive form, meaning a hateful day in which evil is gathered. *ʿaṣab* means that he gathered a band for evil, and from this comes *ʿuṣba* and *ʿiṣāba*, meaning people united in word, that is, united in themselves. The *ʿuṣba* of a man are those united with him by lineage. *Ta'aṣṣabtu li-fulān* means I became like his kinsmen. A man described as *maʿṣūb* (in Raghib's *Mufradat*: "*maʿṣūb al-khalq*" means *mudallaj al-khilqa*, that is, of compact build), meaning compact in creation.

(Allah the Exalted says): ﴿And his people came rushing toward him.﴾ This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Yuhraʿūn* means they hasten. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and other lexicographers said: *ihrāʿ* is only hastening together with trembling. It is said: *ahraʿa al-rajul ihrāʿan*, meaning he hastened in trembling, from cold, anger or fever. The participle is *muhraʿ*. Muhalhil said:
"They came rushing while they were captives, we leading them despite the noses."
Another said:
"With quick ones rushing toward him in haste."
This is like: *ūliʿa fulānun bi-l-amr* (he was obsessed with the matter), *urʿida Zayd* (Zayd trembled), and *zuhiya fulān* (he was proud). It is used only in this sense. It has also been said: *uhrifa*, meaning his greed urged him, and on this view *yuhraʿūn* means they are urged on. Whoever holds the first view says: it has been heard only as *uhriʿa al-rajul*, meaning he hastened, in the passive form. Ibn al-Qutiyya said: *hura'a al-insān hara'an* and *uhri'a*: he was driven and hurried. Al-Harawi said: it is said *hur'a al-rajul* and *uhri'a*, meaning he was urged. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi said: *yuhraʿūn* means they run. Al-Dahhak said: they strive. Ibn 'Uyayna said: as if they are being pushed. Shimr ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a walk between running and a quick trot. Al-Hasan said: a walk between two walks. The meanings are close.

The cause of their hastening, as reported, was that Lot's unbelieving wife, when she saw the guests, their beauty and their appearance, went out and came to the gatherings of her people, saying to them: "Lot has hosted tonight youths the like of whom has not been seen for beauty, and such and such." At that point they came rushing to him. It is also mentioned that when the messengers reached Lot's land, they found Lot in his field. It has been said: they found his daughter drawing water from the river of Sodom, so they asked her to guide them to someone who would host them. She saw their appearance and feared for them from the people of Lot. She said to them: "Wait here!" She went to her father and informed him. He came out to them. They said: "We want you to host us tonight." He said to them: "Have you not heard of the deeds of these people?" They said: "And what are their deeds?" He said: "I bear witness before Allah that they are the worst of people on earth." Allah the Mighty and Majestic had told His angels: "Do not punish them until Lot bears witness against them four times." When Lot made this statement, Gabriel said to his companions: "This is one." The statement was repeated among them until Lot had repeated the testimony four times. Then he brought them into the city.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And before this﴾, that is, before the coming of the messengers. It has also been said: before Lot.

(*kānū yaʿmalūna al-sayyiʾāt*) means that their habit was to come to men. When they came to Lot and approached his guests, Lot stood up to them in defence and said: (﴿These are my daughters﴾). This is a subject and predicate (*mubtadaʾ wa-khabar*). It has been disputed what he meant by "These are my daughters." It was said: he had three daughters from his own loins. It was also said: two, Zaytha and Zaʿwarāʾ. [In the originals and al-Alusi: "Ruthiyya," but in al-Tabari: "Ruthiyya."] It was said that they had two chiefs who were obeyed, and he wished to marry his two daughters to them. It was also said: in that situation he urged them toward marriage. Their custom permitted the marriage of an unbeliever to a believing woman, and this was permitted at the beginning of Islam and then abrogated (*nusikha*, meaning that a ruling was replaced by a later ruling). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married one of his daughters to 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab and the other to Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi' before the revelation, and both were unbelievers. A group, including Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, said: by his words "my daughters" he referred to women in general, since the prophet of a people is a father to them. This is strengthened by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them" (Q. 33:6). Another group said: the statement was only a rebuttal, and he did not intend it to be carried out. This view is reported from Abu 'Ubayda, as one says to someone who is forbidden to eat another's property: "Pork is more lawful to you than this." 'Ikrima said: he did not offer them his daughters or the daughters of his community; he said this only to make them leave.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They are purer for you﴾. This is a subject and predicate, meaning: I will marry them to you, so they are purer for you than what you desire, that is, more lawful. *Al-taṭahhur* means keeping oneself free from what is not lawful. Ibn 'Abbas said: their chiefs had proposed to his daughters and he did not accept them, and on that day he wished to ransom his guests with his daughters. The alif in *aṭhar* is not a comparative form such that one might suppose that there is purity in marrying men. Rather it is like your saying: "Allah is greater (*akbar*), higher (*aʿlā*) and more majestic (*ajall*)," even if there is no comparison. This is a permitted and common usage in the Arabic language, and no one contended against Allah the Exalted so that Allah would be greater than him. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb said on the day of Uhud: "*Uʿlu Hubal*" (exalt Hubal), that is, make your religion prevail. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Umar: "Say: Allah is higher and more majestic." Hubal was never high or majestic.

The majority read *hunna aṭhara* with a *raf*ʿ (nominative) on the *rāʾ*. Al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Amr read *hunna aṭhara* with a *naṣb* (accusative), as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Hunna* here is a pronoun of separation (*ʿimād*). Al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash do not permit *hunna* here to be a pronoun of separation, since it is a pronoun of separation only where the sentence is not complete without what follows, as in *kāna Zayd huwa akhāka*, so that the word *akhāka* is shown not to be a qualifier. Al-Zajjaj said: it shows that *kāna* needs a predicate. Others said: it shows that the predicate is definite or what is near to definite.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests﴾, that is, do not humiliate me and do not abase me. From this is the saying of Hassan:
"May my Lord disgrace you, O 'Utayb ibn Malik, and may He strike you with one of the thunderbolts before death.
You stretched out your hand against the Prophet deliberately, and you struck his mouth, and it was cut with the swords."
It may also be from *al-khazāya*, which is shame and embarrassment. Dhu al-Rumma said:
"Shame, when it overtook him after his tour, from the side of the rope, with anger mixed with it."
Another said:
"Of the white women who are not shamed when the wind presses their garment against them, or when the ornaments slip from their necks."
The word *ḍayf* (guest) applies to one, two, and many, using the form of the singular, since originally it is a verbal noun. The poet said:
"Do not let the knives of the butcher be lacking for the guest, and the guest is the most deserving visitor."
It may also be dual or plural, and the singular is more common, as in your saying: *rijāl ṣawm, fiṭr, zawr*. *Khazia al-rajul khazāyatan* means he felt shame, like *dhalla* and *hāna*. *Khazia khiẓyan* means he was disgraced. Both forms are *yakhzā*.

Then he rebuked them by saying: ﴿Is there not among you a man of rectitude?﴾, that is, a strong man who enjoins the good and forbids the evil. It has also been said: *rashīd* means one who has right guidance, or in the sense of *rāshid* or *murshid*, that is, righteous or one who reforms. Ibn 'Abbas said: a believer. Abu Malik said: one who forbids evil. It has been said: *al-rashīd* means *al-rushd*, and *al-rushd* and *al-rashād* are guidance and uprightness. It is permitted that it means *al-murshid*, like *al-ḥakīm* in the sense of *al-muḥkim*.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They said: "You certainly know that we have no claim on your daughters, and you know what we want."﴾ It is reported that the people of Lot proposed to his daughters, and he refused them, and their custom was that whoever was refused in a proposal to a woman would never be allowed to her. That is the meaning of Allah's words: "They said: 'You certainly know that we have no claim on your daughters.'" It is distant that this particular rule did not apply. The meaning of the statement is that we have no connection to your daughters, they are not our aim, and we have no custom of seeking that.

(*wa-innaka la-taʿlamu mā nurīd*) refers to the guests.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "If only I had strength against you﴾. When he saw their persistence in their error, and he was too weak against them and could not repel them, he wished that he had a helper to turn them back. He said, in a manner of grief and humility: "If only I had strength against you," that is, supporters and helpers. Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant a son. *Anna* is in a position of nominative case with an implied verb, its supposed form being: "if it occurred or happened." This applies to *anna* following *law*. The answer to *law* is omitted, meaning: I would have repelled the people of corruption and placed myself between them and what they wanted.

(أَوْ آوِي إِلى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ) أَيْ أَلْجَأُ وَأَنْضَوِي. وقرى "أَوْ آوِيَ" بِالنَّصْبِ عَطْفًا عَلَى "قُوَّةً" كَأَنَّهُ قَالَ: "لَوْ أَنَّ لِي بِكُمْ قُوَّةً" أَوْ إِيوَاءً إِلَى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ، أَيْ وَأَنْ آوِيَ، فَهُوَ مَنْصُوبٌ بِإِضْمَارِ "أَنْ". وَمُرَادُ لُوطٍ بِالرُّكْنِ الْعَشِيرَةُ، وَالْمَنَعَةُ بِالْكَثْرَةِ. وَبَلَغَ بِهِمْ قَبِيحُ فِعْلِهِمْ إِلَى قَوْلِهِ هَذَا مَعَ عِلْمِهِ بِمَا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى، فَيُرْوَى أَنَّ الْمَلَائِكَةَ وَجِدَتْ عَلَيْهِ حِينَ قَالَ هَذِهِ الْكَلِمَاتِ، وَقَالُوا: إِنَّ رُكْنَكَ لَشَدِيدٌ. وَفِي الْبُخَارِيِّ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ قال: "يَرْحَمُ اللَّهُ لُوطًا لَقَدْ كَانَ يَأْوِي إِلَى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ" الْحَدِيثَ، وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ فِي "الْبَقَرَةِ" [[See vol. 3, p. 298.]]. وَخَرَّجَهُ التِّرْمِذِيُّ وَزَادَ "مَا بَعَثَ اللَّهُ بَعْدَهُ نَبِيًّا إِلَّا فِي ثَرْوَةٍ مِنْ قَوْمِهِ". قَالَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عَمْرٍو: وَالثَّرْوَةُ الْكَثْرَةُ وَالْمَنَعَةُ، حَدِيثٌ حَسَنٌ. وَيُرْوَى أَنَّ لُوطًا عَلَيْهِ
