And it is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "There will come among the last of my Ummah a people whose men will be satisfied with men and whose women with women; when that happens, then await the punishment of the people of Lut, that Allah send upon them stones of sijjil." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: "And it is not far from the wrongdoers."

And in another narration from him, peace be upon him: "The nights and days will not pass until this Ummah makes lawful the backsides of men as they made lawful the backsides of women, and then groups of this Ummah will be struck by stones from your Lord."

It was also said: the meaning is that these towns are not far from the wrongdoers, and they lie between Syria and Medina. "Baʿīd" came in the masculine on the sense of "a far place." Regarding the stones that rained down there are two views: one, that they rained upon the cities when Gabriel lifted them up; the second, that they rained upon those among its people who were not in the cities and were outside of them.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verses 77–83 (part 1 of 3)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them.﴾ When the angels left Abraham, and the distance between Abraham and the town of Lot was four farsakh, two daughters of Lot, who were drawing water, saw the angels and noticed their handsome appearance. They said: "What is your business, and where have you come from?" The angels said: "From such-and-such a place. We want this town." The two girls said: "Its people are men of immorality." The angels said: "Is there anyone in it who will host us?" The two girls said: "Yes, this old man," and they pointed to Lot. When Lot saw their appearance, he feared for them on account of his people.

(*sā'a bihim*) means that their coming distressed him. It is said: *sā'a yasū'u*, which is intransitive, and *sā'ahu yasū'uhu*, which is also transitive. If you wish, you may vowel the *sīn* with a *ḍamma*, because its original vowel is *ḍamma*. The original form is *sūi'a bihim*, from *al-sū'*. The vowel of the *wāw* was transferred to the *sīn*, and so it became a *yā'*. If the *hamza* is lightened, its vowel is placed on the *yā'*, and you say *sī bihim* with a light pronunciation. There is also an irregular dialect with doubling (*shaddah*).

(*wa-ḍāqa bihim dharʿan*) means that his chest was constrained by their coming and he disliked it. It has also been said: his capacity and power were constrained. Its original sense is that a camel stretches its forelegs during its walk, each stride measured by the breadth of its step. When it is loaded beyond its capacity, it is constrained in that, weakens, and stretches out its neck. So "narrowness of the forelegs" is an expression for narrowness of capacity. It has also been said: it comes from *dhara'ahu al-qay'*, meaning that vomiting overcame him, that is, he could not contain the disagreeable matter within himself. His chest was constrained because of them, because of what he saw of their beauty and because of what he knew of the wickedness of his people.

(*wa-qāla hādhā yawmun ʿaṣīb*) means a severe day of evil. The poet said:
"And if you do not satisfy Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will be a grievous day for you in Iraq."
Another said:
"A grievous day that binds the champions, binding them as the strong binds the tall, slender ones."
It is said: *ʿaṣīb* and *ʿaṣʿaṣ* with intensive form, meaning a hateful day in which evil is gathered. *ʿaṣab* means that he gathered a band for evil, and from this comes *ʿuṣba* and *ʿiṣāba*, meaning people united in word, that is, united in themselves. The *ʿuṣba* of a man are those united with him by lineage. *Ta'aṣṣabtu li-fulān* means I became like his kinsmen. A man described as *maʿṣūb* (in Raghib's *Mufradat*: "*maʿṣūb al-khalq*" means *mudallaj al-khilqa*, that is, of compact build), meaning compact in creation.

(Allah the Exalted says): ﴿And his people came rushing toward him.﴾ This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Yuhraʿūn* means they hasten. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and other lexicographers said: *ihrāʿ* is only hastening together with trembling. It is said: *ahraʿa al-rajul ihrāʿan*, meaning he hastened in trembling, from cold, anger or fever. The participle is *muhraʿ*. Muhalhil said:
"They came rushing while they were captives, we leading them despite the noses."
Another said:
"With quick ones rushing toward him in haste."
This is like: *ūliʿa fulānun bi-l-amr* (he was obsessed with the matter), *urʿida Zayd* (Zayd trembled), and *zuhiya fulān* (he was proud). It is used only in this sense. It has also been said: *uhrifa*, meaning his greed urged him, and on this view *yuhraʿūn* means they are urged on. Whoever holds the first view says: it has been heard only as *uhriʿa al-rajul*, meaning he hastened, in the passive form. Ibn al-Qutiyya said: *hura'a al-insān hara'an* and *uhri'a*: he was driven and hurried. Al-Harawi said: it is said *hur'a al-rajul* and *uhri'a*, meaning he was urged. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi said: *yuhraʿūn* means they run. Al-Dahhak said: they strive. Ibn 'Uyayna said: as if they are being pushed. Shimr ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a walk between running and a quick trot. Al-Hasan said: a walk between two walks. The meanings are close.

The cause of their hastening, as reported, was that Lot's unbelieving wife, when she saw the guests, their beauty and their appearance, went out and came to the gatherings of her people, saying to them: "Lot has hosted tonight youths the like of whom has not been seen for beauty, and such and such." At that point they came rushing to him. It is also mentioned that when the messengers reached Lot's land, they found Lot in his field. It has been said: they found his daughter drawing water from the river of Sodom, so they asked her to guide them to someone who would host them. She saw their appearance and feared for them from the people of Lot. She said to them: "Wait here!" She went to her father and informed him. He came out to them. They said: "We want you to host us tonight." He said to them: "Have you not heard of the deeds of these people?" They said: "And what are their deeds?" He said: "I bear witness before Allah that they are the worst of people on earth." Allah the Mighty and Majestic had told His angels: "Do not punish them until Lot bears witness against them four times." When Lot made this statement, Gabriel said to his companions: "This is one." The statement was repeated among them until Lot had repeated the testimony four times. Then he brought them into the city.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And before this﴾, that is, before the coming of the messengers. It has also been said: before Lot.

(*kānū yaʿmalūna al-sayyiʾāt*) means that their habit was to come to men. When they came to Lot and approached his guests, Lot stood up to them in defence and said: (﴿These are my daughters﴾). This is a subject and predicate (*mubtadaʾ wa-khabar*). It has been disputed what he meant by "These are my daughters." It was said: he had three daughters from his own loins. It was also said: two, Zaytha and Zaʿwarāʾ. [In the originals and al-Alusi: "Ruthiyya," but in al-Tabari: "Ruthiyya."] It was said that they had two chiefs who were obeyed, and he wished to marry his two daughters to them. It was also said: in that situation he urged them toward marriage. Their custom permitted the marriage of an unbeliever to a believing woman, and this was permitted at the beginning of Islam and then abrogated (*nusikha*, meaning that a ruling was replaced by a later ruling). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married one of his daughters to 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab and the other to Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi' before the revelation, and both were unbelievers. A group, including Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, said: by his words "my daughters" he referred to women in general, since the prophet of a people is a father to them. This is strengthened by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them" (Q. 33:6). Another group said: the statement was only a rebuttal, and he did not intend it to be carried out. This view is reported from Abu 'Ubayda, as one says to someone who is forbidden to eat another's property: "Pork is more lawful to you than this." 'Ikrima said: he did not offer them his daughters or the daughters of his community; he said this only to make them leave.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They are purer for you﴾. This is a subject and predicate, meaning: I will marry them to you, so they are purer for you than what you desire, that is, more lawful. *Al-taṭahhur* means keeping oneself free from what is not lawful. Ibn 'Abbas said: their chiefs had proposed to his daughters and he did not accept them, and on that day he wished to ransom his guests with his daughters. The alif in *aṭhar* is not a comparative form such that one might suppose that there is purity in marrying men. Rather it is like your saying: "Allah is greater (*akbar*), higher (*aʿlā*) and more majestic (*ajall*)," even if there is no comparison. This is a permitted and common usage in the Arabic language, and no one contended against Allah the Exalted so that Allah would be greater than him. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb said on the day of Uhud: "*Uʿlu Hubal*" (exalt Hubal), that is, make your religion prevail. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Umar: "Say: Allah is higher and more majestic." Hubal was never high or majestic.

The majority read *hunna aṭhara* with a *raf*ʿ (nominative) on the *rāʾ*. Al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Amr read *hunna aṭhara* with a *naṣb* (accusative), as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Hunna* here is a pronoun of separation (*ʿimād*). Al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash do not permit *hunna* here to be a pronoun of separation, since it is a pronoun of separation only where the sentence is not complete without what follows, as in *kāna Zayd huwa akhāka*, so that the word *akhāka* is shown not to be a qualifier. Al-Zajjaj said: it shows that *kāna* needs a predicate. Others said: it shows that the predicate is definite or what is near to definite.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests﴾, that is, do not humiliate me and do not abase me. From this is the saying of Hassan:
"May my Lord disgrace you, O 'Utayb ibn Malik, and may He strike you with one of the thunderbolts before death.
You stretched out your hand against the Prophet deliberately, and you struck his mouth, and it was cut with the swords."
It may also be from *al-khazāya*, which is shame and embarrassment. Dhu al-Rumma said:
"Shame, when it overtook him after his tour, from the side of the rope, with anger mixed with it."
Another said:
"Of the white women who are not shamed when the wind presses their garment against them, or when the ornaments slip from their necks."
The word *ḍayf* (guest) applies to one, two, and many, using the form of the singular, since originally it is a verbal noun. The poet said:
"Do not let the knives of the butcher be lacking for the guest, and the guest is the most deserving visitor."
It may also be dual or plural, and the singular is more common, as in your saying: *rijāl ṣawm, fiṭr, zawr*. *Khazia al-rajul khazāyatan* means he felt shame, like *dhalla* and *hāna*. *Khazia khiẓyan* means he was disgraced. Both forms are *yakhzā*.

Then he rebuked them by saying: ﴿Is there not among you a man of rectitude?﴾, that is, a strong man who enjoins the good and forbids the evil. It has also been said: *rashīd* means one who has right guidance, or in the sense of *rāshid* or *murshid*, that is, righteous or one who reforms. Ibn 'Abbas said: a believer. Abu Malik said: one who forbids evil. It has been said: *al-rashīd* means *al-rushd*, and *al-rushd* and *al-rashād* are guidance and uprightness. It is permitted that it means *al-murshid*, like *al-ḥakīm* in the sense of *al-muḥkim*.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They said: "You certainly know that we have no claim on your daughters, and you know what we want."﴾ It is reported that the people of Lot proposed to his daughters, and he refused them, and their custom was that whoever was refused in a proposal to a woman would never be allowed to her. That is the meaning of Allah's words: "They said: 'You certainly know that we have no claim on your daughters.'" It is distant that this particular rule did not apply. The meaning of the statement is that we have no connection to your daughters, they are not our aim, and we have no custom of seeking that.

(*wa-innaka la-taʿlamu mā nurīd*) refers to the guests.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: "If only I had strength against you﴾. When he saw their persistence in their error, and he was too weak against them and could not repel them, he wished that he had a helper to turn them back. He said, in a manner of grief and humility: "If only I had strength against you," that is, supporters and helpers. Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant a son. *Anna* is in a position of nominative case with an implied verb, its supposed form being: "if it occurred or happened." This applies to *anna* following *law*. The answer to *law* is omitted, meaning: I would have repelled the people of corruption and placed myself between them and what they wanted.

(أَوْ آوِي إِلى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ) أَيْ أَلْجَأُ وَأَنْضَوِي. وقرى "أَوْ آوِيَ" بِالنَّصْبِ عَطْفًا عَلَى "قُوَّةً" كَأَنَّهُ قَالَ: "لَوْ أَنَّ لِي بِكُمْ قُوَّةً" أَوْ إِيوَاءً إِلَى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ، أَيْ وَأَنْ آوِيَ، فَهُوَ مَنْصُوبٌ بِإِضْمَارِ "أَنْ". وَمُرَادُ لُوطٍ بِالرُّكْنِ الْعَشِيرَةُ، وَالْمَنَعَةُ بِالْكَثْرَةِ. وَبَلَغَ بِهِمْ قَبِيحُ فِعْلِهِمْ إِلَى قَوْلِهِ هَذَا مَعَ عِلْمِهِ بِمَا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى، فَيُرْوَى أَنَّ الْمَلَائِكَةَ وَجِدَتْ عَلَيْهِ حِينَ قَالَ هَذِهِ الْكَلِمَاتِ، وَقَالُوا: إِنَّ رُكْنَكَ لَشَدِيدٌ. وَفِي الْبُخَارِيِّ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ قال: "يَرْحَمُ اللَّهُ لُوطًا لَقَدْ كَانَ يَأْوِي إِلَى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ" الْحَدِيثَ، وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ فِي "الْبَقَرَةِ" [[See vol. 3, p. 298.]]. وَخَرَّجَهُ التِّرْمِذِيُّ وَزَادَ "مَا بَعَثَ اللَّهُ بَعْدَهُ نَبِيًّا إِلَّا فِي ثَرْوَةٍ مِنْ قَوْمِهِ". قَالَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عَمْرٍو: وَالثَّرْوَةُ الْكَثْرَةُ وَالْمَنَعَةُ، حَدِيثٌ حَسَنٌ. وَيُرْوَى أَنَّ لُوطًا عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ لَمَّا غَلَبَهُ قَوْمُهُ، وَهَمُّوا بِكَسْرِ الْبَابِ وَهُوَ يُمْسِكُهُ، قَالَتْ لَهُ الرُّسُلُ: تَنَحَّ عَنِ الْبَابِ، فَتَنَحَّى وَانْفَتَحَ الْبَابُ، فَضَرَبَهُمْ جِبْرِيلُ بِجَنَاحِهِ فَطَمَسَ أَعْيُنَهُمْ، وَعَمُوا وَانْصَرَفُوا عَلَى أَعْقَابِهِمْ يَقُولُونَ: النَّجَاءَ، قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَلَقَدْ راوَدُوهُ عَنْ ضَيْفِهِ فَطَمَسْنا أَعْيُنَهُمْ﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 143.]] [القمر: ٣٧] (And they had certainly sought to seduce him from his guests, so We obliterated their eyes). وَقَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ وَأَهْلُ التَّفْسِيرِ: أَغْلَقَ لُوطٌ بَابَهُ وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ مَعَهُ فِي الدَّارِ، وَهُوَ يُنَاظِرُ قَوْمَهُ وَيُنَاشِدُهُمْ مِنْ وَرَاءِ الْبَابِ، وَهُمْ يُعَالِجُونَ تَسَوُّرَ الْجِدَارِ، فَلَمَّا رَأَتِ الْمَلَائِكَةُ مَا لَقِيَ مِنَ الْجَهْدِ وَالْكَرْبِ وَالنَّصَبِ بِسَبَبِهِمْ، قَالُوا: يَا لُوطُ إِنَّ رُكْنَكَ لَشَدِيدٌ، وَإِنَّهُمْ آتِيهِمْ عَذَابٌ غير مردود، وَإِنَّا رُسُلُ رَبِّكَ، فَافْتَحِ الْبَابَ وَدَعْنَا وَإِيَّاهُمْ، فَفَتَحَ الْبَابَ فَضَرَبَهُمْ جِبْرِيلُ بِجَنَاحِهِ عَلَى مَا تَقَدَّمَ. وَقِيلَ: أَخَذَ جِبْرِيلُ قَبْضَةً مِنْ تُرَابٍ فَأَذْرَاهَا فِي وُجُوهِهِمْ، فَأَوْصَلَ اللَّهُ إِلَى عَيْنِ مَنْ بَعُدَ وَمَنْ قَرُبَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ التُّرَابَ فَطَمَسَ أَعْيُنَهُمْ، فَلَمْ يَعْرِفُوا طَرِيقًا، وَلَا اهْتَدَوْا إِلَى بُيُوتِهِمْ، وَجَعَلُوا يَقُولُونَ: النَّجَاءَ النَّجَاءَ! فَإِنَّ فِي بَيْتِ لُوطٍ قَوْمًا هُمْ أَسْحَرُ مَنْ عَلَى وَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ، وَقَدْ سَحَرُونَا فَأَعْمَوْا أَبْصَارَنَا. وَجَعَلُوا يَقُولُونَ: يَا لُوطُ كَمَا أَنْتَ حَتَّى نُصْبِحَ فَسَتَرَى، يَتَوَعَّدُونَهُ.

(قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى:) قالُوا يَا لُوطُ إِنَّا رُسُلُ رَبِّكَ) لَمَّا رَأَتِ الْمَلَائِكَةُ حُزْنَهُ وَاضْطِرَابَهُ وَمُدَافَعَتَهُ عَرَّفُوهُ بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ، فَلَمَّا عَلِمَ أَنَّهُمْ رُسُلٌ مَكَّنَ قَوْمَهُ مِنَ الدُّخُولِ، فَأَمَرَّ جِبْرِيلُ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ يَدَهُ عَلَى أَعْيُنِهِمْ فَعَمُوا، وَعَلَى أَيْدِيهِمْ فَجَفَّتْ.

(لَنْ يَصِلُوا إِلَيْكَ) أَيْ بِمَكْرُوهٍ (فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ) قُرِئَ "فَأَسْرِ" بِوَصْلِ الْأَلِفِ وَقَطْعِهَا، لُغَتَانِ فَصِيحَتَانِ. قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ إِذا يَسْرِ﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 42.]] [الفجر: ٤] (And by the night when it passes), وقال: ﴿سُبْحانَ الَّذِي أَسْرى﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 204.]] [الإسراء: ١] (Glory be to the One who took His servant by night). وَقَالَ النَّابِغَةُ: فَجَمَعَ بَيْنَ اللُّغَتَيْنِ:
أَسْرَتْ [[Another reading: (سرت). He says: the cloud traveled through Orion; therefore he compared it to Orion.]] عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْجَوْزَاءِ سَارِيَةٌ ... تُزْجِي الشِّمَالُ عليه جامد الْبَرَدِ
(A cloud came travelling to him from Orion, driven by the north wind, bearing hard frozen hail.)
وَقَالَ آخَرُ:
حَيِّ النَّضِيرَةَ رَبَّةَ الْخِدْرِ ... أَسْرَتْ إِلَيْكَ وَلَمْ تَكُنْ تَسْرِي
(Greet Al-Nadira, mistress of the curtained litter, who came to you by night, though she had never before travelled by night.)
وَقَدْ قِيلَ: "فَأَسْرِ" بالقطع إذا سار من أول الليل، وَسَرَى إِذَا سَارَ مِنْ آخِرِهِ، وَلَا يُقَالُ فِي النَّهَارِ إِلَّا سَارَ. وَقَالَ لَبِيَدٌ:
إِذَا الْمَرْءُ أَسْرَى لَيْلَةً ظَنَّ أَنَّهُ ... قَضَى عَمَلًا وَالْمَرْءُ مَا عَاشَ عَامِلُ
(When a man travels through the night, he thinks he has finished his task, but a man who lives is always at work.)
وَقَالَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ رَوَاحَةَ:
عِنْدَ الصَّبَاحِ يَحْمَدُ الْقَوْمُ السُّرَى ... وَتَنْجَلِي عَنْهُمْ غَيَابَاتُ الْكَرَى
(At dawn the people praise the night journey, and the shadows of sleep lift from them.)

(بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ) قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ: بِطَائِفَةٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ. الضَّحَّاكُ: بِبَقِيَّةٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ. قَتَادَةُ: بَعْدَ مُضِيِّ صَدْرٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ. الْأَخْفَشُ: بَعْدَ جُنْحٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ. ابْنُ الْأَعْرَابِيِّ: بِسَاعَةٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ. وَقِيلَ: بِظُلْمَةٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ. وَقِيلَ: بَعْدَ هَدْءٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ. وقيل: هزيع مِنَ اللَّيْلِ. وَكُلُّهَا مُتَقَارِبَةٌ، وَقِيلَ: إِنَّهُ نِصْفُ اللَّيْلِ، مَأْخُوذٌ مِنْ قَطَعَهُ نِصْفَيْنِ، وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُ الشاعر [[He is Malik ibn Kinana.]]:
ونائحة تنوح بقطع ليل ... على رجل بِقَارِعَةِ الصَّعِيدِ
(And a wailing woman mourns in the middle of the night over a man at the edge of the highway.)
فَإِنْ قِيلَ: السُّرَى لَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا بِاللَّيْلِ، فَمَا مَعْنَى "بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ"؟ فَالْجَوَابُ: أَنَّهُ لَوْ لَمْ يَقُلْ: "بِقِطْعٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ" جَازَ أَنْ يَكُونَ أَوَّلَهُ.

(وَلا يَلْتَفِتْ مِنْكُمْ أَحَدٌ) أَيْ لَا يَنْظُرُ وَرَاءَهُ مِنْكُمْ أحد، قال مُجَاهِدٌ. ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ: لَا يَتَخَلَّفُ مِنْكُمْ أَحَدٌ. عَلِيُّ بْنُ عِيسَى: لَا يَشْتَغِلُ مِنْكُمْ أَحَدٌ بِمَا يُخَلِّفُهُ مِنْ مَالٍ أَوْ مَتَاعٍ.

(إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ) بِالنَّصْبِ، وَهِيَ الْقِرَاءَةُ الْوَاضِحَةُ الْبَيِّنَةُ الْمَعْنَى، أَيْ فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ. وَكَذَا فِي قِرَاءَةِ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ "فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ" فَهُوَ اسْتِثْنَاءٌ مِنَ الْأَهْلِ. وَعَلَى هَذَا لَمْ يَخْرُجْ بِهَا مَعَهُ. وَقَدْ قَالَ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وجل: ﴿كانَتْ مِنَ الْغابِرِينَ﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 241.]] [الأعراف: ٨٣] (She was among those who remained behind), أَيْ مِنَ الْبَاقِينَ. وَقَرَأَ أَبُو عَمْرٍو وَابْنُ كَثِيرٍ: "إِلَّا امْرَأَتُكُ" بِالرَّفْعِ عَلَى الْبَدَلِ مِنْ "أَحَدٌ". وَأَنْكَرَ هَذِهِ الْقِرَاءَةَ جَمَاعَةٌ مِنْهُمْ أَبُو عُبَيْدٍ، وَقَالَ: لَا يَصِحُّ ذَلِكَ إِلَّا بِرَفْعِ "يَلْتَفِتْ" وَيَكُونُ نَعْتًا، لِأَنَّ الْمَعْنَى يَصِيرُ- إِذَا أُبْدِلَتْ وَجُزِمَتْ- أَنَّ الْمَرْأَةَ أُبِيحَ لَهَا الِالْتِفَاتُ، وَلَيْسَ الْمَعْنَى كَذَلِكَ. قَالَ النَّحَّاسُ: وَهَذَا الْحَمْلُ مِنْ أَبِي عُبَيْدٍ وَغَيْرِهِ عَلَى مِثْلِ أَبِي عَمْرٍو مَعَ جَلَالَتِهِ وَمَحَلِّهِ مِنَ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ لَا يَجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ، وَالرَّفْعُ عَلَى الْبَدَلِ لَهُ مَعْنًى صَحِيحٌ، وَالتَّأْوِيلُ لَهُ عَلَى مَا حَكَى مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ الْوَلِيدِ عَنْ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ يَزِيدَ أَنْ يَقُولَ الرَّجُلَ لِحَاجِبِهِ: لَا يَخْرُجْ فُلَانٌ، فَلَفْظُ النَّهْيِ لِفُلَانٍ وَمَعْنَاهُ لِلْمُخَاطَبِ، أَيْ لَا تَدَعْهُ يَخْرُجُ، وَمِثْلُهُ قَوْلُكَ: لَا يَقُمْ أَحَدٌ إِلَّا زَيْدٌ، يَكُونُ مَعْنَاهُ: انْهَهُمْ عَنِ الْقِيَامِ إِلَّا زَيْدًا، وَكَذَلِكَ النَّهْيُ لِلُوطٍ وَلَفْظُهُ لِغَيْرِهِ، كَأَنَّهُ قَالَ: انْهَهُمْ لَا يَلْتَفِتُ مِنْهُمْ أَحَدٌ إلا امرأتك فإنها تلتفت وتهلك، وأن النَّهْيِ عَنِ الِالْتِفَاتِ لِأَنَّهُ كَلَامٌ تَامٌّ، أَيْ لَا يَلْتَفِتُ، مِنْكُمْ أَحَدٌ إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ فَإِنَّهَا تَلْتَفِتُ وَتَهْلَكُ، وَأَنَّ لُوطًا خَرَجَ بِهَا، وَنَهَى مَنْ مَعَهُ مِمَّنْ أَسْرَى بِهِمْ أَلَّا يَلْتَفِتَ، فَلَمْ يَلْتَفِتْ مِنْهُمْ أَحَدٌ سِوَى زَوْجَتِهِ، فَإِنَّهَا لما سمعت هدة العذاب التفتت وقالت: وا قوماه! فأدركها حجر فقتلها.

(إِنَّهُ مُصِيبُها) أَيْ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ، وَالْكِنَايَةُ فِي "إِنَّهُ" تَرْجِعُ إلى الأمر والشأن، فَإِنَّ الْأَمْرَ وَالشَّأْنَ وَالْقِصَّةَ.

(مُصِيبُها مَا أَصابَهُمْ إِنَّ مَوْعِدَهُمُ الصُّبْحُ) لَمَّا قَالَتِ الْمَلَائِكَةُ: ﴿إِنَّا مُهْلِكُوا أَهْلِ هذِهِ الْقَرْيَةِ﴾ [العنكبوت: ٣١] (Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town) قَالَ لُوطٌ: الْآنَ الْآنَ. اسْتَعْجَلَهُمْ بِالْعَذَابِ لِغَيْظِهِ عَلَى قَوْمِهِ، فَقَالُوا: (أَلَيْسَ الصُّبْحُ بِقَرِيبٍ) (Is not the morning near?) وَقَرَأَ عِيسَى بْنُ عُمَرَ "أَلَيْسَ الصُّبُحُ" بِضَمِّ الْبَاءِ وَهِيَ لُغَةٌ. وَيَحْتَمِلُ أَنْ يَكُونَ جَعَلَ الصُّبْحَ مِيقَاتًا لِهَلَاكِهِمْ، لِأَنَّ النُّفُوسَ فِيهِ أَوْدَعُ، وَالنَّاسَ فِيهِ أَجْمَعُ. وَقَالَ بَعْضُ أَهْلِ التَّفْسِيرِ: إِنَّ لُوطًا خَرَجَ بِابْنَتَيْهِ لَيْسَ مَعَهُ غَيْرُهُمَا عِنْدَ طُلُوعِ الْفَجْرِ، وَأَنَّ الْمَلَائِكَةَ قَالَتْ لَهُ: إِنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ وَكَّلَ بِهَذِهِ الْقَرْيَةِ مَلَائِكَةً مَعَهُمْ صَوْتُ رَعْدٍ، وَخَطْفُ بَرْقٍ، وَصَوَاعِقُ عَظِيمَةٌ، وَقَدْ ذَكَرْنَا لَهُمْ أَنَّ لُوطًا سَيَخْرُجُ فَلَا تُؤْذُوهُ، وَأَمَارَتُهُ أَنَّهُ لَا يَلْتَفِتُ، وَلَا تَلْتَفِتُ ابْنَتَاهُ فَلَا يَهُولَنَّكَ مَا تَرَى. فَخَرَجَ لُوطٌ وَطَوَى اللَّهُ لَهُ الْأَرْضَ فِي وَقْتِهِ حَتَّى نَجَا وَوَصَلَ إِلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ.

(قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى:) فَلَمَّا جاءَ أَمْرُنا) أَيْ عَذَابُنَا.

(جَعَلْنا عالِيَها سافِلَها) وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ جِبْرِيلَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ أَدْخَلَ جَنَاحَهُ تَحْتَ قُرَى قَوْمِ لُوطٍ، وَهِيَ خَمْسٌ: سَدُومُ- وَهِيَ الْقَرْيَةُ الْعُظْمَى،- وَعَامُورَا، وَدَادُومَا، وضعوه، وَقَتَمُ [[In manuscripts ع, ز and ك: Qamwara, Radma and Sa'wa; there is disagreement over the spelling of these towns.]]، فَرَفَعَهَا مِنْ تُخُومِ الْأَرْضِ حَتَّى أَدْنَاهَا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ بما في فِيهَا، حَتَّى سَمِعَ أَهْلُ السَّمَاءِ نَهِيقَ حُمُرِهِمْ وَصِيَاحَ دِيَكَتِهِمْ، لَمْ تَنْكَفِئْ لَهُمْ جَرَّةٌ، وَلَمْ ينكسر [[In manuscript ى: "ينكشف" (was not uncovered).]] لهم إناء، ثم نكسوا على رؤوسهم، وَأَتْبَعَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِالْحِجَارَةِ. مُقَاتِلٌ. أُهْلِكَتْ أَرْبَعَةٌ، وَنَجَتْ ضعوه. وَقِيلَ: غَيْرُ هَذَا، وَاللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ. قَوْلُهُ تعالى: (وَأَمْطَرْنا عَلَيْهِمْ حِجارَةً مِنْ سِجِّيلٍ) دَلِيلٌ عَلَى أَنَّ مَنْ فَعَلَ فِعْلَهُمْ حُكْمُهُ الرَّجْمُ، وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ فِي "الْأَعْرَافِ" [[See vol. 7, p. 243.]]. وَفِي التَّفْسِيرِ: أَمْطَرْنَا فِي الْعَذَابِ، وَمَطَرْنَا فِي الرَّحْمَةِ. وَأَمَّا كَلَامُ الْعَرَبِ فَيُقَالُ: مَطَرَتِ السماء وأمطرت: حكاه الهروي. واختلف في "سِجِّيلٍ" فَقَالَ النَّحَّاسُ [[Thus in manuscript أ; in manuscripts ز, ع, ك and ووى: "al-Bukhari".]]: السِّجِّيلُ الشَّدِيدُ الْكَثِيرُ، وَسِجِّيلٌ وَسِجِّينٌ اللَّامُ وَالنُّونُ أُخْتَانِ. وَقَالَ أَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ: السِّجِّيلُ الشَّدِيدُ، وَأَنْشَدَ [[The full line will appear later on p. 83.]]
ضَرْبًا تَوَاصَى بِهِ الْأَبْطَالُ سِجِّينًا قَالَ النَّحَّاسُ: وَرَدَّ عَلَيْهِ هَذَا الْقَوْلَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ مُسْلِمٍ وَقَالَ: هَذَا سِجِّينٌ وَذَلِكَ سِجِّيلٌ فَكَيْفَ يُسْتَشْهَدُ بِهِ؟! قَالَ النَّحَّاسُ: وَهَذَا الرَّدُّ لَا يَلْزَمُ، لِأَنَّ أَبَا عُبَيْدَةَ ذَهَبَ إِلَى أَنَّ اللَّامَ تُبْدَلُ مِنَ النُّونِ لِقُرْبِ إِحْدَاهُمَا مِنَ الْأُخْرَى، وَقَوْلُ أَبِي عُبَيْدَةَ يُرَدُّ مِنْ جِهَةٍ أُخْرَى، وَهِيَ أَنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ عَلَى قَوْلِهِ لَكَانَ حِجَارَةً سِجِّيلًا، لِأَنَّهُ لَا يُقَالُ: حِجَارَةٌ مِنْ شَدِيدٍ، لِأَنَّ شَدِيدًا نَعْتٌ. وَحَكَى أَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ عَنِ الْفَرَّاءِ أَنَّهُ قَدْ يُقَالُ لِحِجَارَةِ الْأَرْحَاءِ سِجِّيلٌ. وَحَكَى عَنْهُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ الْجَهْمِ أَنَّ سِجِّيلًا طِينٌ يُطْبَخُ حَتَّى يَصِيرَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْأَرْحَاءِ. وَقَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْهُمُ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ وَسَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ وَابْنُ إِسْحَاقَ: إِنَّ سِجِّيلًا لَفْظَةٌ غَيْرُ عَرَبِيَّةٍ عُرِّبَتْ، أَصْلُهَا سنج وجيل. وَيُقَالُ: سنك وكيل، بِالْكَافِ مَوْضِعَ الْجِيمِ، وَهُمَا بِالْفَارِسِيَّةِ حَجَرٌ وَطِينٌ عَرَّبَتْهُمَا الْعَرَبُ فَجَعَلَتْهُمَا اسْمًا وَاحِدًا. وَقِيلَ: هُوَ مِنْ لُغَةِ الْعَرَبِ. وَقَالَ قَتَادَةُ وَعِكْرِمَةُ: السِّجِّيلُ الطِّينُ بِدَلِيلِ قَوْلِهِ ﴿لِنُرْسِلَ عَلَيْهِمْ حِجارَةً مِنْ طِينٍ﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 47.]] [الذاريات: ٣٣] (To send down upon them stones of clay). وَقَالَ الْحَسَنُ: كَانَ أَصْلُ الْحِجَارَةِ طِينًا فَشُدِّدَتْ. وَالسِّجِّيلُ عِنْدَ الْعَرَبِ كُلُّ شَدِيدٍ صُلْبٍ. وَقَالَ الضَّحَّاكُ: يَعْنِي الْآجُرَّ. وَقَالَ ابْنُ زَيْدٍ: طِينٌ طُبِخَ حَتَّى كَانَ كَالْآجُرِّ، وَعَنْهُ أَنَّ سِجِّيلًا اسْمُ السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا، ذَكَرَهُ الْمَهْدَوِيُّ، وَحَكَاهُ الثَّعْلَبِيُّ عَنْ أَبِي الْعَالِيَةِ، وَقَالَ ابْنُ عَطِيَّةَ: وَهَذَا ضَعِيفٌ يَرُدُّهُ وَصْفُهُ بِ "مَنْضُودٍ". وَعَنْ عِكْرِمَةَ: أَنَّهُ بَحْرٌ مُعَلَّقٌ فِي الْهَوَاءِ بَيْنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ مِنْهُ نَزَلَتِ الْحِجَارَةُ. وَقِيلَ: هِيَ جِبَالٌ فِي السَّمَاءِ، وَهِيَ الَّتِي أَشَارَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى إِلَيْهَا بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَيُنَزِّلُ مِنَ السَّماءِ مِنْ جِبالٍ فِيها مِنْ بَرَدٍ﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 289.]] [النور: ٤٣] (And He sends down from the sky mountains containing hail). وَقِيلَ: هُوَ مِمَّا سُجِّلَ لَهُمْ أَيْ كُتِبَ لَهُمْ أَنْ يُصِيبَهُمْ، فَهُوَ فِي مَعْنَى سِجِّينٍ، قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَما أَدْراكَ مَا سِجِّينٌ. كِتابٌ مَرْقُومٌ﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 254.]] [المطففين: ٨] (And what can make you know what Sijjin is? It is a written register) قَالَهُ الزَّجَّاجُ وَاخْتَارَهُ. وَقِيلَ: هُوَ فِعِّيلٌ مِنْ أَسْجَلْتُهُ أَيْ أَرْسَلْتُهُ، فَكَأَنَّهَا مُرْسَلَةٌ عَلَيْهِمْ. وَقِيلَ: هُوَ مِنْ أَسْجَلْتُهُ إِذَا أَعْطَيْتُهُ، فَكَأَنَّهُ عَذَابٌ أُعْطُوهُ، قَالَ [[The verse is by al-Fadl ibn al-Abbas ibn Utba ibn Abi Lahab. "Musajala" means a contest in which two drawers of water each draw a bucket equal to the other's; whoever falters loses, and the Arabs used it as a figure for boasting. "Al-Karab" is the rope tied around the bucket below the first rope.]]:
مَنْ يُسَاجِلْنِي يُسَاجِلْ مَاجِدًا ... يَمْلَأُ الدلو إلى عقد الكرب
(Whoever competes with me in drawing water will meet a noble man who fills the bucket up to the knot of the rope.)
وَقَالَ أَهْلُ الْمَعَانِي: السِّجِّيلُ وَالسِّجِّينُ الشَّدِيدُ مِنَ الْحَجَرِ وَالضَّرْبِ، قَالَ ابْنُ مُقْبِلٍ:

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 77–83 (part 3 of 3):

وَرَجْلَةٍ يَضْرِبُونَ الْبَيْضَ ضَاحِيَةً [[Another narration in Lisan: (yadribuna al-bayḍa ʿan ʿaraḍ).]] ... ḍarban tawaṣṣā bihi al-abṭālu sijjīnā

(Manḍūd) Ibn ʿAbbas said: consecutive (mutatābiʿ). Qatadah said: some of them placed upon others (nuḍida baʿḍuhā fawqa baʿḍ). al-Rabiʿ said: some of it was placed upon other parts until it became one body (ḥattā ṣāra jasadan wāḥidan). ʿIkrimah said: arranged in rows (maṣfūf). Some of them said: compacted (marṣūṣ), and the meaning is close. It is said: "I piled up the goods and the milk" (naḍadtu al-matāʿ wa al-laban) when I placed some of it upon others; so it is manḍūd, naḍīd and naḍad. He said:

wa-raffaʿtuhu ilā al-sijfayni fa-l-naḍad

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said: prepared (muʿadd), meaning it is of what Allah prepared for His oppressive enemies.

(Musawwamah) i.e. marked (muʿallamah), from al-simā, which is the sign; that is, there were on them things like seals. It was also said: on every stone was written the name of the one it was thrown at, and they did not resemble the stones of the earth. al-Farrāʾ said: they claimed that they were with redness and blackness in whiteness, and that is their being marked (taswīmuhā). Kaʿb said: they were marked with whiteness and redness. The poet said:

[[The verse is by Usayd ibn ʿUnqaʾ al-Fazari, praising ʿUmayla when he divided his wealth with him, and after it:
As if al-Thurayya were hung upon his neck, and upon his neck al-Shiʿra, and upon his face the moon.
And His saying: (He has a appearance that does not burden the sight), i.e. whoever sees him rejoices in him.]]

ghulāmun ramāhu Allāhu bi-l-ḥusni yāfiʿan ... lahu simyāʾu lā tashuqqu ʿalā al-baṣar

And "musawwamah" is an attribute of stones. And "manḍūd" is an attribute of "sijjīl." And in His saying: (with your Lord) there is evidence that they are not of the stones of the earth, as said by al-Hasan.

(wa-mā hiya mina al-ẓālimīna bi-baʿīd) meaning the people of Lut, i.e. it would not miss them. Mujahid said: it terrifies Quraysh; the meaning is: the stones are not far from the oppressors of your people, O Muhammad. Qatadah and ʿIkrimah said: it means the oppressors of this Ummah; by Allah, Allah has not protected any oppressor from it since. And it is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "There will come among the last of my Ummah a people whose men will be satisfied with men and whose women with women; when that happens, then await the punishment of the people of Lut, that Allah send upon them stones of sijjil." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: "And it is not far from the wrongdoers."

And in another narration from him, peace be upon him: "The nights and days will not pass until this Ummah makes lawful the backsides of men as they made lawful the backsides of women, and then groups of this Ummah will be struck by stones from your Lord."

It was also said: the meaning is that these towns are not far from the wrongdoers, and they lie between Syria and Medina. "Baʿīd" came in the masculine on the sense of "a far place." Regarding the stones that rained down there are two views: one, that they rained upon the cities when Gabriel lifted them up; the second, that they rained upon those among its people who were not in the cities and were outside of them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 84–95 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾. That is, We sent [him] to Madyan, and Madyan is the people of Shu'ayb. Regarding their being called by this name there are two opinions. The first is that they are the sons of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, so it is said "Madyan" while meaning "the sons of Madyan," just as one says "Mudar" while meaning "the sons of Mudar." The second is that it is the name of their city, and they were attributed to it. Al-Nahhas said: Madyan is not declined, because it is the name of a city. This meaning, with additions, has already been discussed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 257.]].

(﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾). This has already been covered.

(﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance﴾). Despite their disbelief, they were people of cheating and fraud. When a seller came to them with food, they took it by a greater measure, and they exacted to the utmost of what they could [[from ع.]] and did wrong. And if a buyer came to them for food, they sold to him by a short measure, and were stingy with him to the utmost of their ability. So they were commanded to belief, abandoning shirk, and to fulfil [the measure], forbidding fraud.

(﴿Indeed I see you in prosperity﴾), that is, in abundance of provision and plenty of blessings. Al-Hasan said: their prices were cheap.

(﴿And indeed I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾). He described the day as "encompassing," and he meant that day was described as encompassing them, for when the day of punishment encompasses them, the punishment has encompassed them. It is like your saying: "a severe day," meaning its heat is severe. Opinions differ about that punishment. It is said: it is the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. It is said: it is the punishment of annihilation in this world. It is said: it is the high price of goods; this meaning was related from Ibn 'Abbas. And in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No people have displayed fraud in measure and balance except that Allah afflicts them with drought and high prices." This has already been mentioned.

The Exalted said: ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice﴾. He commanded fulfilment after forbidding fraud, for emphasis. Al-Iyfa' is completion. "With justice" means with equity and right, and the intent is that each one who has a share should receive his share. He does not mean fulfilling the measure and the weighed thing, because he did not say "fulfil with the measure and with the balance"; rather he meant that you should not reduce the size of the measure below what is customary, and likewise the weights.

(﴿And do not deprive people of their things﴾), that is, do not diminish for them anything of what they deserve.

(﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, acting corruptly﴾). He made clear that dishonesty in measure and balance is an exaggeration of corruption on the earth. More on this has passed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 248.]], and praise be to Allah.

The Exalted said: (﴿What remains from Allah is better for you﴾), that is, what Allah leaves for you after giving rights in justice is more blessed and better in outcome than what you keep for yourselves from the surplus of fraud through tyranny and injustice. Al-Tabari and others said this. Mujahid said: "What remains from Allah is better for you" means His obedience. Al-Rabi' said: the charge of Allah. Al-Farra' said: the watchfulness of Allah. Ibn Zayd: the mercy of Allah. Qatadah and al-Hasan: your portion from your Lord is better for you. Ibn 'Abbas said: the provision of Allah is better for you.

(﴿If you are believers﴾). He made this conditional because they would only recognise the truth of this if they were believers. It was said: it is possible that they acknowledged that Allah is their Creator, so he addressed them with this.

(﴿And I am not a watcher over you﴾), that is, a guardian watching you at your measuring and weighing; that is, it is not possible for me to witness every dealing that proceeds from you so that I may hold you to account for giving the right. It was said: that is, it is not within my power to protect you from the removal of Allah's blessings upon you through your disobediences.

(The Exalted said:) They said: ﴿O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped﴾? (It is also read "aslatuka" without the plural.)

(﴿Or that we not do with our wealth what we please﴾). "An" is in the accusative position. Al-Kisa'i said: its position is genitive, by the implied preposition "ba'".

It is related that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, used to pray much, persistent in worship, both obligatory and voluntary, and he would say: "Prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing." So when he commanded them and forbade them, they reproached him for what they saw him constantly doing of much prayer, and they mocked him, saying what Allah reported of them. It was said: here "prayer" means recitation; this was said by Sufyan from al-A'mash, that is, your recitation commands you. By this it is shown that they were disbelievers. Al-Hasan said: Allah did not send any prophet without making prayer and zakat obligatory upon him.

(﴿Or that we do with our wealth what we will﴾). Al-Farra' claimed that the sense is: "Or that you forbid us to do with our wealth what we will." Al-Sulami and al-Dahhak ibn Qays read "aw an taf'ala fi amwalina ma tasha'" with "ta" in both verbs, and the meaning is: what you will, O Shu'ayb. Al-Nahhas said: "aw an" in this reading is conjoined to the first "an." It is related from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: among what he forbade them was clipping the dirhams [[Clipping means cutting something from its edges.]]. It was also said: the meaning of "or that we do with our wealth what we will" is: if we agree among ourselves to diminish, why do you prevent us from it?

(﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾). They meant: in your own estimation, by your claim. Similar to this is what is said about Abu Jahl: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 151.]] [al-Dukhan: 49], that is, in your own estimation, by your claim. It was said: they said it in the manner of mockery and derision; Qatadah said so. From this is their saying to the Abyssinian: "Abu al-Bayda'," and to the white man: "Abu al-Jawn" [[al-Jawn here means the black one.]]; and from this is the saying of the guardians of Hell to Abu Jahl: "Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: the Arabs describe a thing by its opposite for euphemism and optimism, as the stung one is called "safe" and the desert "mafaza." It was said: it is an allusion intended as abuse. The best of all these, and what precedes it confirms its soundness, is that: indeed you are truly the forbearing, the rightly guided; how then do you command us to abandon what our fathers worshipped! It is also indicated by "Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped," which they denied, seeing his much prayer and worship, and that he is forbearing and rightly guided, in that he should command them to abandon what their fathers used to worship. And after it, there is also what indicates this: ﴿He said: O my people, have you considered if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me from Himself good provision﴾, that is, shall I not forbid you from misguidance? All of this indicates that they said it in its literal sense, and that this was their belief concerning him. Similar to this meaning is the saying of the Jews of Banu Qurayza to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said to them: "O brothers of the apes" [[In one manuscript: "the apes and the swine." It has passed in vol. 6, p. 236 that this was also said by the Muslims to them.]]; they said: "O Muhammad, we did not know you to be ignorant!"

Issue: The people of tafsir said: among what he forbade them, and for which they were punished, was cutting dinars and dirhams. They used to nibble from the edges of the sound coins so that the shavings would be a surplus for them; they dealt with the sound coins by count, and with the clipped ones by weight, and they cheated in weighing. Ibn Wahb said Malik said: they used to break dinars and dirhams. Likewise a group of the earlier exegetes said, such as Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Zayd ibn Aslam and others, and breaking them is a great sin. In the Book of Abu Dawud, from 'Alqama ibn 'Abd Allah, from his father, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that the currency of the Muslims that is current among them be broken, except out of necessity, for if it is sound its value stands and its benefit appears, and if it is broken it becomes mere goods and its benefit is lost, which harms the people; and for this reason it is forbidden. It has been said regarding the interpretation of Allah's words: ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 215.]] [al-Naml: 48], that they used to break dirhams; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: they claimed that after Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi there was no one in Medina more knowledgeable in the interpretation of the Qur'an than Zayd ibn Aslam.

Issue: Asbagh said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim ibn Khalid ibn Junada, client of Zayd ibn al-Harith al-'Utaqi, said: whoever breaks them, his testimony is not accepted, and if he pleads ignorance he is not excused; this is not a place for excuse. Ibn al-'Arabi said: as for his saying that his testimony is not accepted, it is because he has committed a major sin, and major sins remove uprightness, not minor ones. As for his saying that his plea of ignorance in this is not accepted, it is because this is a clear matter that is not hidden from anyone; an excuse is accepted only when the truthfulness of it appears, or when the truth of it is hidden and Allah knows it better than the servant, as Malik said.

Issue: When this is disobedience and corruption, by which testimony is rejected, the one who does it is punished. Ibn al-Musayyab passed by a man who had been flogged, and said: "What is this?" A man said: "He clips the dinars and dirhams." Ibn al-Musayyab said: "This is of the corruption on the earth," and he did not object to his flogging; similar is related from Sufyan. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Nujaybi said: I was sitting with 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, who was then governor of Medina [[In one manuscript: "in Medina"; in another: "Commander of the Believers."]], when a man was brought who clipped dirhams, and it had been witnessed against him; he beat him, shaved his head, and ordered that he be paraded, and commanded him to say: "This is the punishment of whoever clips dirhams." Then he ordered that he be returned to him [i.e., his place], and said: "What prevented me from cutting off your hand was only that I had not previously set down a ruling on this before today, and I have now set it down; whoever wishes, let him cut." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: as for his being whipped with the whip, there is no dispute about it; as for shaving his head, 'Umar did it, and I myself, during the days of my judgeship among the people, used to beat and shave; I used to do that only to one whose hair is an aid to him in disobedience and a means to adorn himself in corruption, and this is what is obligatory for every means to disobedience: that it be cut off, if it does not affect the body. As for cutting off his hand, 'Umar took that from the section on theft, for clipping dirhams is not breaking them, since breaking is destroying their quality while clipping is diminishing their quantity; it is taking wealth in a hidden manner. If it is said: is not guarding the basis for amputation? We say: it is possible that 'Umar held that preparing them for distinguishing between creatures, a dinar or a dirham, is their guard, and the guard of each thing is according to its condition. Ibn al-Zubayr also implemented this and cut off the hand of a man for clipping dinars and dirhams. Our scholars, the Malikis, have said: the dinars and dirhams are the seals of Allah, upon which is His name; if one who breaks a seal of Allah were to be amputated according to the view of the people of interpretation, he would deserve it; or whoever breaks a ruler's seal bearing his name is disciplined, but Allah's seal is that by which needs are fulfilled, so the two are not equal in punishment. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I hold that one should be amputated for clipping them, not for breaking them. I used to do this during my tenure as judge, but I was surrounded by the ignorant, and I did not love to be [[In manuscript ع: "I was not beaten"; in others: "I liked."]] exposed to the talk of envious misguided people, so whoever is able to do it one day, from the people of truth, let him do it seeking reward from Allah the Exalted.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verses 84–95 (part 2 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾. This was discussed earlier. (﴿And He has provided me from Himself with good provision﴾), meaning abundant and lawful. Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was wealthy. This is what Ibn 'Abbas and others said. It was also said that he meant by it guidance, success, knowledge and understanding. There is an ellipsis in the speech, which is what we have mentioned, meaning: "Shall I not forbid you from error?" It was also said that the meaning is: "Tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, shall I follow the misguided?" It was also said that the meaning is: "Tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, [will] you order me [[In (ʿ): afa-tamurūnanī, "will you order me?"]] to disobey in cheating and short-measuring, when God has made me independent of it [[from (ʿ) and (ā)]]?"

(﴿And I do not wish to oppose you﴾): the phrase is in the accusative position governed by "urīdu" (I wish).

(﴿in what I forbid you from﴾): meaning, I do not forbid you from anything and then commit it myself, just as I do not abandon what I have commanded you to do.

(﴿I only wish reform, as much as I am able﴾): meaning, I only wish to do what is right, that you may reform your worldly affairs through justice and your hereafter through worship. He said "as much as I am able" because ability is one of the conditions of the act, not of the wish. The word "mā" here is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: "I only wish reform with my utmost effort and capacity."

(﴿And my success is not but through God﴾): meaning, my right guidance. Tawfīq (success) means right guidance.

(﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾): meaning, I have depended upon Him.

(﴿and to Him I turn in repentance﴾): meaning, I return to Him in whatever calamities befall me. It was also said: "To Him I return in the Hereafter." It was also said that inābah (turning) means supplication, and the meaning is: "To Him I supplicate."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, let not my opposition bring upon you﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "yujrimannakum" (cause you to incur).

(﴿my opposition﴾) is in the nominative position.

(﴿that there befall you﴾) is in the accusative position. Meaning: let not my enmity toward you lead you to abandon faith, so that there befalls you what befell the disbelievers [[from (ʿ) and (wāw)]] before you. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said: "Let not my opposition earn you the punishment, so that you are struck by it as it struck those before you," as said by al-Zajjaj. The meaning of "yajrimannakum" has already been mentioned in "al-Ma'idah" [[See vol. 6, p. 44 and following.]], and "al-shiqaq" (opposition) in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 143.]]. It means enmity, as said by al-Suddi, and from it is the verse of al-Akhtal:

*Is there no one who conveys from me a message [[Here "rasūl" means "message." In the Diwan: "mubhigh qabasan" (a messenger of a firebrand).]]...*
*So how did you find the taste of opposition?*

al-Hasan al-Basri [[from (ʿ)]] said: "its harm to me" (iḍrārī). Qatadah said: "my separation" (firāqī).

(﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾): this is because they were recent in time to the destruction of the people of Lot. It was also said: the dwellings of the people of Lot are not far from you, meaning in a distant place, which is why "al-ba'īd" (far) is in the singular. al-Kisa'i said: meaning, their dwellings are near your dwellings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾. This was discussed earlier. (﴿Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾): these are two of His names, glorified is He, and we have explained them in the book "al-Asna fi Sharh al-Asma' al-Husna" (The Most Excellent in Explaining the Most Beautiful Names). al-Jawhari said: "I loved (waddadtu) the man, I love him with love (wuddan) when I have loved him. Al-wadud is the one who loves, and al-wudd, al-widd, al-wudd, and al-mawaddah all mean love." It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that whenever he mentioned Shu'ayb he said: "That is the orator of the prophets."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say﴾, meaning we do not comprehend, because you impose upon us matters unseen, of resurrection and rising, and admonish us with things for which we have no precedent. It was also said: they said this turning away from listening to him and belittling his speech. It is said: "faqiha yafqahu" when one understands with understanding (fiqh), and al-Kisa'i related: "faqiha fiqhan and fiqhan" when one becomes a jurist [[The text of the originals here is confused; it has been corrected from lexicographical works. The text of the original reads: "Faqaha yafqahu idha fahima fiqhan wa fiqhan wa hakā al-Kisā'ī: fiqhan, and faqaha fiqhan idha sāra faqīhan."]].

(﴿And we see you among us as weak﴾). It was said: he had lost his sight. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. [[Shu'ayb the Prophet, peace be upon him, was not blind, because this attribute contradicts infallibility in a way that is defective. The blind Shu'ayb is the companion of Musa, who was not a prophet, and between them were three hundred years.]] It was also said: he was weak of sight. This was said by al-Thawri, and al-Nahhas related from him a view similar to that of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. al-Nahhas said: the lexicographers related that Himyar would call a blind man "ḍa'īf" (weak), meaning that he has become weak through the loss of his sight, just as it is said of him "ḍarīr" (afflicted), meaning he has been harmed by the loss of his sight, and as it is said of him "makfūf" (restrained), meaning he has been restrained from looking through the loss of his sight. al-Hasan said: its meaning is "mahīn" (despised). It was also said: the meaning is weak in body, related by 'Ali ibn 'Isa. al-Suddi said: "alone, you have no army or helpers by which you could oppose us." It was also said: he had little knowledge of worldly interests and the governance of its people. "Ḍa'īfan" is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

(﴿And were it not for your clan﴾): it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. The "rahṭ" of a man is his tribe, on whom he relies and by whom he is strengthened. From it comes "al-rāhiṭā'" for the burrow of the jerboa, because it secures itself by it and hides its young in it. The meaning of (﴿we would have stoned you﴾) is: we would have killed you by stoning. They used to kill a person by pelting him with stones, and his clan were of his religious community. It was also said: the meaning of "larajamnāka" is: we would have reviled you. From it is the verse of al-Ja'di:

*We exchanged bitter words, until we became like two horses racing.*

"Al-rajm" also means cursing, and from it comes "al-shayṭān al-rajīm" (the accursed Satan).

(﴿And you are not against us mighty﴾): meaning, you are not against us a victor, nor one who prevails, nor one who is protected.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: O my people, is my clan﴾. "Arahṭī" is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and the meaning is: is my clan, in your hearts (﴿more honored by you than God﴾), greater, more majestic, and more exalted, while He is the one who possesses you.

(﴿and you have cast Him behind your backs﴾): meaning, you have taken what I have brought you of God's command and cast it behind your backs, and you refrained from killing me out of fear of my people. It is said: "I made his affair (bi-ẓahr)" when I neglected it. This has passed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 40.]]. (﴿Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾): meaning, of disbelief and disobedience.

(﴿Encompassing﴾): meaning knowing. It was also said: guarding.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. You will know﴾. This is a threat and a warning. It has been discussed earlier in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 89.]].

(﴿upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾): meaning, that will destroy him. "Man" is in the accusative position, like the verse (﴿He knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾) [[See vol. 3, p. 62.]] [al-Baqarah: 220].

(﴿and who is a liar﴾): it is coordinated with the preceding. It was also said: meaning, "and you will know who among us is the liar." It was also said: it is in the nominative position, the estimate being: "and it will disgrace the one who is a liar." It was also said: its estimate is "and who is a liar, then his lie will be known, and he will taste the consequence of his affair." al-Farra' claimed that they only used "huwa" in "wa man huwa kādhib" because they do not say "man qā'im" (who is standing); they say "man qāma" (who stood), "man yaqūm" (who stands), and "man al-qā'im" (who is the one standing), so they added "huwa" to make a sentence that stands in place of a verb that acts. al-Nahhas said: what contradicts this is the saying of [[He is 'Amr ibn Abi Rabi'a.]]:

*Who is my messenger to the Pleiades, that I am constrained in my patience at its separation and at the letter?*

(﴿And wait; indeed, I am with you a watcher﴾): meaning, wait for the punishment and the wrath, for I am awaiting victory and mercy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our command came﴾. It was said: Jibril cried out at them with one cry, and their souls left their bodies. (﴿We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and the cry seized those who had wronged﴾), meaning the cry of Jibril. He made the verb feminine according to the wording "al-ṣayḥah" (the cry). In the story of Salih he said: "and the cry seized those who had wronged," making it masculine according to the meaning "al-ṣiyāḥ" (the shouting). Ibn 'Abbas said: God did not destroy two communities with one punishment except the people of Salih and the people of Shu'ayb. God destroyed them with the cry, except that the cry seized the people of Salih from beneath them, and the cry seized the people of Shu'ayb from above them.

(﴿So they became in their homes prostrate, as if they had never prospered there. Unquestionably, away with Madyan, as Thamud was taken away﴾). Its meaning has been discussed earlier. al-Kisa'i related that Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "kamā ba'idat Thamūd" with a damma on the 'ayn. al-Nahhas said: what is known in the language is that one says "ba'ida yab'adu ba'adan and bu'dan" when one perishes. al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "ba'idat" with a damma on the 'ayn, it is a dialect used for both good and evil, and its verbal noun is "al-bu'd," while "ba'idat" is used for evil alone, as in "ba'ida yab'adu ba'adan." So "al-ba'ad" according to the recitation of the majority means a curse. The two dialects may coincide in meaning because of their closeness in meaning, so it is among those whose verbal noun came in a form other than its verb, due to the closeness of meanings.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 84–95 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾. That is, We sent [him] to Madyan, and Madyan is the people of Shu'ayb. Regarding their being called by this name there are two opinions. The first is that they are the sons of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, so it is said "Madyan" while meaning "the sons of Madyan," just as one says "Mudar" while meaning "the sons of Mudar." The second is that it is the name of their city, and they were attributed to it. Al-Nahhas said: Madyan is not declined, because it is the name of a city. This meaning, with additions, has already been discussed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 257.]].

(﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾). This has already been covered.

(﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance﴾). Despite their disbelief, they were people of cheating and fraud. When a seller came to them with food, they took it by a greater measure, and they exacted to the utmost of what they could [[from ع.]] and did wrong. And if a buyer came to them for food, they sold to him by a short measure, and were stingy with him to the utmost of their ability. So they were commanded to belief, abandoning shirk, and to fulfil [the measure], forbidding fraud.

(﴿Indeed I see you in prosperity﴾), that is, in abundance of provision and plenty of blessings. Al-Hasan said: their prices were cheap.

(﴿And indeed I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾). He described the day as "encompassing," and he meant that day was described as encompassing them, for when the day of punishment encompasses them, the punishment has encompassed them. It is like your saying: "a severe day," meaning its heat is severe. Opinions differ about that punishment. It is said: it is the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. It is said: it is the punishment of annihilation in this world. It is said: it is the high price of goods; this meaning was related from Ibn 'Abbas. And in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No people have displayed fraud in measure and balance except that Allah afflicts them with drought and high prices." This has already been mentioned.

The Exalted said: ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice﴾. He commanded fulfilment after forbidding fraud, for emphasis. Al-Iyfa' is completion. "With justice" means with equity and right, and the intent is that each one who has a share should receive his share. He does not mean fulfilling the measure and the weighed thing, because he did not say "fulfil with the measure and with the balance"; rather he meant that you should not reduce the size of the measure below what is customary, and likewise the weights.

(﴿And do not deprive people of their things﴾), that is, do not diminish for them anything of what they deserve.

(﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, acting corruptly﴾). He made clear that dishonesty in measure and balance is an exaggeration of corruption on the earth. More on this has passed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 248.]], and praise be to Allah.

The Exalted said: (﴿What remains from Allah is better for you﴾), that is, what Allah leaves for you after giving rights in justice is more blessed and better in outcome than what you keep for yourselves from the surplus of fraud through tyranny and injustice. Al-Tabari and others said this. Mujahid said: "What remains from Allah is better for you" means His obedience. Al-Rabi' said: the charge of Allah. Al-Farra' said: the watchfulness of Allah. Ibn Zayd: the mercy of Allah. Qatadah and al-Hasan: your portion from your Lord is better for you. Ibn 'Abbas said: the provision of Allah is better for you.

(﴿If you are believers﴾). He made this conditional because they would only recognise the truth of this if they were believers. It was said: it is possible that they acknowledged that Allah is their Creator, so he addressed them with this.

(﴿And I am not a watcher over you﴾), that is, a guardian watching you at your measuring and weighing; that is, it is not possible for me to witness every dealing that proceeds from you so that I may hold you to account for giving the right. It was said: that is, it is not within my power to protect you from the removal of Allah's blessings upon you through your disobediences.

(The Exalted said:) They said: ﴿O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped﴾? (It is also read "aslatuka" without the plural.)

(﴿Or that we not do with our wealth what we please﴾). "An" is in the accusative position. Al-Kisa'i said: its position is genitive, by the implied preposition "ba'".

It is related that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, used to pray much, persistent in worship, both obligatory and voluntary, and he would say: "Prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing." So when he commanded them and forbade them, they reproached him for what they saw him constantly doing of much prayer, and they mocked him, saying what Allah reported of them. It was said: here "prayer" means recitation; this was said by Sufyan from al-A'mash, that is, your recitation commands you. By this it is shown that they were disbelievers. Al-Hasan said: Allah did not send any prophet without making prayer and zakat obligatory upon him.

(﴿Or that we do with our wealth what we will﴾). Al-Farra' claimed that the sense is: "Or that you forbid us to do with our wealth what we will." Al-Sulami and al-Dahhak ibn Qays read "aw an taf'ala fi amwalina ma tasha'" with "ta" in both verbs, and the meaning is: what you will, O Shu'ayb. Al-Nahhas said: "aw an" in this reading is conjoined to the first "an." It is related from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: among what he forbade them was clipping the dirhams [[Clipping means cutting something from its edges.]]. It was also said: the meaning of "or that we do with our wealth what we will" is: if we agree among ourselves to diminish, why do you prevent us from it?

(﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾). They meant: in your own estimation, by your claim. Similar to this is what is said about Abu Jahl: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 151.]] [al-Dukhan: 49], that is, in your own estimation, by your claim. It was said: they said it in the manner of mockery and derision; Qatadah said so. From this is their saying to the Abyssinian: "Abu al-Bayda'," and to the white man: "Abu al-Jawn" [[al-Jawn here means the black one.]]; and from this is the saying of the guardians of Hell to Abu Jahl: "Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: the Arabs describe a thing by its opposite for euphemism and optimism, as the stung one is called "safe" and the desert "mafaza." It was said: it is an allusion intended as abuse. The best of all these, and what precedes it confirms its soundness, is that: indeed you are truly the forbearing, the rightly guided; how then do you command us to abandon what our fathers worshipped! It is also indicated by "Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped," which they denied, seeing his much prayer and worship, and that he is forbearing and rightly guided, in that he should command them to abandon what their fathers used to worship. And after it, there is also what indicates this: ﴿He said: O my people, have you considered if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me from Himself good provision﴾, that is, shall I not forbid you from misguidance? All of this indicates that they said it in its literal sense, and that this was their belief concerning him. Similar to this meaning is the saying of the Jews of Banu Qurayza to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said to them: "O brothers of the apes" [[In one manuscript: "the apes and the swine." It has passed in vol. 6, p. 236 that this was also said by the Muslims to them.]]; they said: "O Muhammad, we did not know you to be ignorant!"

Issue: The people of tafsir said: among what he forbade them, and for which they were punished, was cutting dinars and dirhams. They used to nibble from the edges of the sound coins so that the shavings would be a surplus for them; they dealt with the sound coins by count, and with the clipped ones by weight, and they cheated in weighing. Ibn Wahb said Malik said: they used to break dinars and dirhams. Likewise a group of the earlier exegetes said, such as Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Zayd ibn Aslam and others, and breaking them is a great sin. In the Book of Abu Dawud, from 'Alqama ibn 'Abd Allah, from his father, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that the currency of the Muslims that is current among them be broken, except out of necessity, for if it is sound its value stands and its benefit appears, and if it is broken it becomes mere goods and its benefit is lost, which harms the people; and for this reason it is forbidden. It has been said regarding the interpretation of Allah's words: ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 215.]] [al-Naml: 48], that they used to break dirhams; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: they claimed that after Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi there was no one in Medina more knowledgeable in the interpretation of the Qur'an than Zayd ibn Aslam.

Issue: Asbagh said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim ibn Khalid ibn Junada, client of Zayd ibn al-Harith al-'Utaqi, said: whoever breaks them, his testimony is not accepted, and if he pleads ignorance he is not excused; this is not a place for excuse. Ibn al-'Arabi said: as for his saying that his testimony is not accepted, it is because he has committed a major sin, and major sins remove uprightness, not minor ones. As for his saying that his plea of ignorance in this is not accepted, it is because this is a clear matter that is not hidden from anyone; an excuse is accepted only when the truthfulness of it appears, or when the truth of it is hidden and Allah knows it better than the servant, as Malik said.

Issue: When this is disobedience and corruption, by which testimony is rejected, the one who does it is punished. Ibn al-Musayyab passed by a man who had been flogged, and said: "What is this?" A man said: "He clips the dinars and dirhams." Ibn al-Musayyab said: "This is of the corruption on the earth," and he did not object to his flogging; similar is related from Sufyan. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Nujaybi said: I was sitting with 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, who was then governor of Medina [[In one manuscript: "in Medina"; in another: "Commander of the Believers."]], when a man was brought who clipped dirhams, and it had been witnessed against him; he beat him, shaved his head, and ordered that he be paraded, and commanded him to say: "This is the punishment of whoever clips dirhams." Then he ordered that he be returned to him [i.e., his place], and said: "What prevented me from cutting off your hand was only that I had not previously set down a ruling on this before today, and I have now set it down; whoever wishes, let him cut." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: as for his being whipped with the whip, there is no dispute about it; as for shaving his head, 'Umar did it, and I myself, during the days of my judgeship among the people, used to beat and shave; I used to do that only to one whose hair is an aid to him in disobedience and a means to adorn himself in corruption, and this is what is obligatory for every means to disobedience: that it be cut off, if it does not affect the body. As for cutting off his hand, 'Umar took that from the section on theft, for clipping dirhams is not breaking them, since breaking is destroying their quality while clipping is diminishing their quantity; it is taking wealth in a hidden manner. If it is said: is not guarding the basis for amputation? We say: it is possible that 'Umar held that preparing them for distinguishing between creatures, a dinar or a dirham, is their guard, and the guard of each thing is according to its condition. Ibn al-Zubayr also implemented this and cut off the hand of a man for clipping dinars and dirhams. Our scholars, the Malikis, have said: the dinars and dirhams are the seals of Allah, upon which is His name; if one who breaks a seal of Allah were to be amputated according to the view of the people of interpretation, he would deserve it; or whoever breaks a ruler's seal bearing his name is disciplined, but Allah's seal is that by which needs are fulfilled, so the two are not equal in punishment. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I hold that one should be amputated for clipping them, not for breaking them. I used to do this during my tenure as judge, but I was surrounded by the ignorant, and I did not love to be [[In manuscript ع: "I was not beaten"; in others: "I liked."]] exposed to the talk of envious misguided people, so whoever is able to do it one day, from the people of truth, let him do it seeking reward from Allah the Exalted.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verses 84–95 (part 2 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾. This was discussed earlier. (﴿And He has provided me from Himself with good provision﴾), meaning abundant and lawful. Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was wealthy. This is what Ibn 'Abbas and others said. It was also said that he meant by it guidance, success, knowledge and understanding. There is an ellipsis in the speech, which is what we have mentioned, meaning: "Shall I not forbid you from error?" It was also said that the meaning is: "Tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, shall I follow the misguided?" It was also said that the meaning is: "Tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, [will] you order me [[In (ʿ): afa-tamurūnanī, "will you order me?"]] to disobey in cheating and short-measuring, when God has made me independent of it [[from (ʿ) and (ā)]]?"

(﴿And I do not wish to oppose you﴾): the phrase is in the accusative position governed by "urīdu" (I wish).

(﴿in what I forbid you from﴾): meaning, I do not forbid you from anything and then commit it myself, just as I do not abandon what I have commanded you to do.

(﴿I only wish reform, as much as I am able﴾): meaning, I only wish to do what is right, that you may reform your worldly affairs through justice and your hereafter through worship. He said "as much as I am able" because ability is one of the conditions of the act, not of the wish. The word "mā" here is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: "I only wish reform with my utmost effort and capacity."

(﴿And my success is not but through God﴾): meaning, my right guidance. Tawfīq (success) means right guidance.

(﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾): meaning, I have depended upon Him.

(﴿and to Him I turn in repentance﴾): meaning, I return to Him in whatever calamities befall me. It was also said: "To Him I return in the Hereafter." It was also said that inābah (turning) means supplication, and the meaning is: "To Him I supplicate."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, let not my opposition bring upon you﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "yujrimannakum" (cause you to incur).

(﴿my opposition﴾) is in the nominative position.

(﴿that there befall you﴾) is in the accusative position. Meaning: let not my enmity toward you lead you to abandon faith, so that there befalls you what befell the disbelievers [[from (ʿ) and (wāw)]] before you. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said: "Let not my opposition earn you the punishment, so that you are struck by it as it struck those before you," as said by al-Zajjaj. The meaning of "yajrimannakum" has already been mentioned in "al-Ma'idah" [[See vol. 6, p. 44 and following.]], and "al-shiqaq" (opposition) in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 143.]]. It means enmity, as said by al-Suddi, and from it is the verse of al-Akhtal:

*Is there no one who conveys from me a message [[Here "rasūl" means "message." In the Diwan: "mubhigh qabasan" (a messenger of a firebrand).]]...*
*So how did you find the taste of opposition?*

al-Hasan al-Basri [[from (ʿ)]] said: "its harm to me" (iḍrārī). Qatadah said: "my separation" (firāqī).

(﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾): this is because they were recent in time to the destruction of the people of Lot. It was also said: the dwellings of the people of Lot are not far from you, meaning in a distant place, which is why "al-ba'īd" (far) is in the singular. al-Kisa'i said: meaning, their dwellings are near your dwellings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾. This was discussed earlier. (﴿Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾): these are two of His names, glorified is He, and we have explained them in the book "al-Asna fi Sharh al-Asma' al-Husna" (The Most Excellent in Explaining the Most Beautiful Names). al-Jawhari said: "I loved (waddadtu) the man, I love him with love (wuddan) when I have loved him. Al-wadud is the one who loves, and al-wudd, al-widd, al-wudd, and al-mawaddah all mean love." It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that whenever he mentioned Shu'ayb he said: "That is the orator of the prophets."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say﴾, meaning we do not comprehend, because you impose upon us matters unseen, of resurrection and rising, and admonish us with things for which we have no precedent. It was also said: they said this turning away from listening to him and belittling his speech. It is said: "faqiha yafqahu" when one understands with understanding (fiqh), and al-Kisa'i related: "faqiha fiqhan and fiqhan" when one becomes a jurist [[The text of the originals here is confused; it has been corrected from lexicographical works. The text of the original reads: "Faqaha yafqahu idha fahima fiqhan wa fiqhan wa hakā al-Kisā'ī: fiqhan, and faqaha fiqhan idha sāra faqīhan."]].

(﴿And we see you among us as weak﴾). It was said: he had lost his sight. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. [[Shu'ayb the Prophet, peace be upon him, was not blind, because this attribute contradicts infallibility in a way that is defective. The blind Shu'ayb is the companion of Musa, who was not a prophet, and between them were three hundred years.]] It was also said: he was weak of sight. This was said by al-Thawri, and al-Nahhas related from him a view similar to that of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. al-Nahhas said: the lexicographers related that Himyar would call a blind man "ḍa'īf" (weak), meaning that he has become weak through the loss of his sight, just as it is said of him "ḍarīr" (afflicted), meaning he has been harmed by the loss of his sight, and as it is said of him "makfūf" (restrained), meaning he has been restrained from looking through the loss of his sight. al-Hasan said: its meaning is "mahīn" (despised). It was also said: the meaning is weak in body, related by 'Ali ibn 'Isa. al-Suddi said: "alone, you have no army or helpers by which you could oppose us." It was also said: he had little knowledge of worldly interests and the governance of its people. "Ḍa'īfan" is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

(﴿And were it not for your clan﴾): it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. The "rahṭ" of a man is his tribe, on whom he relies and by whom he is strengthened. From it comes "al-rāhiṭā'" for the burrow of the jerboa, because it secures itself by it and hides its young in it. The meaning of (﴿we would have stoned you﴾) is: we would have killed you by stoning. They used to kill a person by pelting him with stones, and his clan were of his religious community. It was also said: the meaning of "larajamnāka" is: we would have reviled you. From it is the verse of al-Ja'di:

*We exchanged bitter words, until we became like two horses racing.*

"Al-rajm" also means cursing, and from it comes "al-shayṭān al-rajīm" (the accursed Satan).

(﴿And you are not against us mighty﴾): meaning, you are not against us a victor, nor one who prevails, nor one who is protected.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: O my people, is my clan﴾. "Arahṭī" is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and the meaning is: is my clan, in your hearts (﴿more honored by you than God﴾), greater, more majestic, and more exalted, while He is the one who possesses you.

(﴿and you have cast Him behind your backs﴾): meaning, you have taken what I have brought you of God's command and cast it behind your backs, and you refrained from killing me out of fear of my people. It is said: "I made his affair (bi-ẓahr)" when I neglected it. This has passed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 40.]]. (﴿Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾): meaning, of disbelief and disobedience.

(﴿Encompassing﴾): meaning knowing. It was also said: guarding.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. You will know﴾. This is a threat and a warning. It has been discussed earlier in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 89.]].

(﴿upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾): meaning, that will destroy him. "Man" is in the accusative position, like the verse (﴿He knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾) [[See vol. 3, p. 62.]] [al-Baqarah: 220].

(﴿and who is a liar﴾): it is coordinated with the preceding. It was also said: meaning, "and you will know who among us is the liar." It was also said: it is in the nominative position, the estimate being: "and it will disgrace the one who is a liar." It was also said: its estimate is "and who is a liar, then his lie will be known, and he will taste the consequence of his affair." al-Farra' claimed that they only used "huwa" in "wa man huwa kādhib" because they do not say "man qā'im" (who is standing); they say "man qāma" (who stood), "man yaqūm" (who stands), and "man al-qā'im" (who is the one standing), so they added "huwa" to make a sentence that stands in place of a verb that acts. al-Nahhas said: what contradicts this is the saying of [[He is 'Amr ibn Abi Rabi'a.]]:

*Who is my messenger to the Pleiades, that I am constrained in my patience at its separation and at the letter?*

(﴿And wait; indeed, I am with you a watcher﴾): meaning, wait for the punishment and the wrath, for I am awaiting victory and mercy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our command came﴾. It was said: Jibril cried out at them with one cry, and their souls left their bodies. (﴿We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and the cry seized those who had wronged﴾), meaning the cry of Jibril. He made the verb feminine according to the wording "al-ṣayḥah" (the cry). In the story of Salih he said: "and the cry seized those who had wronged," making it masculine according to the meaning "al-ṣiyāḥ" (the shouting). Ibn 'Abbas said: God did not destroy two communities with one punishment except the people of Salih and the people of Shu'ayb. God destroyed them with the cry, except that the cry seized the people of Salih from beneath them, and the cry seized the people of Shu'ayb from above them.

(﴿So they became in their homes prostrate, as if they had never prospered there. Unquestionably, away with Madyan, as Thamud was taken away﴾). Its meaning has been discussed earlier. al-Kisa'i related that Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "kamā ba'idat Thamūd" with a damma on the 'ayn. al-Nahhas said: what is known in the language is that one says "ba'ida yab'adu ba'adan and bu'dan" when one perishes. al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "ba'idat" with a damma on the 'ayn, it is a dialect used for both good and evil, and its verbal noun is "al-bu'd," while "ba'idat" is used for evil alone, as in "ba'ida yab'adu ba'adan." So "al-ba'ad" according to the recitation of the majority means a curse. The two dialects may coincide in meaning because of their closeness in meaning, so it is among those whose verbal noun came in a form other than its verb, due to the closeness of meanings.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 84–95 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾. That is, We sent [him] to Madyan, and Madyan is the people of Shu'ayb. Regarding their being called by this name there are two opinions. The first is that they are the sons of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, so it is said "Madyan" while meaning "the sons of Madyan," just as one says "Mudar" while meaning "the sons of Mudar." The second is that it is the name of their city, and they were attributed to it. Al-Nahhas said: Madyan is not declined, because it is the name of a city. This meaning, with additions, has already been discussed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 257.]].

(﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾). This has already been covered.

(﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance﴾). Despite their disbelief, they were people of cheating and fraud. When a seller came to them with food, they took it by a greater measure, and they exacted to the utmost of what they could [[from ع.]] and did wrong. And if a buyer came to them for food, they sold to him by a short measure, and were stingy with him to the utmost of their ability. So they were commanded to belief, abandoning shirk, and to fulfil [the measure], forbidding fraud.

(﴿Indeed I see you in prosperity﴾), that is, in abundance of provision and plenty of blessings. Al-Hasan said: their prices were cheap.

(﴿And indeed I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾).
