Al-A'mash, Hafs, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-amma alladhina su'idu" with a ḍammah on the sin [i.e., su'idu]. Abu 'Amr said: the proof that it is su'idu is that the first is "shaqu" and he did not say "ushqu."

Al-Nahhas said: I saw 'Ali ibn Sulayman marvelling at al-Kisa'i's reading "su'idu," despite his knowledge of Arabic grammar, since this is an impermissible solecism (laḥn), for one says only: "sa'ida fulan" and "as'adahu Allah" (Allah made him happy), and "as'ada" follows the pattern of "amraḍa." Al-Kisa'i only argued with their saying "mas'ud," but he has no proof in it, because one says "makan mas'ud fihi" (a place where one is made happy), then the preposition is dropped and it is used as a name.

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "su'idu" with a ḍammah is following their saying "mas'ud," and it is anomalous and rare, because one does not say "sa'idahu Allah"; one says only "as'adahu Allah."

Al-Tha'labi said: "su'idu" with a ḍammah means they were granted happiness. One says "sa'ida" and "as'ada" with the same meaning. The rest read "su'idu" with a fatḥah on the sin, by analogy with "shaqu," and this is what Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-sa'adah" is the opposite of "al-shaqawah." You say from it: "sa'ida al-rajulu" with a kasrah, so he is "sa'id," like "salima" so he is "salim," and "sa'ida" so he is "mas'ud." One does not say "mus'ad" concerning him, as if they dispensed with it in favour of "mas'ud."

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim said: "sa'idahu Allah" has been reported, so he is "mas'ud," and "as'adahu Allah," so he is "mus'ad." This strengthens the opinion of the Kufans.

Sibawayh said: one does not say "sa'ida fulan," just as one does not say "shaqiya fulan," because it is one of those verbs that do not take an object (la yata'addá).

(**ʿaṭāʾan ghayra majdhūdh**) That is, not cut off, from "jadhdhahu, yajudhdhuhu," meaning "he cut it." Al-Nabigha said:

*It cuts the Salawqi mail, its weave doubled, and kindles with the flint the fire of al-Habahib* [[The line is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, describing swords. It is also transmitted as "taqiddu" and "yuwqidun." The salawqi is armour attributed to Salawq, a village in Yemen. The muḍā'af is that whose links are woven double. The ṣifāḥ are broad stones. The ḥabāḥib are a kind of fly that has a glow at night; it is said that the fire of al-ḥabāḥib is the spark that flies into the air when two stones collide.]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not be﴾ is a jussive (jazm) after the prohibition, and the nūn was dropped because of its frequent use.

(**fī miryah**) That is, in doubt.

(**mimmā yaʿbudu hāʾulāʾ**) That is, concerning the gods, that they are falsehood. Better than this: that is, say, O Muhammad, to everyone who doubts: "So do not be in doubt about what these worship," that Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not command them to it, and they worship them only as their fathers used to do, out of imitation of them.

(**wa-innā la-muwaffūhum naṣībahum ghayra manqūṣ**) Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: their share of provision. Said by Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: their share of punishment. Said by Ibn Zayd. The third: what they were promised of good or evil. Said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

This is the first part of the commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah Hud (11), verses 100–109.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That is from the reports of the towns which We relate to you.﴾ "That" (dhalika) is in the nominative by an implied subject, meaning: the matter is that. It may also be read as a subject (mubtada'), and the meaning is: that report mentioned above, from the reports of the towns, We relate to you.

(Among them are standing and reaped.) Qatadah said: "The standing" is that which remains upright over its roofs (khawiyah 'ala 'urushiha), and "the reaped" is that which has no trace left. It was also said: "the standing" is the inhabited, and "the reaped" is the ruined; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Mujahid said: "standing" means the empty ones upon their roofs, and "reaped" means uprooted, that is, cut down like crops when they are harvested. A poet said:

"And people, in the distribution of death among them,
are like crops: some standing, and some reaped."

Another said [the verse is by al-Tirimmah, as in Lisan al-'Arab]:
"We are only like a tender shoot of crop;
so when its time comes, its reaper comes."

Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: "ḥaṣīd" means maḥṣūd (reaped); its plural is ḥaṣdā and ḥiṣād, like marḍā and mirāḍ. He said: for those who have intellect, it is ḥaṣdā, like qatīl and qatlā.

(And We did not wrong them.) The root meaning of wronging (ẓulm) in the language is placing a thing in other than its place; this has already been discussed fully in "al-Baqarah" (see vol. 1, p. 309 onward).

(But they wronged themselves) by disbelief and sins. Sibawayh reported that one says: ẓalama iyyāhu (he wronged him).

(So their gods, whom they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them) i.e., did not repel anything from them. (Any thing) — there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: those which they used to worship, i.e., invoked.

(When the command of your Lord came, they did not add to them anything but ruin.) i.e., nothing but loss (takhsīr). Mujahid and Qatadah said this. Labid said:

"I have grown old, and every companion of youth
returns to decay, and that is the tatbīb."

Tabab means destruction and loss. There is an implied element here: the worship of idols did not add to them except that their worship of them had caused them to lose the reward of the Hereafter; so the governing noun is omitted.

(Thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns) i.e., just as He seized these towns, which belonged to Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, so He seizes all wrongdoing towns. 'Asim al-Jahdari and Talhah ibn Musarrif read: "Thus is the seizing of your Lord, when He seized the towns." It is also reported from al-Jahdari: "Thus is the seizing (akhdh) of your Lord," as the majority read "when He seized the towns."

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "wa-kadhālika akhdh rabbika idh akhadh" (with the past tense), it is an report about what has been the custom in the destruction of earlier nations, and the meaning is: thus is the seizing of your Lord of those nations which He seized when He seized them. The reading of the majority treats it as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the meaning is: thus is the seizing of your Lord of whomever He intends to destroy whenever He seizes him; here "idh" refers to the past, i.e., when He seized the towns, and "idha" to the future. (While it is wrongdoing) i.e., and its people are wrongdoers; the noun (ahl, people) is omitted, as in: "And ask the town" [Yusuf: 82].

(Indeed His seizing is painful and severe.) i.e., His punishment for the people of polytheism is painful and harsh. In the Sahih of Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Musa, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not release him," then he recited: "Thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns..." to the end of the verse. Abu 'Isa said: this is a hasan sahih gharib hadith.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ i.e., surely a lesson and an admonition.

(For whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter.)

(That is a day) — a subject and predicate.

(Gathered) — is an attribute of it.

(For it mankind is gathered) — the subject of what has not been named as agent (nā'ib al-fa'il); for this reason it does not say "majmū'ūn" (plural). If you take "the people" as the subject (mubtada') and the predicate "majmū' lahu" (gathered for it), then it does not say "majmū'ūn" under this analysis, because "lahu" stands in place of the agent. Al-jam' means al-ḥashr, i.e., they will be gathered for that day.

(And that is a witnessed day) — i.e., the righteous and the wicked witness it, and the people of heaven witness it. We have mentioned these two names along with others of the names of the Resurrection in the book "al-Tadhkirah," and clarified them, praise be to Allah.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We do not delay it﴾ — i.e., We do not delay that day.

(Except for a limited term) — i.e., for a term whose decree has preceded from Us, and it is numbered in Our reckoning.

(On the day it comes) — it has been read as "yawma ya'ti" (without the yā' in pause). The yā' is dropped when there is a kasra before it, as one says: "lā adri" (I do not know); al-Qushayri mentioned this. Al-Nahhas said: the people of Medina, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with the yā' in continuous recitation and omitted in pause; it is reported that Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read "yawma ya'ti" with the yā' both in pause and in connection. Al-A'mash and Hamzah read "yawma ya'ti" without a yā' both in pause and connection. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: the correct position regarding this is not to pause on it, and to connect it with the yā', because a group of grammarians said: the yā' is not dropped, and a thing is not apocopated without an apocopating particle. As for pausing without the yā', there is an opinion of al-Kisa'i, who said: because a sound verb is paused upon like the jussive, so the yā' is dropped as the damma is dropped. As for the reading of Hamzah, Abu 'Ubayd argued for dropping the yā' in connection and pause on two grounds: first, he claimed he saw it in the Imam known as the Mushaf of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) without a yā'; second, he reported that it is the dialect of Hudhayl, who say "mā adri." Al-Nahhas said: as for his argument from the Mushaf of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), most scholars refute it. Malik ibn Anas (may Allah have mercy on him) said: I asked about the Mushaf of 'Uthman, and I was told it had been lost. As for his argument from their saying "mā adri," there is no proof in it, because this omission has been reported by the early grammarians, who mentioned its cause and said it is not to be analogized upon. Al-Farra' recited, for the omission of the yā':

"Your palm is a palm that does not give a dirham in generosity,
and another gives the blood by the sword."

i.e., "tu'ṭī." Sibawayh and al-Khalil reported that the Arabs say "lā adri," dropping the yā' and making do with the kasra, except that they claim this is due to frequency of use. Al-Zajjaj said: the better in grammar is to affirm the yā'. He said: what I see is to follow the Mushaf and the consensus of the reciters, because recitation is a sunnah, and similar things have come in Arabic speech.

(No soul speaks except by His permission.) The original is "tatakallamu"; one of the two tā's is dropped for lightness. There is an implied element: no soul speaks in it except with what is permitted of good speech, because they are compelled to abandon the ugly. It was also said: the meaning is, no soul speaks with a proof or intercession except by His permission. It was also said: for them there is a time at the place of standing when they are prevented from speaking except by His permission. The people of atheism in religion ask most about this verse, saying: why did He say "no soul speaks except by His permission," and "This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to make excuses" [al-Mursalat: 36]? He said in another place mentioning the Resurrection: "And some of them turn to others, questioning one another" [al-Saffat: 27]; and He said: "The day every soul will come pleading for itself" [al-Nahl: 111]; and He said: "Stop them, for they are to be questioned" [al-Saffat: 24]; and He said: "So on that day no one will be asked about his sin, man or jinn" [al-Rahman: 39]. The answer is what we have mentioned, that they do not speak with a proof that is due to them; they only speak with acknowledgment of their sins, and blaming some of them others, and some of them casting their sins upon others. As for speaking and uttering a proof in their favor, no. This is like when you say to one who addresses you much, but his address is void of proof: "You have not spoken anything, and you have not uttered anything"; so one who speaks without proof is called, regarding that, a non-speaker. Others said: that day is long, and has stations and places; in some of them they are prevented from speaking, and in some of them speech is granted to them. This indicates that no soul speaks except by His permission.

(Among them are wretched and happy.) i.e., among the souls, or among the people, whom He mentioned in His saying: "a day on which mankind is gathered for it." The wretched is the one for whom wretchedness has been written, and the happy is the one for whom happiness has been written. Labid said:

"Among them is the happy, taking his share;
and among them is the wretched, content with his livelihood."

Al-Tirmidhi reported from Ibn 'Umar, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: when this verse was revealed, "Among them are wretched and happy," I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Prophet of Allah, then for what do we work? For something already finished, or for something not yet finished?" He said: "Rather, for something already finished and the pens have run with it, O 'Umar; but each is made easy for what he was created for." He said: this is a hasan gharib hadith from this route; we do not know it except from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar. This has been mentioned before in "al-A'raf."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿As for those who were wretched﴾ — this is a subject (mubtada').

(Then in the Fire) — this is in the position of the predicate; likewise (for them therein is groaning and wailing). Abu al-'Aliyah said: the zafir is from the chest, and the shahiq is from the throat; and he also said the opposite of that. Al-Zajjaj said: the zafir is from the intensity of moaning, and the shahiq is from a very high moan. He said: the lexicographers of Kufa and Basra claim that the zafir is like the beginning of the donkey's bray, and the shahiq like the end of the donkey's bray. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said the reverse: the zafir is a strong sound, and the shahiq is a weak sound. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: the zafir is like the first bray of the donkey, and the shahiq is like its last, when it finishes its sound. The poet said [the poet is al-'Ajjaj, and the verse is from a qasidah of his describing the desert, whose opening is:
"Dark in its depths, empty of its passage,
its landmarks confused, its mirages gleaming":]
"Groaning within the belly, a sahīl, or a shahaq,
until one says: it brays, and it has not brayed."
It was also said: the zafir is the expulsion of breath, which is when the belly is filled with distress and it comes out with breath; and the shahiq is the return of breath. It was also said: the zafir is the repeated drawing of breath from intense grief, taken from zafr, which is carrying on the back because of its heaviness; and the shahiq is a long extended breath, taken from their saying: a shahiq mountain, i.e., tall. The zafir and shahiq are among the sounds of the grieving.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ — "mā dāmati" is in the accusative position as an adverbial of time, meaning: the duration of the heavens and the earth; and the implied sense is: at the time of that. There has been difference over the interpretation of this. A group, including al-Dahhak, said: the meaning is as long as the heavens of Paradise and Hell and their earths endure; "the heaven" is everything that rises above you and shades you, and "the earth" is what your foot rests upon. In the revelation: "And He has made us inherit the earth; we settle in Paradise wherever we will" [al-Zumar: 74]. It was also said: it refers to the heaven and earth known in this world, and this follows the custom of the Arabs in speaking about the permanence and perpetuity of a thing, as in their saying: "I will not come to you as long as a night is covered (janna layl), or a torrent flows (sāla sayl), or the night and day alternate (mā ikhtalafa al-layl wa al-nahar), or the dove mourns (mā nāḥa al-ḥamām), or the heavens and the earth endure," and similar expressions by which they mean length without end. Thus Allah made the disbelievers' eternal abode understood by this, even though He has informed of the passing away of the heavens and the earth. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that all created things originally derive from the light of the Throne, and that in the Hereafter the heavens and the earth will be returned to the light from which they were taken; so they are both enduring forever in the light of the Throne.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verses 100–109 (part 2 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except what your Lord wills﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb), because it is an exception (istithna') that is not from the first part [of the sentence]. Scholars have differed about it in ten opinions.

The first: it is an exception from his saying, "then in the Fire," as if He said: "Except what your Lord wills of delaying a people from that." This is an opinion narrated by Abu Nadra from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Jabir, may Allah be pleased with them both. He did not say "man sha'a" (whoever He wills) because the intended meaning is a number and not individuals, like His saying: ﴿what is good for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3].[[See vol. 5, p. 12.]] And from Abu Nadra, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Except whoever He wills not to enter them, even though they were wretched through disobedience."

The second: the exception is only for the sinful among the believers, concerning their being brought out of the Fire after a period. On this view, his saying "As for those who were wretched" is general, covering both disbelievers and sinners, and the exception is from "abiding therein" (khalidin). This was said by Qatada, al-Dahhak, Abu Sinan, and others. In the authentic collection, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Some people will enter Jahannam until, when they have become like coal [[al-humam: ashes, charcoal, and anything burnt by fire; its singular is hummah.]], they will be brought out of it and enter Paradise, and they will be called 'the people of Jahannam.'" This meaning has already been mentioned in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 332.]] and elsewhere.

The third: the exception is from the groaning and the wailing, meaning: for them therein is groaning and wailing, except what your Lord wills of the kinds of punishment that He did not mention. Likewise for the people of Paradise there is the bliss that is mentioned and what is not mentioned. This was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ means they will not die therein and will not be brought out of it, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, which is that He commands the Fire to consume them and annihilate them, and then re-creates them.

I say: this opinion applies only to the disbeliever, and the exception concerns his being consumed and his re-creation.

The fifth: that "illa" (except) means "siwa" (other than), as you say in speech: "There is no man with me except Zayd," and "I have on you two thousand dirhams except the thousand that I have on you." It is said: the meaning is "as long as the heavens and the earth endure, other than what your Lord wills of eternity."

The sixth: that it is an exception from the bringing out, and He does not intend to bring them out of it. As you say in speech: "I intended to do that, except that I will to do something else," while you remain upon that act. So the meaning is that if He willed to bring them out, He would have brought them out, but He has informed them that they are abiding therein. Al-Zajjaj reported these two opinions from the linguists (ahl al-lughah), and he said: "The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) have two other opinions. One of the two: ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ refers to the length of their standing at the heads of their graves, for the reckoning, the length of their stay in the world, in the barzakh, and in standing for the reckoning. The other opinion: the exception occurs concerning an increase upon the bliss and the punishment, and its meaning is: ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ of an increase in bliss for the people of bliss, and an increase in punishment for the people of the Blazing Fire."

I say: The exception concerning the increase is from the eternity (khulud) over the duration of the existence of the heaven and earth known in this world. This was preferred by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Ali, meaning: abiding therein for the measure of the endurance of the heavens and the earth, which is the duration of the world. The heaven and the earth have a time at which they will change, and this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿the Day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48].[[See p. 382 of this part.]] Allah created the children of Adam and dealt with them, and bought from them their selves and their wealth in exchange for Paradise, and upon that He made a covenant with them on the Day of the Covenant. Whoever fulfils that covenant has Paradise, and whoever goes with his neck (i.e., is lost) will abide in the Fire for the measure of the endurance of the heavens and the earth. They endure only for the transaction. Likewise, the people of Paradise abide in Paradise for that measure. When this transaction is complete, everything falls under the will of Allah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38–39].[[See vol. 16, pp. 147 and 289.]] So the people of both abodes abide for the measure of their endurance, and that is the right of Lordship (rububiyyah) at that measure of greatness. Then He made eternity (al-abad) binding for them in both abodes, by the right of His Oneness (ahadiyyah). Whoever meets Him as one who affirms His oneness remains in his abode forever, and whoever meets Him associating with His oneness a god remains in the prison forever. So Allah informed the servants of the measure of eternity, then said: "except what your Lord wills" of an increase in the duration that hearts are unable to grasp, because it has no end. Thus by [the] belief, their eternity in both abodes is everlasting.

It has been said that "illa" here means "wa" (and), said by al-Farra' and some people of reflection. This is the eighth opinion, and the meaning is: "and what your Lord wills of an increase in eternity over the duration of the heavens and the earth in this world."

It has been said concerning His saying: ﴿except those who did wrong﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150],[[See vol. 2, p. 128.]] that it means "and not those who did wrong." The poet said:[[The line is by 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib, and it is also said to be by Hadrami ibn 'Amir. It is permissible that "illa" here means "ghayr" (other than). Sibawayh said: it is as if he said: "and every brother, other than the two stars (al-Farqadan), is forsaken by his brother," so he described "kull" with it.]]

*And every brother, the one who is parted from by his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqadan [stars]*

That is: "and the two Farqadan." Abu Muhammad Makki said: this opinion, that "illa" means "wa," is distant according to the Basrans, and its explanation has already passed in "al-Baqarah."[[See vol. 2, p. 128.]]

It was also said: its meaning is "as your Lord willed," like His saying: ﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 22], that is, "as has already passed." This is the ninth opinion.

The tenth: His saying, "except what your Lord wills," is only by way of the exception that the Law has encouraged to use in every speech. It is in the manner of His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath: 27].[[See vol. 16, pp. 147 and 289.]] This is an exception concerning something obligatory, and this exception is, in ruling, like a condition, as if He said: "if your Lord wills." It is therefore not described as connected (muttasil) or disconnected (munqati'). This is supported and strengthened by His saying: ﴿a gift not cut off﴾ [Hud: 108]. Abu 'Ubayd said something similar: the decree of the will of Allah, exalted is He, concerning the eternity of both groups in both abodes, has preceded, so the word of exception came, though the decree concerning eternity had already preceded. He said: this is like His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath: 27], though He knows that they will enter it definitely. So the exception in both places does not imply optional choice, since the will has preceded with the decree concerning eternity in both abodes and entry into the Sacred Mosque. Something similar was said by al-Farra'.

And a saying: the eleventh: the wretched are the happy, and the happy are the wretched, and no others. The exception in both places refers to them. Its explanation: "ma" means "man" (whoever). Allah the Mighty and Majestic excepted, from those who enter the Fire and abide therein, those from the community of Muhammad ﷺ who will be brought out of it because of the faith they have. And He excepted, from those who enter Paradise and abide therein, those who enter the Fire because of their sins before entering Paradise, and then are brought out of it into Paradise. These are the ones upon whom the second exception falls. It is as if He said: "As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is groaning and wailing, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills" of not making them abide therein forever. These are the ones brought out of it from the community of Muhammad ﷺ by their faith and by the intercession of Muhammad ﷺ. So by their entry into the Fire they are called "the wretched," and by their entry into Paradise they are called "the happy," as al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas when he said: "Those who were made happy were made wretched by entering the Fire, then were made happy by their coming out of it and entering Paradise."

Al-A'mash, Hafs, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-amma alladhina su'idu" with a ḍammah on the sin [i.e., su'idu]. Abu 'Amr said: the proof that it is su'idu is that the first is "shaqu" and he did not say "ushqu."

Al-Nahhas said: I saw 'Ali ibn Sulayman marvelling at al-Kisa'i's reading "su'idu," despite his knowledge of Arabic grammar, since this is an impermissible solecism (laḥn), for one says only: "sa'ida fulan" and "as'adahu Allah" (Allah made him happy), and "as'ada" follows the pattern of "amraḍa." Al-Kisa'i only argued with their saying "mas'ud," but he has no proof in it, because one says "makan mas'ud fihi" (a place where one is made happy), then the preposition is dropped and it is used as a name.

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "su'idu" with a ḍammah is following their saying "mas'ud," and it is anomalous and rare, because one does not say "sa'idahu Allah"; one says only "as'adahu Allah."

Al-Tha'labi said: "su'idu" with a ḍammah means they were granted happiness. One says "sa'ida" and "as'ada" with the same meaning. The rest read "su'idu" with a fatḥah on the sin, by analogy with "shaqu," and this is what Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-sa'adah" is the opposite of "al-shaqawah." You say from it: "sa'ida al-rajulu" with a kasrah, so he is "sa'id," like "salima" so he is "salim," and "sa'ida" so he is "mas'ud." One does not say "mus'ad" concerning him, as if they dispensed with it in favour of "mas'ud."

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim said: "sa'idahu Allah" has been reported, so he is "mas'ud," and "as'adahu Allah," so he is "mus'ad." This strengthens the opinion of the Kufans.

Sibawayh said: one does not say "sa'ida fulan," just as one does not say "shaqiya fulan," because it is one of those verbs that do not take an object (la yata'addá).

(**ʿaṭāʾan ghayra majdhūdh**) That is, not cut off, from "jadhdhahu, yajudhdhuhu," meaning "he cut it." Al-Nabigha said:

*It cuts the Salawqi mail, its weave doubled, and kindles with the flint the fire of al-Habahib* [[The line is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, describing swords. It is also transmitted as "taqiddu" and "yuwqidun." The salawqi is armour attributed to Salawq, a village in Yemen. The muḍā'af is that whose links are woven double. The ṣifāḥ are broad stones. The ḥabāḥib are a kind of fly that has a glow at night; it is said that the fire of al-ḥabāḥib is the spark that flies into the air when two stones collide.]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not be﴾ is a jussive (jazm) after the prohibition, and the nūn was dropped because of its frequent use.

(**fī miryah**) That is, in doubt.

(**mimmā yaʿbudu hāʾulāʾ**) That is, concerning the gods, that they are falsehood. Better than this: that is, say, O Muhammad, to everyone who doubts: "So do not be in doubt about what these worship," that Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not command them to it, and they worship them only as their fathers used to do, out of imitation of them.

(**wa-innā la-muwaffūhum naṣībahum ghayra manqūṣ**) Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: their share of provision. Said by Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: their share of punishment. Said by Ibn Zayd. The third: what they were promised of good or evil. Said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And had it not been for a word that had preceded from your Lord﴾. "The word" refers to Allah's decree, Mighty and Majestic is He, that He would defer them until the Day of Resurrection, because of the benefit He knew to be in that. Had it not been for that, He would have judged between them concerning their term by rewarding the believer and punishing the disbeliever. It was said: the intended meaning is between those who differed concerning the Book of Musa (Moses), for they were divided between one who affirmed it [bihi [[من اوووى.]]] and one who denied it. It was also said: it refers to those who differ concerning you, O Muhammad, by hastening the punishment, but the decree had preceded to defer the punishment of this nation until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾. If it is taken to refer to the people of Musa, then the meaning is: they are in doubt about the Book of Musa, so they are in doubt about the Qur'an.

**Translation:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, to each, your Lord will fully repay their deeds﴾. That is, each of the nations We have enumerated will see the recompense of their deeds, and likewise your people, O Muhammad. The reciters differed concerning the reading of "wa-inna kullan lamma". The people of the two Sanctuaries (Ahl al-Haramayn): Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr along with them, read "wa-in kullan lamma" with the light (takhfif) form, taking it as the lightened "in" (in al-mukhaffafa min al-thaqila) functioning as an active particle (mu'mala). This was mentioned by al-Khalil and Sibawayh. Sibawayh said: "Someone I trust told us that he heard the Arabs say: *in Zaydan la-munṭaliq* (indeed Zayd is certainly departing)." He recited the line of the poet [[It is by Ibn Sarim al-Yashkuri; the first half of the verse is: "And at times she meets us with a face that is radiant (muqsam)." The accusative of *al-zabya* can be governed by *kaana*, as an imitation of the verb when it is elided and still exerts its governance, and the predicate is omitted because the listener knows it. It is also permissible to put *al-zabya* in the genitive, on the assumption of "ka-zabya" (like a gazelle), and *an* is then a superfluous emphatic particle.]]:

*ka-anna zabyatan ta'ṭū ilā wāriqi al-salam*
(as if a gazelle were stretching its neck toward the leaves of the salam tree)

He intended *ka-annaha zabyatun* (as if she were a gazelle), so he lightened it and put the following word in the accusative. The Basrans permit lightening the heavy *inna* while still governing (ila'a) with it. Al-Kisa'i rejected this and said: "I do not know on what basis *wa-in kullan* was read!" Al-Farra' claimed that in the reading of the one who lightened it, *kullan* is in the accusative governed by the verb *la-yuwaffiyannahum*, meaning: "and indeed, [He will surely fully repay] *kullan*." All the grammarians rejected this and said: "This is a great error; it is not permitted by anyone to say *Zaydan la-adribannahu*." [[al-Tabari said: That is because the Arabs do not put a noun before the oath-lam in the accusative governed by a verb after it.]]

The rest read "inna" with the heavy form and put "kullan" in the accusative governed by it, as is its original form. 'Asim, Hamza, and Ibn 'Amir read "lamma" with the heavy form (tashdid). The rest read it lightened, meaning: "wa-inna kullan la-yuwaffiyannahum," treating "ma" as a relative/pleonastic element (ṣila). It was also said that it came to separate the two lams that accompany the oath, both of which are open, so they were separated by "ma". Al-Zajjaj said: the lam of "lamma" is the lam of "inna," and "ma" is a superfluous emphatic particle. You say: *inna Zaydan la-munṭaliq*. Inna requires that its predicate or its subject be preceded by a lam, as in your saying: *inna Allaha la-ghafurun raḥim* (indeed God is most forgiving, most merciful), and His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 245.]]. The lam in "la-yuwaffiyannahum" is the one with which the oath is introduced; it enters upon the verb and must be accompanied by the heavy or light nun. When the two lams came together, they were separated by "ma," and "ma" is a superfluous emphatic particle.

Al-Farra' said: "ma" has the meaning of "man" (who), as in His saying: ﴿And indeed among you is one who will surely lag behind﴾ [al-Nisa': 72], meaning: "and indeed, [it is] for those who [He will surely fully repay]." The lam in "la-yuwaffiyannahum" is for the oath. This meaning returns to the saying of al-Zajjaj, except that according to al-Zajjaj "ma" is superfluous, while according to al-Farra' it is a noun meaning "man."

It was also said: it is not superfluous, rather it is a noun to which the lam of emphasis is attached, and it is the predicate of "inna," and "la-yuwaffiyannahum" is the answer to the oath. The implied meaning: "and indeed, every one [who] was created, your Lord will surely fully repay them their deeds."

It was also said: "ma" has the meaning of "man," as in His saying: ﴿So marry what is good for you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3], meaning "whoever." All of this is precisely the saying of al-Farra'.

As for the one who doubled "lamma" and read "wa-inna kullan lamma" with the heavy form in both places, namely Hamza and those who agree with him, it was said: it is a grammatical error (laḥn). It is transmitted from Muhammad ibn Zayd that this is not permitted, and one does not say: *inna Zaydan illa la-adribannahu* (indeed Zayd… except I will surely strike him), nor *lamma la-ḍarabtuhu*. Al-Kisa'i said: "God knows best about this reading, and I do not know a valid basis for it." He and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the doubling in both places is problematic (mushkil). Al-Nahhas and others said: the grammarians have several opinions on this.

The first: its original form is *li-man ma*, the nun was changed into a mim, three mims came together, so the middle one was dropped, and it became "lamma" and "ma." According to this view, "ma" has the meaning of "man," and the intended sense is: "wa-inna kullan li-man alladhina" (and indeed each [one] of those who…), like their saying:

*wa-innī lamma uṣdiru al-amra wajhahu ... idhā huwa a'yā bi-l-sabīli maṣādiruhu*
(And indeed, when I issue the command in its direction, when it becomes difficult, its outlets are [clear] by the path)

Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: "man" is a noun of two letters, so it is not permitted to delete it.

The second: the original form is *li-min ma*, and the broken mim was dropped because of the coming together of the mims. The intended sense: "wa-inna kullan li-min khalqin la-yuwaffiyannahum" (and indeed each [one] of the creation, He will surely fully repay them).

It was also said: "lamma" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "lamma," and it came without tanwin, treating the connected form as if it were the pause form. On this view it is like His saying: ﴿And you devour the inheritance, devouring greedily (aklan lamman)﴾ [al-Fajr: 19], meaning gathering the wealth that is consumed. So the intended sense is: "wa-inna kullan la-yuwaffiyannahum rabbuka a'malahum tawfiyatan lamman," that is, a gathering of their deeds in full. It is like your saying: *qiyaman la-aqumanna* (standing, I will surely stand). Al-Zuhri read "lamman" with tashdid and tanwin in this sense.

The third: "lamma" has the meaning of "illa" (except). The lexicographers transmit: *as'aluka bi-llahi lamma fa'alta* (I ask you by God, except that you did it), meaning "illa fa'alta." A similar usage is His saying: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4], meaning "illa 'alayha" (except over it). So the meaning of the verse is: "There is no one of them except that He will surely fully repay them." Al-Qushayri said: al-Zajjaj rejected this view on the grounds that there is no negation in His saying "wa-inna kullan lamma," such that "illa" would have to be understood. And one does not say: *dhahaba al-nasu lamma Zaydin* (the people went, except Zayd).

The fourth: Abu 'Uthman al-Mazini said: the original is "wa-inna kullan lamma," with "lamma" lightened, and then it was made heavy, like the line of Ru'ba:

*laqad khashitu an ara jadban ... fi 'āminā dhā ba'da mā akhṣabbā*
(Indeed I feared that I would see drought in this year of ours, after it had been fertile)

Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error; the heavy form is lightened, but the light form is not made heavy.

The fifth: Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: it is possible that the doubling comes from their saying: *lamamtu al-shay'alummuhu lamman* (I gathered the thing, I gather it, gathering), and then the form *fa'lā* was derived from it, as was read in His saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession (tatra)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 44], without tanwin and with tanwin. On this view, the alif is for the feminine, and it may be pronounced with imala (inclination) according to those who practise imala. Al-Zajjaj said: the view that in my opinion is the only permissible one is that it is the lightened form of the heavy (in al-thaqila), and it has the meaning of "ma," like: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4]. Likewise it is also doubled in its original form, and it has the meaning of "ma," and "lamma" has the meaning of "illa." Khalil, Sibawayh, and all the Basrans transmitted this, and that "lamma" is used with the meaning of "illa."

I say: this view which al-Zajjaj approved, al-Nahhas and others transmitted from him, and a similar view and al-Zajjaj's criticism of it were mentioned earlier. However, the correct form of that view is: "in" in it is a negative particle, whereas here it is the lightened form of the heavy, so they differ. [[The following phrase appears in one manuscript as a correction of al-Qurtubi's wording, with a marginal note: (Marginal note): (The correct statement of what the Shaykh, may God have mercy on him, mentioned is that he should say: "Except that this view, 'in' in it is a negative particle, and the preceding view, 'in' in it is the lightened form of the heavy; so they differ.")]]

Two readings remain. Abu Hatim said: in the reading of Ubayy: ﴿wa-inna kullan illa la-yuwaffiyannahum﴾ [[In manuscript ya: "wa-inna kullan illa la-yuwaffiyannahum." In the irregular readings: "wa-inna kull" with the kaf open and the lam lightened "lamma."]] [Hud: 111]. And it is transmitted from al-A'mash: "wa-in kullun lamma," with "in" lightened, "kullun" in the nominative, and "lamma" heavy. Al-Nahhas said: these readings that contradict the consonantal text (al-sawad) are to be understood with "in" meaning "ma" only, and they are to be taken as interpretation (tafsir), because it is not permitted to recite in a way that contradicts the consonantal text except in this manner.

(*innahu bi-ma ya'malūna khabīr*) This is a threat and a warning.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 112:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to others besides him. It was also said: the address is to him, but what is meant is his community (ummah), as said by al-Suddi. It was also said: "istaqim" means ask (utlub) for steadfastness in the religion from God and ask Him for it. In that case the sin (al-sin) is the sin of request (sin al-su'al), just as you say: "astaghfiru Allah" (I ask God's forgiveness), meaning "I ask Him for forgiveness." And istiqamah (steadfastness) is persistence in one direction without deviating to the right or the left; so be steadfast in complying with God's command.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Sufyan ibn Abd Allah al-Thaqafi, who said: I said, "O Messenger of God, tell me something about Islam such that I will not need to ask anyone about it after you!" He said: "Say: I have believed in God, then be steadfast."

Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad related in his Musnad, on the authority of Uthman ibn Hadir al-Azdi, who said: I entered upon Ibn Abbas and said, "Advise me!" He said: "Yes! Upon you is the fear of God and steadfastness. Follow, and do not innovate."

(And those who turned with you) meaning: be steadfast, you and they, meaning his companions who repented from polytheism, and those who came after them from among his community who followed him. Ibn Abbas said: No verse was revealed to the Messenger of God ﷺ that was harder or more burdensome upon him than this verse. For this reason he said to his companions when they said to him: "Grey hair has come to you quickly!" He said: "Hud and its sister surahs have made me grey." This has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah. It is also related on the authority of Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: I heard Abu Ali al-Sari [in the original (al-Shatawi), corrected from (al-Durr al-Manthur)] say: I saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream and I said: "O Messenger of God! It has been related from you that you said: 'Hud has made me grey.'" He said: "Yes." I said to him: "What about it has made you grey?" "The stories of the prophets and the destruction of the nations!" He said: "No, rather His saying: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾."

[See vol. 18, p. 262.]

(And do not transgress) He forbade transgression (al-tughyan), and tughyan is exceeding the limit, and from it comes: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed﴾. It was also said: that is, do not tyrannize over anyone.

**First**: Concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿Do not incline﴾. *Rukun* (inclining, relying) literally means leaning on something, depending on it, feeling at ease with it, and being content with it. Qatadah said: its meaning is, "Do not show affection for them and do not obey them." Ibn Jurayj said: "Do not lean toward them." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "Do not approve of their deeds." All of these are close in meaning. Ibn Zayd said: *rukun* here means *idhhan* (flattery)[[al-idhhan: al-musana'ah (appeasement, placating)]], which is that one does not denounce their disbelief.

**Second**: The majority of readers recite *tarkanu* with a fatha on the *kaf*. Abu 'Amr said: this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Talhah ibn Musarrif, Qatadah and others recite *tarkunu* with a damma on the *kaf*. Al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of Tamim and Qays. Some scholars also permitted *rakana, yarkanu*, like *mana'a, yamna'u*[[The verse is of the *ta'iba* pattern.]].

**Third**: Concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿those who have done wrong﴾. It was said: they are the polytheists. It was also said: it is general, covering them and the sinners, in the manner of His words, exalted is He, ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs﴾ [al-An'am: 68], and the rest of the verse, which has already been discussed. This is the correct view regarding the meaning of the verse, and that it indicates the shunning of people of disbelief and sin, including people of innovation (*bid'ah*) and others. For keeping company with them is disbelief or sin, since companionship is only born of affection. The poet Tarafah ibn al-'Abd, the wise man, said:

*Do not ask about the man; ask about his companion,*
*For every companion follows the one he accompanies.*

If keeping company is out of necessity and *taqiyyah* (precautionary dissimulation), the ruling on it has already been discussed in "Al 'Imran"[[See vol. 4, p. 57.]] and "al-Ma'idah"[[See vol. 6, p. 12, and vol. 5, pp. 217 and 417.]]. Keeping company with a wrongdoer out of *taqiyyah* is excepted from the prohibition in the case of compulsion. And God knows best.

**Fourth**: Concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿and the Fire will touch you﴾, meaning it will burn you, through mixing with them, keeping their company, colluding with them in their aversion[[In manuscript Y: "their aims and their associates."]], and agreeing with them in their affairs.

There are six issues here.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾. No one among the exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) has disagreed that the "prayer" in this verse means the obligatory prayers. He singled it out for mention because it is the second pillar of faith, and people turn to it in times of calamity. When a matter grieved the Prophet (ﷺ), he would turn to prayer. (*Hazaba-hu*: a serious matter befell him, or distress afflicted him.)

Some of the Sufi shaykhs said that the verse means occupying the times entirely with worship, obligatory and voluntary. [Note in the edition: so in MS ʿ and W. In Ibn al-ʿArabi it reads: it does not cover this, neither obligatory nor voluntary, since they are five prayers.] Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This view is weak. The command covers only what is obligatory, not voluntary acts, since the regular supererogatory devotions are known, and the times of the recommended voluntary prayers are limited. Any other time is open to recommended acts on a substitute basis, not in a comprehensive way, and that is beyond human capacity.

**The second issue:** God's words, ﴿the two ends of the day﴾. Mujahid said: the first end is the dawn prayer (Subh), and the second end is the noon (Zuhr) and afternoon (ʿAsr) prayers. Ibn ʿAtiyyah chose this view. It was also said: the two ends are dawn and sunset (Maghrib), as Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said. It is also reported from al-Hasan: the second end is the afternoon prayer alone, as Qatadah and al-Dahhak said. It was said: the two ends are noon and afternoon. The "zulaf" (nearer parts) are sunset, night and dawn; it seems this speaker considered the audible recitation. Al-Mawardi reported that the first end is the dawn prayer by consensus. I say: this consensus is undermined by the view preceding it. Al-Tabari preferred that the two ends are dawn and sunset, and said that this is apparent. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: It was rebutted on the ground that sunset does not enter into it, since it is part of the night prayer. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: What is strange about al-Tabari is that he holds the two ends of the day to be dawn and sunset, which are the two ends of the night! He turned the bow into a leather cup (*sarat al-qaws rikwah*: the proverb is used for reversal and the overturning of affairs), and swerved from the target (*al-burjas*: a mark placed on the tip of a spear or the like; *al-ghalwah*: the distance of an arrow's shot) by a whole range. Al-Tabari said: The evidence for it is the consensus of all that one of the two ends is dawn, which indicates that the other end is sunset, and no one agreed with him on that.

I say: This is an unjust attack by Ibn al-ʿArabi in refutation, and no one agreed with him on that. We have already mentioned from Mujahid that the first end is the dawn prayer, and there is agreement, except for an outlier, that whoever eats or has intercourse after dawn deliberately, believing that day to be a day of fasting-breaking, must make up the day and pay expiation. That only applies to what comes after dawn of the day. This indicates the soundness of what al-Tabari said regarding dawn. Sunset remains, and the rebuttal to it has been mentioned above. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** God's words, ﴿and at the nearer parts of the night﴾, meaning "at nearer parts of the night." The *zulaf* are hours close to one another, and from this root Muzdalifah is named, because it is a station after ʿArafat near Makkah. Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Ibn Abi Ishaq and others read *wa-zulufan* with a damma on the lam, as the plural of *zalif*, since *zalif* has been spoken. It is also possible that its singular is *zulfah* in the dialect of those who vowel the sin with a damma, like *busrah* and *busr*. Ibn Muhaysin read *wa-zulfan* with a sukun on the lam; its singular is *zulfah*, pluralised like collective nouns that denote individuals, such as *durrah* and *durr*, *burrah* and *burr*. Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin also read *zulfa*, like *qurba*. The rest read *wa-zulafan* with a fatha on the lam, like *ghurfah* and *ghuraf*. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: *al-zulaf* are the hours, whose singular is *zulfah*. Some said: *al-zulfah* is the first hour of the night after the sun sets. On this view, the "nearer parts of the night" means the night prayer (ʿAtamah), as Ibn ʿAbbas said. Al-Hasan said: Maghrib and ʿIshaʾ. It was also said: Maghrib, ʿIshaʾ and dawn, as already mentioned. Al-Akhfash said: it means the night prayer, without specifying.

**The fourth issue:** God's words, ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾. The majority of the early exegetes among the Companions and Successors [may God be pleased with them all] held that the "good deeds" here are the five daily prayers. Mujahid said: the good deeds are a person's saying "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is given as an example of good deeds. What appears is that the wording is general regarding good deeds and specific regarding evil deeds, due to the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Major sins are avoided."

I say: The occasion of revelation supports the majority view. It was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar. It was said: he was Abu al-Yusr ibn ʿAmr. And it was said: his name was ʿAbbad. He was alone with a woman, kissed her, and enjoyed her short of intercourse. Al-Tirmidhi transmitted from ʿAbdullah who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "I had an encounter with a woman at the far end of Madinah, and I touched her short of intercourse. Here I am; judge me as you wish." ʿUmar said to him: "God has covered you! If you had covered yourself..." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave him no answer, and the man went off. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent someone after him and called him, and recited to him: "Establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and at the nearer parts of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember," to the end of the verse. A man among the people said: "Is this for him specifically?" He said: "No, rather for all people." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sound hadith (hasan sahih).

He also transmitted from Ibn Masʿud that a man had obtained a forbidden kiss from a woman, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about its expiation, and then this was revealed: "Establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and at the nearer parts of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds." The man said: "Is this for me, O Messenger of God?" He said: "For you and for whoever of my community acts upon it." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sound hadith (hasan sahih).

It is also related from Abu al-Yusr who said: A woman came to me to buy dates. I said: "There are dates in the house better than these." She entered the house with me, and I leaned toward her and kissed her. I went to Abu Bakr and told him of that. He said: "Cover yourself, repent, and tell no one." But I could not bear it, so I went to ʿUmar and told him. He said: "Cover yourself, repent, and tell no one." But I could not bear it, so I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and told him. He said: "Did you betray a warrior fighting in the way of God in his household with the like of this?" Until he wished that he had not embraced Islam except that hour, and until he thought he was among the people of the Fire. He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) lowered his head until God revealed to him: "Establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and at the nearer parts of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember." Abu al-Yusr said: I came to him, and he recited it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). His Companions said: "O Messenger of God! Is this for him specifically, or for people generally?" He said: "No, rather for people generally." Abu ʿIsa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a hasan gharib hadith [Note in the edition: in the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi it reads sahih instead of gharib]. Qays ibn al-Rabiʿ was weakened by Waki and others. It has also been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) turned away from him, and the ʿAsr prayer was called. When he had finished, Jibril (peace be upon him) came down to him with the verse, and he summoned him and said: "Did you attend the prayer with us?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Go, for it is an expiation for what you did." It is also related that when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse to him, he said: "Get up and pray four rakʿahs." And God knows best.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim, in *Nawadir al-Usul*, transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have not seen anything better in seeking nor quicker in overtaking than a new good deed to an old sin," and then: "Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember."

**The fifth issue:** The verse, together with these hadiths, indicates that a forbidden kiss and a forbidden touch do not incur the prescribed punishment (hadd). It may be used as evidence that there is no hadd nor discretionary punishment (adab) upon a man and a woman even if they were found under one garment. This is the view chosen by Ibn al-Mundhir, because when the disagreement of the scholars on this question was mentioned, he cited this hadith, indicating that nothing is obligatory upon them. What the scholars hold on this will come in *al-Nur* [see vol. 12, pp. 161 and 98], God willing.

**The sixth issue:** God, glory be to Him, mentioned in His Book the prayer with its bowing, prostration, standing, recitation and names. He said: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, the verse. And He said: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra: 78], the verse. And He said: ﴿So glorify God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning. And to Him is praise in the heavens and the earth, and at dusk and when you reach midday﴾ [al-Rum: 17–18] [see vol. 14, p. 14]. And He said: ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ [Taha: 130] [see vol. 11, p. 260]. And He said: ﴿Bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77]. And He said: ﴿And stand before God in devotion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238] [see vol. 3, p. 213]. And He said: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 204] [see vol. 7, p. 353], as already mentioned. And He said: ﴿Do not recite your prayer aloud, nor be silent in it﴾ [al-Isra: 110], meaning your recitation. All of this is general (mujmal), which He stated generally in His Book, and He referred its explanation to His Prophet, saying, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44]. So the Prophet (ﷺ) explained the times of the prayers, the number of rakʿahs and prostrations, the description of all the prayers, their obligatory and recommended parts, what the prayer is not valid without from the obligatory elements, and what is recommended in them of sunan and virtues. He said in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: "Pray as you have seen me pray." This was transmitted from him by the whole body from the whole body, as is well known. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not die until he had made clear everything people needed, completing the religion and making the path plain. God, Most High, said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and approved Islam as your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] [see vol. 6, p. 61].

God's words, ﴿That is a reminder for those who remember﴾: that is, the Qur'an is an admonition and a repentance for whoever takes heed and remembers. He singled out "those who remember" for mention because they are the ones who benefit from the reminder. *Al-dhikra* is a verbal noun that came with the feminine suffix.

﴿And be patient﴾, that is, over the prayer, as in His saying: ﴿Enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132].[[See vol. 11, p. 263.]] It was also said: the meaning is, "Be patient, O Muhammad, over what you suffer of harm."

(Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers), meaning those who pray. His saying (So why was it not) means: why was there not.

(among the generations before you), that is, among the nations that came before you.

(people of virtue), that is, people of obedience, religion, intellect and insight.

(forbidding) their people

(from corruption on earth), because of the intellects Allah had given them and the signs He had shown them. This is a rebuke to the disbelievers. It was also said: here "lawla" (why not) is for negation, meaning "there was not, among the generations before you," as in His saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed﴾ [Yunus: 98], meaning "there was not."

(except a few), an exception of the disjunctive kind (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ, an exception not of the same category as what precedes it), meaning "but only a few."

(of those We rescued from among them), who forbade corruption on earth. It was said: they were the people of Yunus (Jonah), based on His saying: "except the people of Yunus." It was also said: they were the followers of the prophets and the people of truth.

(And those who did wrong followed), that is, they associated partners with Allah and disobeyed.

(the luxury in which they were given ease), that is, their preoccupation with wealth and pleasures and their preferring these over the Hereafter.

(And they were criminals).

The Exalted said: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns﴾, meaning the people of the towns.

(wrongfully) meaning through polytheism and disbelief.

(while their people are reforming) meaning in their dealings with one another regarding rights. That is, He would not destroy them for disbelief alone unless corruption was added to it, just as He destroyed the people of Shu'ayb for cheating in measure and weight, and the people of Lut for sodomy. This indicates that sins bring the punishment of total annihilation in this world closer than polytheism does, though the punishment for polytheism in the Hereafter is more severe. In the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi (the Sahih collection of al-Tirmidhi), on the authority of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When people see the wrongdoer and do not restrain his hands, Allah is about to encompass them all with a punishment from Him." This has already been discussed [[See vol. 6, p. 342 and following.]]. It has also been said: the meaning is, "And your Lord would never destroy the towns wrongfully while their people are Muslims," for that would be an injustice to them and a diminishing of their rights. That is, He did not destroy any people except after giving them a warning and a admonition. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is: your Lord would never destroy anyone while that person is wronging him, even if he were in the utmost state of righteousness, because that is a disposal of His own dominion. Its proof is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 346.]] [Yunus: 44]. It has also been said: the meaning is, "And Allah would never destroy them for their sins while they are reforming," that is, sincere in faith. On this view, "wrongdoing" means sins.

The Exalted said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: upon the religion of Islam alone. Al-Dahhak said: a people of one religion, whether of misguidance or of guidance.

(And they will continue to differ) meaning in various religions. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

(Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy) This is an exception of disconnected type, meaning: but those upon whom your Lord has mercy, through faith and guidance, do not differ. It has also been said: they differ in provision, so this one is rich and that one is poor, "except those upon whom your Lord has mercy" through contentment. This was said by al-Hasan.

(And for that He created them) Al-Hasan, Muqatil, and 'Ata' [and Yaman [[From ʿ, ā, w, y.]]] said: the reference is to the difference, meaning: and for the difference He created them. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak said: and for His mercy He created them. He said "wa-li-dhalika" and not "wa-li-tilka," and mercy is feminine because it is a verbal noun; and also because the feminine form of "mercy" is not a true feminine, so it was treated as meaning "grace." It has also been said: the reference of "dhalika" is to both the difference and the mercy, and "dhalika" may be used to refer to two opposites, as in His saying: ﴿Neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 448.]] [al-Baqarah: 68], and He did not say "between those two" or "between these two." He also said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever between that, a moderate way﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 72.]] [al-Furqan: 67], and He said: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer or silent therein, but seek between that a way﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 343.]] [al-Isra': 110]. Similarly His saying: ﴿Say: "By the bounty of Allah and His mercy, so in that let them rejoice"﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 353.]] [Yunus: 58]. This is the best of the opinions, if Allah wills, because it is comprehensive, meaning: and for what has been mentioned He created them. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) pointed to this, as narrated from him by Ashhab. Ashhab said: I asked Malik about this verse, and he said: He created them so that there would be a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze; that is, He created the people of difference for difference, and the people of mercy for mercy. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: He created them as two groups, a group He has mercy upon and a group He does not have mercy upon. Al-Mahdawi said: in the wording according to this interpretation there is an inversion: the meaning is, "And they will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: 'I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together,' and for that He created them." It has also been said: it is connected to His saying: ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ [Hud: 103], and the meaning is: for witnessing that Day He created them. It has also been said: it is connected to His saying: ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ [Hud: 105], meaning: for happiness and wretchedness He created them.

The Exalted said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾. The meaning of "has been fulfilled" is that it was established as He informed and decreed it in His eternity. The fulfilment of the word is its being immune to alteration and change.

(I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together) "Min" here is explanatory of the kind, meaning: from the kind of jinn and the kind of mankind. "Ajma'in" is an emphasis. Just as He informed that He would fill His Fire, so He also informed, through the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ), that He would fill His Paradise, by his saying: "And each one of you has its fill." Al-Bukhari recorded it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and it has already been mentioned.

In the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi (the Sahih collection of al-Tirmidhi), on the authority of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When people see the wrongdoer and do not restrain his hands, Allah is about to encompass them all with a punishment from Him." This has already been discussed [[See vol. 6, p. 342 and following.]]. It has also been said: the meaning is, "And your Lord would never destroy the towns wrongfully while their people are Muslims," for that would be an injustice to them and a diminishing of their rights. That is, He did not destroy any people except after giving them a warning and a admonition. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is: your Lord would never destroy anyone while that person is wronging him, even if he were in the utmost state of righteousness, because that is a disposal of His own dominion. Its proof is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 346.]] [Yunus: 44]. It has also been said: the meaning is, "And Allah would never destroy them for their sins while they are reforming," that is, sincere in faith. On this view, "wrongdoing" means sins.

The Exalted said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: upon the religion of Islam alone. Al-Dahhak said: a people of one religion, whether of misguidance or of guidance.

(And they will continue to differ) meaning in various religions. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

(Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy) This is an exception of disconnected type, meaning: but those upon whom your Lord has mercy, through faith and guidance, do not differ. It has also been said: they differ in provision, so this one is rich and that one is poor, "except those upon whom your Lord has mercy" through contentment. This was said by al-Hasan.

(And for that He created them) Al-Hasan, Muqatil, and 'Ata' [and Yaman [[From ʿ, ā, w, y.]]] said: the reference is to the difference, meaning: and for the difference He created them. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak said: and for His mercy He created them. He said "wa-li-dhalika" and not "wa-li-tilka," and mercy is feminine because it is a verbal noun; and also because the feminine form of "mercy" is not a true feminine, so it was treated as meaning "grace." It has also been said: the reference of "dhalika" is to both the difference and the mercy, and "dhalika" may be used to refer to two opposites, as in His saying: ﴿Neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 448.]] [al-Baqarah: 68], and He did not say "between those two" or "between these two." He also said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever between that, a moderate way﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 72.]] [al-Furqan: 67], and He said: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer or silent therein, but seek between that a way﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 343.]] [al-Isra': 110]. Similarly His saying: ﴿Say: "By the bounty of Allah and His mercy, so in that let them rejoice"﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 353.]] [Yunus: 58]. This is the best of the opinions, if Allah wills, because it is comprehensive, meaning: and for what has been mentioned He created them. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) pointed to this, as narrated from him by Ashhab. Ashhab said: I asked Malik about this verse, and he said: He created them so that there would be a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze; that is, He created the people of difference for difference, and the people of mercy for mercy. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: He created them as two groups, a group He has mercy upon and a group He does not have mercy upon. Al-Mahdawi said: in the wording according to this interpretation there is an inversion: the meaning is, "And they will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: 'I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together,' and for that He created them." It has also been said: it is connected to His saying: ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ [Hud: 103], and the meaning is: for witnessing that Day He created them. It has also been said: it is connected to His saying: ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ [Hud: 105], meaning: for happiness and wretchedness He created them.

The Exalted said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾. The meaning of "has been fulfilled" is that it was established as He informed and decreed it in His eternity. The fulfilment of the word is its being immune to alteration and change.

(I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together) "Min" here is explanatory of the kind, meaning: from the kind of jinn and the kind of mankind. "Ajma'in" is an emphasis. Just as He informed that He would fill His Fire, so He also informed, through the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ), that He would fill His Paradise, by his saying: "And each one of you has its fill." Al-Bukhari recorded it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and it has already been mentioned.

"Concerning His words, the Exalted: ﴿And all [that] We relate to you of the news of the messengers﴾. "Kullan" is in the accusative, governed by "naqussu" (We relate). Its meaning: and all that you need of the news of the messengers, We relate to you. Al-Akhfash said: "kullan" is a fronted circumstantial accusative (hal muqaddamah), as in your saying: "Kullan darabtu al-qawm" (I struck all the people).

(of the news of the messengers) That is, of their reports and their patience over the harm inflicted upon them by their peoples.

(by which We strengthen your heart) That is, to convey the message and to be patient over the harm that reaches you in it. It was also said: We increase you in steadfastness and certainty through it. Ibn Abbas said: "ma nashuddu bihi qalbaka" (that by which We firm up your heart). Ibn Jurayj said: "nusabbiru bihi qalbaka" (We make your heart patient through it), so that it does not despair. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "nuttayyibu" (We comfort), and the meaning is close. "Ma" is a substitution (badal) for "kullan." The meaning: We relate to you from the news of the messengers that by which We strengthen your heart.

(and there has come to you in this the truth) That is, in this surah, according to Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa and others. He singled out this surah because it contains the reports of the prophets, Paradise and Hell. It was also said: He singled it out for mention for emphasis, although the truth is in the whole Qur'an. Qatada and al-Hasan said: the meaning is "in this world" (fi hadhihi al-dunya), meaning prophethood.

(and an admonition and a reminder for the believers) The admonition (mawi'zah) is that by which one is admonished through the destruction of past nations and the bygone generations who denied. This is an honouring of this surah, because other surahs also contain the truth, the admonition, and the reminder, but it does not say of them what it says of this one, as a specification. "And a reminder for the believers": that is, they remember what befell those who were destroyed, so they repent. He specified the believers because they are the ones who take admonition when they hear the stories of the prophets.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 11, verses 121–123:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say to those who do not believe: "Act according to your position; indeed we are acting."﴾ This is a threat and a warning.

(﴿Indeed we are acting. And wait; indeed we are waiting.﴾) is another threat, and its meaning has already passed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, the unseen of them and the witnessed of them, and something is omitted because the meaning indicates it. Ibn 'Abbas said: the treasuries of the heavens and the earth. Al-Dahhak said: all that is hidden from the servants within them. And the others said: the unseen of the heavens and the earth is the descent of punishment from the sky and its emergence from the earth. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth," that is, He knows what is hidden within them. He attributed the unseen, which is an annexed noun, to the object by way of extension (tawassu'), because the preposition was dropped; you say: "I was absent in the land" and "I was absent in a city such-and-such."

(﴿And to Him the whole matter is returned﴾) That is, on the Day of Resurrection, since no created thing has any command except by His permission. Nafi' and Hafs read "yurja'u" with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the jim, meaning yuradd (is returned).

(﴿So worship Him and put your trust in Him﴾) That is, take refuge in Him and be confident in Him.

(﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾) That is, He will recompense each one for his deed. The people of Madina, Syria and Hafs read with ta' (tu'malun) in the address form; the rest read with ya' (ya'malun) in the narrative form. Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: "ya'malun" is used when the Prophet ﷺ is not addressed along with them; and some said: "ta'malun" with ta' because He addressed the Prophet ﷺ and said: say to them, "And your Lord is not unaware of what you do." Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the conclusion of the Torah is the conclusion of Hud, from the saying "And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth" to the end of the surah. The surah of Hud is complete, and it is followed by the surah of Yusuf (peace be upon him).
